PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
CON
This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.
FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
CON
This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.

and Life Savings, a coalition of

business and taxpayers

Support dwindles for wealth tax, voter ID ballot measures, new poll shows
Seema Mehta
Thu, October 29, 2026 at 10:00 AM UTC
8 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) speaks at the "Ballots Over Billionaires" rally on Oct. 5 in Los Angeles. Supporters of Proposition 40, which establishes a one-time wealth tax on billionaires, have been vastly outspent by the opposition. (Jason Armond/Los Angeles Times)
California voters are souring on a Nov. 3 ballot measure to impose a one-time tax on billionaires to help fund healthcare programs, a proposal that has triggered one of the most expensive political battles in state history.
Half of likely voters plan to vote against Proposition 40, the proposed wealth tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) on billionaires' assets, while 42% support it, according to a new poll by UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies that was co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times. The findings mark a significant decline in support of the measure, which was crafted by an influential California healthcare union to compensate for an estimated $100 billion in federal healthcare cuts approved by President Trump and congressional Republicans.
The survey also found that a solid majority of likely voters opposed Proposition 39, which would require Californians to provide identification when voting and election officials to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens. The findings come as the Trump administration continues to attack California as a haven for voter fraud, including unfounded allegations of rampant illegal voting by undocumented immigrants.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Read more: Your guide to Proposition 40: California's billionaire tax proposal (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide?utm_source=yahoo&utm_medium=promo_module&utm_campaign=rss_feed)
Mark DiCamillo, the poll's director, said previous surveys showed support for Proposition 40 has been fragile, and the most recent shows its prospects have dimmed as election day approaches.
The increase in opposition to Proposition 40 is "broad-based and spans virtually all major segments of the electorate," DiCamillio said. The ballot measure was leading in a Berkeley poll conducted just six weeks ago, albeit by a slim margin, so its reversal of fortune is significant, he said.
The declining support comes after an onslaught of money spent opposing Proposition 40, including a torrent of television and social media ads airing everywhere from NFL games to "Everybody Loves Raymond" reruns. Nearly $368 million has been contributed to efforts opposing the billionaire tax, while $36 million has been donated to support the proposed levy.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the assets of billionaires who resided in California as of Jan. 1, with some exceptions. Democrats and their allies are splintered over the proposal. Some, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, argue it will prompt the wealthy to flee California, further harming its volatile budget, which is dependent on the state's richest residents. The California Democratic Party and leading progressives support the measure, with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) calling it a modest tax necessary to help Californians struggling because of cuts imposed by Republicans to pay for tax breaks for the wealthy.
While Republican voters overwhelmingly oppose Proposition 40, nearly two-thirds of Democrats support it and more than a quarter opposing it. There is also a generational divide, with 6 out of 10 voters 65 years old or older opposing the measure, while more than two-thirds of those under 30 supporting it, according to the poll.
The findings are similar to a Public Policy Institute of California poll released Tuesday, which found 52% of likely voters would vote against Proposition 40, while 46% supported it.
The campaign against the wealth tax, funded by some of California's richest tech moguls, is centered on three intertwined ballot initiatives: Proposition 40 and Propositions 41 and 42, both of which would undercut Proposition 40 through a series of changes to state tax laws and spending restrictions.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Proposition 41 would cut wasteful government spending (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) by requiring audits of new state special taxes and would bar new state taxes that are exempt from a state spending limit. Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on retirement holdings, individually owned assets and other personal savings. Both Propositions 41 and 42 would nullify the billionaire tax if it passes, provided either measure receives more votes.
A plurality of voters oppose Propositions 41 and 42, a reversal from just six week ago, according to the poll.
In mid-September, voters were closely divided about Proposition 41 — 37% in favor and 33% opposed — (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2zw023kt) with a large number of undecided. In the current poll, 38% of likely voters favor the measure and 47% oppose it. Proposition 42 led by 9 percentage points in the Berkeley/L.A. Times poll in September — 43% in favor and 34% opposed. Now, 43% of likely voters support it and 45% oppose it.
DiCamillo said backers of a ballot measure also should be concerned any time support registers below 50%, since voters who are undecided or unsure tend to vote no.
Advertisement
Advertisement
"It's below 50%, and it's trending down. Both of those are ominous signs," DiCamillo said. Proposition 42 is "still very close. I'm not saying it's definitely going down, but it's moving in the wrong direction late in the campaign, and usually movement in a late poll is even more significant than the actual numbers themselves."
He added that while many voters were unaware the two proposed ballot measures were designed as poison pills to kill the billionaire tax, among those who knew, the opposition was significantly greater.
If all three measures fail, that still would be a victory for the billionaires who spent aggressively to tank the wealth tax.
Another notable finding was voters' support of Proposition 3, which would make permanent a higher income tax rate on the wealthy (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) that funds education. A majority of voters — 54% — support continuing the levy, while 37% oppose it, according to the poll. DiCamillo says the disparity in support of the proposed billionaire tax and the extension of the existing wealth tax has been consistent in IGS's polls, and is likely because of the differing foundations of the levies.
Advertisement
Advertisement
"Proposition 3 is already in place, and if you read the fiscal impact, if this were to pass, it maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual funding," he said, "It's a big revenue generator, and I think that is something that's already in place."
"Voters kind of understand the progressive nature of California's tax system, and they kind of support that, but they don't support nearly as much the idea of some new kind of tax, the wealth tax, which is taxing assets rather than income," he said. "So that's the distinction."
These ballot measures are among 14 that voters will decide (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits) on Nov. 3, as well as statewide, congressional, local and judicial elections.
Read more: 14 propositions that could remake California taxes, housing, healthcare and elections (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits?utm_source=yahoo&utm_medium=promo_module&utm_campaign=rss_feed)
Advertisement
Advertisement
Among the other controversial measures is Proposition 39, a measure pushed by Republicans that would require all voters in future elections to show government-issued identification every time they vote in person or provide a special PIN or the last four digits of their Social Security number when submitting mail-in ballots.
The measure also would require the California secretary of state and county election officials to verify that registered voters are U.S. citizens by "using government data," which according to supporters could include information in the federal Social Security Administration database, jury summons information and other government records.
Nearly 6 in 10 likely voters oppose the effort, while more than a third support it, split largely along party lines. More than half of voters who are registered as "no party preference" or with a smaller political party oppose the proposal, which DiCamillo said was an indication of trouble for the proposition given the state's Democratic majority electorate and the proximity of the election.
"It's hard for Republicans to push something over the finish line by themselves," he said.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Other prominent ballot measures:
Proposition 43, which would prohibit local governments (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-43-threshold-local-special-tax-voter-guide) from imposing certain new special taxes unless two-thirds of voters approve the proposal. Such proposals need a simple majority vote to be approved. While 46% of likely voters oppose the proposal, 36% support it, challenging numbers this close to election day, DiCamillo said. "It needs to get to 50," he said. "We'll see how you do that this late in the campaign."
Proposition 4, which would repeal a prohibition of public financing of campaigns (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-4-public-campaign-financing-voter-guide), allowing state and local governments to support candidates if they abide by several rules. Likely voters are evenly split about the proposal, with 41% supporting it and opposing it, and 18% undecided. "It's close, but it's still below 50%. Most voters tend to vote no in the late going if they're not convinced," DiCamillo said, adding that he viewed the lack of support among voters who do not affiliate with a political party as a signal of potential failure.
The poll of 2,787 registered California voters was conducted online in English and Spanish Oct. 19-25 and has a margin of error of about 3 percentage points in either direction.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) speaks at the "Ballots Over Billionaires" rally on Oct. 5 in Los Angeles. Supporters of Proposition 40, which establishes a one-time wealth tax on billionaires, have been vastly outspent by the opposition. (Jason Armond/Los Angeles Times)
California voters are souring on a Nov. 3 ballot measure to impose a one-time tax on billionaires to help fund healthcare programs, a proposal that has triggered one of the most expensive political battles in state history.
Half of likely voters plan to vote against Proposition 40, the proposed wealth tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) on billionaires' assets, while 42% support it, according to a new poll by UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies that was co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times. The findings mark a significant decline in support of the measure, which was crafted by an influential California healthcare union to compensate for an estimated $100 billion in federal healthcare cuts approved by President Trump and congressional Republicans.
The survey also found that a solid majority of likely voters opposed Proposition 39, which would require Californians to provide identification when voting and election officials to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens. The findings come as the Trump administration continues to attack California as a haven for voter fraud, including unfounded allegations of rampant illegal voting by undocumented immigrants.

Support dwindles for wealth tax, voter ID ballot measures, new poll shows
Seema Mehta
Thu, October 29, 2026 at 10:00 AM UTC
8 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) speaks at the "Ballots Over Billionaires" rally on Oct. 5 in Los Angeles. Supporters of Proposition 40, which establishes a one-time wealth tax on billionaires, have been vastly outspent by the opposition. (Jason Armond/Los Angeles Times)
California voters are souring on a Nov. 3 ballot measure to impose a one-time tax on billionaires to help fund healthcare programs, a proposal that has triggered one of the most expensive political battles in state history.
Half of likely voters plan to vote against Proposition 40, the proposed wealth tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) on billionaires' assets, while 42% support it, according to a new poll by UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies that was co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times. The findings mark a significant decline in support of the measure, which was crafted by an influential California healthcare union to compensate for an estimated $100 billion in federal healthcare cuts approved by President Trump and congressional Republicans.
The survey also found that a solid majority of likely voters opposed Proposition 39, which would require Californians to provide identification when voting and election officials to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens. The findings come as the Trump administration continues to attack California as a haven for voter fraud, including unfounded allegations of rampant illegal voting by undocumented immigrants.

Read more: Your guide to Proposition 40: California's billionaire tax proposal (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide?utm_source=yahoo&utm_medium=promo_module&utm_campaign=rss_feed)
Mark DiCamillo, the poll's director, said previous surveys showed support for Proposition 40 has been fragile, and the most recent shows its prospects have dimmed as election day approaches.
The increase in opposition to Proposition 40 is "broad-based and spans virtually all major segments of the electorate," DiCamillio said. The ballot measure was leading in a Berkeley poll conducted just six weeks ago, albeit by a slim margin, so its reversal of fortune is significant, he said.
The declining support comes after an onslaught of money spent opposing Proposition 40, including a torrent of television and social media ads airing everywhere from NFL games to "Everybody Loves Raymond" reruns. Nearly $368 million has been contributed to efforts opposing the billionaire tax, while $36 million has been donated to support the proposed levy.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the assets of billionaires who resided in California as of Jan. 1, with some exceptions. Democrats and their allies are splintered over the proposal. Some, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, argue it will prompt the wealthy to flee California, further harming its volatile budget, which is dependent on the state's richest residents. The California Democratic Party and leading progressives support the measure, with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) calling it a modest tax necessary to help Californians struggling because of cuts imposed by Republicans to pay for tax breaks for the wealthy.
While Republican voters overwhelmingly oppose Proposition 40, nearly two-thirds of Democrats support it and more than a quarter opposing it. There is also a generational divide, with 6 out of 10 voters 65 years old or older opposing the measure, while more than two-thirds of those under 30 supporting it, according to the poll.
The findings are similar to a Public Policy Institute of California poll released Tuesday, which found 52% of likely voters would vote against Proposition 40, while 46% supported it.
The campaign against the wealth tax, funded by some of California's richest tech moguls, is centered on three intertwined ballot initiatives: Proposition 40 and Propositions 41 and 42, both of which would undercut Proposition 40 through a series of changes to state tax laws and spending restrictions.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Proposition 41 would cut wasteful government spending (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) by requiring audits of new state special taxes and would bar new state taxes that are exempt from a state spending limit. Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on retirement holdings, individually owned assets and other personal savings. Both Propositions 41 and 42 would nullify the billionaire tax if it passes, provided either measure receives more votes.
A plurality of voters oppose Propositions 41 and 42, a reversal from just six week ago, according to the poll.
In mid-September, voters were closely divided about Proposition 41 — 37% in favor and 33% opposed — (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2zw023kt) with a large number of undecided. In the current poll, 38% of likely voters favor the measure and 47% oppose it. Proposition 42 led by 9 percentage points in the Berkeley/L.A. Times poll in September — 43% in favor and 34% opposed. Now, 43% of likely voters support it and 45% oppose it.
DiCamillo said backers of a ballot measure also should be concerned any time support registers below 50%, since voters who are undecided or unsure tend to vote no.
Advertisement
Advertisement
"It's below 50%, and it's trending down. Both of those are ominous signs," DiCamillo said. Proposition 42 is "still very close. I'm not saying it's definitely going down, but it's moving in the wrong direction late in the campaign, and usually movement in a late poll is even more significant than the actual numbers themselves."
He added that while many voters were unaware the two proposed ballot measures were designed as poison pills to kill the billionaire tax, among those who knew, the opposition was significantly greater.
If all three measures fail, that still would be a victory for the billionaires who spent aggressively to tank the wealth tax.
Another notable finding was voters' support of Proposition 3, which would make permanent a higher income tax rate on the wealthy (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) that funds education. A majority of voters — 54% — support continuing the levy, while 37% oppose it, according to the poll. DiCamillo says the disparity in support of the proposed billionaire tax and the extension of the existing wealth tax has been consistent in IGS's polls, and is likely because of the differing foundations of the levies.
Advertisement
Advertisement
"Proposition 3 is already in place, and if you read the fiscal impact, if this were to pass, it maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual funding," he said, "It's a big revenue generator, and I think that is something that's already in place."
"Voters kind of understand the progressive nature of California's tax system, and they kind of support that, but they don't support nearly as much the idea of some new kind of tax, the wealth tax, which is taxing assets rather than income," he said. "So that's the distinction."
These ballot measures are among 14 that voters will decide (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits) on Nov. 3, as well as statewide, congressional, local and judicial elections.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Among the other controversial measures is Proposition 39, a measure pushed by Republicans that would require all voters in future elections to show government-issued identification every time they vote in person or provide a special PIN or the last four digits of their Social Security number when submitting mail-in ballots.
The measure also would require the California secretary of state and county election officials to verify that registered voters are U.S. citizens by "using government data," which according to supporters could include information in the federal Social Security Administration database, jury summons information and other government records.
Nearly 6 in 10 likely voters oppose the effort, while more than a third support it, split largely along party lines. More than half of voters who are registered as "no party preference" or with a smaller political party oppose the proposal, which DiCamillo said was an indication of trouble for the proposition given the state's Democratic majority electorate and the proximity of the election.
"It's hard for Republicans to push something over the finish line by themselves," he said.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Other prominent ballot measures:
Proposition 43, which would prohibit local governments (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-43-threshold-local-special-tax-voter-guide) from imposing certain new special taxes unless two-thirds of voters approve the proposal. Such proposals need a simple majority vote to be approved. While 46% of likely voters oppose the proposal, 36% support it, challenging numbers this close to election day, DiCamillo said. "It needs to get to 50," he said. "We'll see how you do that this late in the campaign."
Proposition 4, which would repeal a prohibition of public financing of campaigns (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-4-public-campaign-financing-voter-guide), allowing state and local governments to support candidates if they abide by several rules. Likely voters are evenly split about the proposal, with 41% supporting it and opposing it, and 18% undecided. "It's close, but it's still below 50%. Most voters tend to vote no in the late going if they're not convinced," DiCamillo said, adding that he viewed the lack of support among voters who do not affiliate with a political party as a signal of potential failure.
The poll of 2,787 registered California voters was conducted online in English and Spanish Oct. 19-25 and has a margin of error of about 3 percentage points in either direction.

But the polling after this spending still shows the race tied/slightly behind, which suggests the ads aren't working well enough, or that the No side's message ("billionaire trick") resonates.

Also consider: Prop 40's failure. Prop 40 is polling at 42-46% yes (both IGS and PPIC show it losing). If Prop 40 is clearly going down, does that affect Prop 42? The No on 42 campaign's main argument is that Prop 42's "only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax." If voters know Prop 40 is going to fail anyway, the poison-pill rationale weakens... but voters don't think that way; they just react to ads.

Another angle: how does Prop 42 do with demographic breakdown? PPIC October: "most Republicans and independents would vote yes, while most Democrats would vote no." The 2026 midterm electorate in California will be Democratic-leaning (midterm with governor race; Dems are energized against Trump?). Actually in 2026, midterm turnout in CA will skew older and more Democratic. Older voters — the Yes campaign targets seniors worried about retirement taxes. Older voters turn out more in midterms — that helps Yes.

Let me try to get the IGS crosstabs PDF through a different approach, and look for the AIMSA poll's No number, plus any final polls (Nov 1-2). Also check editorial endorsements (LA Times, SF Chronicle, etc.).

Also — very important — let me double-check whether there are any newer polls (e.g., released Nov 1-2) and what the final IGS crosstabs show by party, age, region.","format":"unknown","index":0}]

Hmm wait, "62% of YES money came from billionaires and wealthy individuals; 25% from labor unions; 11% from corporations" — for which prop? Not sure. Then "Endorsed by Gov. Gavin Newsom; California Democratic Party; California Apartment Association; California Labor Federation (AFL-CIO)..." — this might be for Prop 37 or Prop 1, not 42. The layout is garbled.

Hmm, wait. The "Endorsed by Gov. Gavin Newsom" and "PAC whose top donors are Sergey Brin and John Doerr" — several measures. The structure of that page is unclear. Let me not rely on it.

From the californiatoday.com guide: "Governor Gavin Newsom endorsed it on October 9." — Prop 42. Newsom opposes Prop 40 and endorsed Prop 42.

From abc30: "Gov. Gavin Newsom, who opposes Prop. 40, has now come out publicly in support of Prop. 42, going against his own party and some labor unions."

So the California Democratic Party — does it oppose Prop 42? The Democratic Party supports Prop 40. Actually, from the earlier LA Times article: "The California Democratic Party and leading progressives support the measure [Prop 40]." And Newsom endorsed Prop 42 "going against his own party."

Opponents of Prop 42: Bernie Sanders, SEIU-UHW, Teamsters California, AFSCME California (per caprops.org). No side funding: $32.4 million (FPPC) — including California Business Roundtable Issues PAC? No wait, that's in support. Let me re-read.

From FPPC November 2026 General Election top contributors list:
"Prop. 42 ... Support: $157,272,537.26 | Oppose: $32,386,200.51"

Supporting: Yes on 42 committee with $157.1 million from Building a Better California.
Opposing: $32.4 million — the snippet shows "California Business Roundtable Issues PAC, Top Donors: Peter Thiel; Eric Schmidt, $10,690,000" — hmm, that would be supporting. Confusing. Actually the "Opposing" committee for Prop 42 might be "Tax the Ultra-Rich Now, Yes on 3 & 40, No on 41 & 42" or "Working Families Say No to Propositions 41 and 42 sponsored by labor unions".

Anyway, the Yes side has outspent the No side roughly 5:1 ($157M vs $32M).

Now, let me think about which poll is more reliable and how to weigh the evidence:

Berkeley IGS: reads official ballot title and summary to respondents (including fiscal impact statement "Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future"). IGS uses online panel via voter file (PDI). IGS allows undecided. IGS final numbers: 43-45.

PPIC: reads ballot title and label. PPIC's methodology: they ask "would you vote yes or no" — PPIC reports only yes/no with don't know. 51-47 with 2% don't know. PPIC surveys adults, then filters likely voters. PPIC's "likely voter" screens.

Let's compute: Dems 47% × 42% yes = 19.7; Reps 24% × 78% = 18.7; NPP 23% × 55% = 12.7. Total yes ≈ 51%. That's consistent with PPIC's 51%. If the remaining 12% undecided breaks similarly (say 3:1 No), final would be Yes 45-46 / No 54-55 → No wins by ~8. If undecided breaks 50/50, Yes 49 / No 51 → No wins narrowly.

PPIC trend: Sept 54/43 → Oct 51/47. Downward Yes. If this continues... but PPIC has almost no undecided (2%).

The average of final polls: IGS: Yes 43/No 45 (+2 No); PPIC: Yes 51/No 47 (+4 Yes); AIMSA: 50% yes (unknown no, likely ~35-40% no with 10-15% undecided?). Hmm.

Actually, let me look at the AIMSA poll details more carefully to get the No number. And also check for any other late polls (Emerson, SurveyUSA, IVC Media follow-up, Data for Progress, etc.). Let me also try to get the IGS crosstabs for party breakdown.

Also, I should consider: the "early vote" — with most ballots cast by mail in California, and voting starting Oct 5, a large share of the electorate voted before the late movement. Berkeley IGS's Oct 19-25 poll found among those who already voted vs. those not yet voted — the "already voted" may have voted when support was higher. Hmm, but the poll's overall numbers include both.

Let me also think about which poll to weight more. PPIC vs IGS discrepancy: IGS reads the full ballot title + summary + fiscal impact. PPIC reads title + label only. The label for Prop 42: "Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer's past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure." Hmm, "Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026" — the nullification language might remind voters of the poison-pill aspect. Not sure.

One more important consideration: IGS's likely-voter model and the online PDI sample may slightly undercount... hard to say.

Let me look at how IGS vs PPIC performed historically on 2024 ballot measures. In 2024, IGS final polls were pretty accurate (e.g., Prop 36, Prop 32). PPIC also decent. In 2020, PPIC overestimated support for Prop 15 (their Sept poll had 53% yes; it lost). IGS in 2020 had Prop 15 at 51% in September, lost by 3.5.

For final IGS polls (late October), in 2020 IGS found Prop 15 at 49% yes / 41% no (Oct 25 - Nov 1) — final result 48.4% yes. Pretty accurate. In 2024, IGS final poll: Prop 32 (minimum wage) 50% yes → final 52.5%? Hmm, actually Prop 32 narrowly won by ~1%. IGS had Prop 5 in 2024... no wait, Prop 5 was 2024? No — Prop 5 (2024) lowered vote threshold for housing bonds; IGS final had 42/35; it lost 40-60. Prop 33 rent control: IGS 40/32, lost 40-60. Prop 34: IGS... won narrowly 50.8.

Overall IGS late polls tend to slightly overestimate yes support or be close. In this case, IGS shows Yes 43/No 45. If IGS overestimates yes, then No wins by more.

PPIC in 2024 final (Oct): Prop 32 at 53% (result: 52.2% yes — close); Prop 5 at 47% (result 40.3% — overestimate by 7!); Prop 33 at 40% (result 40.2% — close); Prop 36 at 71% (result 68.6% — close); Prop 6 at 41% (result 43.6% — under). Prop 35 at 64% (result 66.3% — close). So PPIC's only big miss was Prop 5 (overestimated by 7 points).

Hmm interesting. Both pollsters were mostly accurate in recent cycles, with a tendency to slightly overestimate yes on some measures.

Now, the key insight from political science: for California ballot initiatives, the rule of thumb is that measures below 50% support in final polls usually fail. Prop 42's final polling average: IGS 43, PPIC 51, AIMSA 50 → average ~48% yes. Undecided voters (mostly in IGS's 12%) break toward No. This suggests Prop 42 is slightly more likely to fail than pass.

But wait — there's a countervailing factor: the Yes campaign's massive spending advantage ($157M vs $32M) and heavy late advertising. Campaigns with big spending advantages can win close races. The Yes side ads are everywhere. But the polling after this spending still shows the race tied/slightly behind, which suggests the ads aren't working well enough, or that the No side's message ("billionaire trick") resonates.

Also consider: Prop 40's failure. Prop 40 is polling at 42-46% yes (both IGS and PPIC show it losing). If Prop 40 is clearly going down, does that affect Prop 42? The No on 42 campaign's main argument is that Prop 42's "only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax." If voters know Prop 40 is going to fail anyway, the poison-pill rationale weakens... but voters don't think that way; they just react to ads.

Another angle: how does Prop 42 do with demographic breakdown? PPIC October: "most Republicans and independents would vote yes, while most Democrats would vote no." The 2026 midterm electorate in California will be Democratic-leaning (midterm with governor race; Dems are energized against Trump?). Actually in 2026, midterm turnout in CA will skew older and more Democratic. Older voters — the Yes campaign targets seniors worried about retirement taxes. Older voters turn out more in midterms — that helps Yes.

Let me try to get the IGS crosstabs PDF through a different approach, and look for the AIMSA poll's No number, plus any final polls (Nov 1-2). Also check editorial endorsements (LA Times, SF Chronicle, etc.).

Also — very important — let me double-check whether there are any newer polls (e.g., released Nov 1-2) and what the final IGS crosstabs show by party, age, region.

Frequently asked questions
Is Prop 39 (voter ID) passing?
It trails in PPIC (Oct. 16–22: 41% yes, 58% no) and IGS (Oct. 19–25: 37% yes, 57% no, 5% undecided, explicitly printed in Table 2). It led in SurveyUSA (49% yes, 42% no, 10% undecided) and IVP (43% yes, 40% no, 17% undecided). These are polls, not election results.
Is Prop 40 (billionaire tax) passing?
It trails in PPIC (Oct. 16–22: 46% yes, 52% no, 2% don’t know) and IGS (Oct. 19–25: 42% yes, 50% no, 8% undecided). SurveyUSA (Oct. 19–24) had it at 44% yes, 43% no, 13% undecided, a one-point lead within its interval. These are polls, not election results.
Are Props 41 and 42 leading?
Both trail in IGS: Prop 41 is 38% yes and 47% no; Prop 42 is 43% yes and 45% no. PPIC had Prop 42 at 51% yes, 47% no and 2% don’t know. These are polls, not election results.

Methodology Note:
Findings are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents, conducted online using the Ipsos KnowledgePanel. Interviews were conducted in
English and Spanish according to the respondents’ preferences. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. Interviewing took place
from October 16—22, 2026.
These crosstabs are based on a subgroup of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error, taking design effects from weighting into consideration, is ±3.8
percent at the 95 percent confidence level for the unweighted sample of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error for unweighted likely voter subgroups
is larger. Sampling error is only one type of error to which surveys are subject. Results may also be affected by factors such as question wording,
question order, and survey timing.
If you have any questions or require additional information regarding this survey, please contact surveys@ppic.org

Full Crosstabs–Likely Voters Only
Methodology Note:
Findings are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents, conducted online using the Ipsos KnowledgePanel. Interviews were conducted in
English and Spanish according to the respondents’ preferences. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. Interviewing took place
from October 16—22, 2026.
These crosstabs are based on a subgroup of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error, taking design effects from weighting into consideration, is ±3.8
percent at the 95 percent confidence level for the unweighted sample of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error for unweighted likely voter subgroups
is larger. Sampling error is only one type of error to which surveys are subject. Results may also be affected by factors such as question wording,
question order, and survey timing.

is larger. Sampling error is only one type of error to which surveys are subject. Results may also be affected by factors such as question wording,

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
CON
This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.
FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

California voters are souring on a Nov. 3 ballot measure to impose a one-time tax on billionaires to help fund healthcare programs, a proposal that has triggered one of the most expensive political battles in state history.
Half of likely voters plan to vote against Proposition 40, the proposed wealth tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) on billionaires' assets, while 42% support it, according to a new poll by UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies that was co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times. The findings mark a significant decline in support of the measure, which was crafted by an influential California healthcare union to compensate for an estimated $100 billion in federal healthcare cuts approved by President Trump and congressional Republicans.
The survey also found that a solid majority of likely voters opposed Proposition 39, which would require Californians to provide identification when voting and election officials to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens. The findings come as the Trump administration continues to attack California as a haven for voter fraud, including unfounded allegations of rampant illegal voting by undocumented immigrants.

Mark DiCamillo, the poll's director, said previous surveys showed support for Proposition 40 has been fragile, and the most recent shows its prospects have dimmed as election day approaches.
The increase in opposition to Proposition 40 is "broad-based and spans virtually all major segments of the electorate," DiCamillio said. The ballot measure was leading in a Berkeley poll conducted just six weeks ago, albeit by a slim margin, so its reversal of fortune is significant, he said.
The declining support comes after an onslaught of money spent opposing Proposition 40, including a torrent of television and social media ads airing everywhere from NFL games to "Everybody Loves Raymond" reruns. Nearly $368 million has been contributed to efforts opposing the billionaire tax, while $36 million has been donated to support the proposed levy.

The California Democratic Party and leading progressives support the measure, with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) calling it a modest tax necessary to help Californians struggling because of cuts imposed by Republicans to pay for tax breaks for the wealthy.
While Republican voters overwhelmingly oppose Proposition 40, nearly two-thirds of Democrats support it and more than a quarter opposing it. There is also a generational divide, with 6 out of 10 voters 65 years old or older opposing the measure, while more than two-thirds of those under 30 supporting it, according to the poll.
The findings are similar to a Public Policy Institute of California poll released Tuesday, which found 52% of likely voters would vote against Proposition 40, while 46% supported it.
The campaign against the wealth tax, funded by some of California's richest tech moguls, is centered on three intertwined ballot initiatives: Proposition 40 and Propositions 41 and 42, both of which would undercut Proposition 40 through a series of changes to state tax laws and spending restrictions.

He added that while many voters were unaware the two proposed ballot measures were designed as poison pills to kill the billionaire tax, among those who knew, the opposition was significantly greater.
If all three measures fail, that still would be a victory for the billionaires who spent aggressively to tank the wealth tax.
Another notable finding was voters' support of Proposition 3, which would make permanent a higher income tax rate on the wealthy (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) that funds education. A majority of voters — 54% — support continuing the levy, while 37% oppose it, according to the poll. DiCamillo says the disparity in support of the proposed billionaire tax and the extension of the existing wealth tax has been consistent in IGS's polls, and is likely because of the differing foundations of the levies.

Nearly 6 in 10 likely voters oppose the effort, while more than a third support it, split largely along party lines. Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days.
Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and
state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition,
the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of
these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind,
with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on
topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’
initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race.
Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63%
to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the
Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six
percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic
about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1
(60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three
legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title
and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37
(65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and
Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and
support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at
least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least
“somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and
the economy as well as housing costs and availability as
the most important issues facing California today.
Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is
headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming
majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in
the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49
percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults
and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big
problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of
confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
3/40
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At
the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52
House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters
will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’
initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter
engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton
(R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led
Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (61% to 36%).
Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats
support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the
Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra
over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions
and threats to democratic values and norms as the most
important problems facing the nation today.
Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think
the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and
expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next
12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President
Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action
against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is
working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for
Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
4/40
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the
November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the
gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey), the 2022 general
election (62% October 2022 survey), and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey). Today,
majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of
independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with
the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions
are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election
(22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following
news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten
were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (25% very,
35% fairly) and in October 2018 (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69%
Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters
(65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic
candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were
similar in September (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (64%
Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more
Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most
independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to
37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic
candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
5/40
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are
more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half
or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an
“enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and
between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-
one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, shortly before the
June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024, ahead of the last congressional
election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more
enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature
placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say
they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds
for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey, 55 percent said
they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan
groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54%

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days.
Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and
state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition,
the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of
these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind,
with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on
topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’
initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race.
Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63%
to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the
Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six
percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic
about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1
(60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three
legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title
and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37
(65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and
Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and
support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at
least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least
“somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and
the economy as well as housing costs and availability as
the most important issues facing California today.
Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is
headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming
majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in
the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49
percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults
and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big
problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of
confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.

November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At
the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52
House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters
will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’
initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter
engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton
(R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led
Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (61% to 36%).
Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats
support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the
Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra
over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions
and threats to democratic values and norms as the most
important problems facing the nation today.
Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think
the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and
expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next
12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President
Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action
against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is
working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for
Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days.
Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and
state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition,
the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of
these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind,
with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on
topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’
initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race.
Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63%
to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the
Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six
percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic
about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1
(60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three
legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title
and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37
(65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and
Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and
support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at
least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least
“somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and
the economy as well as housing costs and availability as
the most important issues facing California today.
Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is
headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming
majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in
the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49
percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults
and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big
problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of
confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
3/40
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At
the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52
House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters
will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’
initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter
engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton
(R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led
Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (61% to 36%).
Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats
support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the
Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra
over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions
and threats to democratic values and norms as the most
important problems facing the nation today.
Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think
the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and
expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next
12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President
Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action
against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is
working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for
Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
4/40
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the
November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the
gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey), the 2022 general
election (62% October 2022 survey), and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey). Today,
majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of
independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with
the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions
are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election
(22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following
news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten
were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (25% very,
35% fairly) and in October 2018 (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69%
Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters
(65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic
candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were
similar in September (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (64%
Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more
Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most
independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to
37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic
candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
5/40
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are
more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half
or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an
“enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and
between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-
one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, shortly before the
June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024, ahead of the last congressional
election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more
enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.

Hmm, so two columns at 84% yes (col6, col10) — Rep and Con. Two at ~25-32% yes (col8, col11) — Dem and Lib. And the "middle" columns: col1 (47/51), col2 (54/44), col3 (47/52), col4 (49/46), col5 (56/42), col7 (53/44), col9 (53/43).

Given PPIC's commentary "most Republicans and independents would vote yes": which middle columns are "independents"? An independent column should be around 50-55% yes. Col2 (54/44), col5 (56/42), col7 (53/44), col9 (53/43) are all "yes-leaning" middles; col1 (47/51) and col3 (47/52) are "no-leaning" middles.

If col7 = Central Valley (53/44)? Hmm, CV should be more yes... or col7 = Ind (53/44) — matches "most independents would vote yes" ✓.
If col9 = Central Valley (53/43) — plausible-ish.
Then col4 = Ind? col4 (49/46) — hmm, or col4 = Mod?

Anyway: the pattern is clear. The electorate's partisan composition will decide this. In a midterm with heavy Dem turnout (early vote: Dem ballots 51.2% of returned, Rep 27.7%, other 21.5% as of Nov 2), let's model:

Suppose final electorate: Dem 47%, Rep 25%, Ind/NPP 28%.
- Dem: ~53% no / 43% yes (say 25-47% yes... let me use the strongly-no Democratic column ~25-32% yes? Hmm, but the commentary says "most Democrats would vote no" — the Dem column in the crosstabs is either col8 (25 yes) or col11 (32 yes)... 

Hmm, but wait — one of those is Dem and the other is Lib. Democrats: 25-32% yes? That seems strongly no. But then how does the total get to 51% yes? Let's compute: Dem 47% × 0.30 yes = 14.1; Rep 25% × 0.84 = 21.0; Ind 28% × 0.53 = 14.8. Total = 49.9% ≈ 51% ✓ (with rounding). OK, that's consistent with PPIC's 51%.

But this is knife-edge: if the actual electorate is even slightly more Democratic than PPIC's likely-voter sample, Prop 42 fails. If more Republican/independent, it passes.

Now, the crucial question: what will the actual turnout composition be? Early voting data (Nov 2): returned ballots: Dem 3.19M (51.2%), Rep 1.72M (27.7%), Other 1.34M (21.5%). Hmm, that's the ballot return party split as of Nov 2 (27% overall turnout). Election-day votes will add more Republicans typically (though in CA, most votes are VBM). The final electorate might be ~49-50% Dem, ~26% Rep, ~24% Ind/other. Hmm, wait, the "other" category includes NPP (22% of registration) plus third parties. NPP voters tend to have lower turnout.

Hmm, note the early vote percentages: 51.2% Dem is a bit high vs 2022's 46.7%, but early-in-the-cycle returns skew Dem; later returns (Election Day drop-offs) add more Reps/NPPs.

- Dem: 30% yes → 14.4
- Rep: 84% yes → 21.8
- Ind/NPP: 53% yes → 13.8
Total ≈ 50.0%. Toss-up.

Alternatively, with IGS's numbers (43 yes / 45 no), it's leaning No.

1. IGS's final poll (the last poll released, Oct 29, fielded Oct 19-25) has No +2, and the IGS trend shows No gaining (34→45). PPIC's Oct 16-22 has Yes +4, with Yes declining (54→51). Both pollsters show the same directional trend: movement toward No.

2. Undecided: IGS has 12% undecided. The classic pattern: undecideds break No on ballot initiatives, especially when the initiative is the side that must achieve majority. Mark DiCamillo explicitly warns about this.

3. The Yes side has vastly more money ($157M+ raised for Yes on 42; $32M for No). But the No side's messaging is potent in a Democratic-leaning state: "billionaire-funded trick." Also, Bernie Sanders and labor unions are campaigning against. Meanwhile the Yes side's ads ("protect retirement savings") are well-funded and appealing.

Gavin Newsom and other Democrats, would block new taxes..." Let me check the CA Democratic Party's official position. The abc30 article says Newsom endorsing "goes against his own party and some labor unions." The CA Democratic Party probably took a "No on 42" position (since they support Prop 40).

5. Editorial boards: major papers (LA Times, SF Chronicle, Sac Bee, etc.) likely recommend No on 42. Let me verify quickly. Editorials typically matter at the margins.

6. Historical base rate for California tax-limitation initiatives: In 2020, Prop 15 (split-roll property tax) failed 48.4%–51.6% despite polling ~51% in Sept/Oct. In 2018, Prop 6 (gas tax repeal) failed 43-57. In 2022, no tax measures. In 2016, Prop 55 (extend tax on rich) passed; Prop 56 passed. Those were tax increases on specific groups though. For a "ban future taxes" measure — this is unusual. Prop 42's support among older voters (who dominate midterms) is probably higher... but the No campaign ties it to the billionaire tax, which polls show voters dislike billionaires.

7. The "competing measures" dynamic: If Prop 40 fails (which both polls show — trailing by 6-8 points), the strategic reason to vote No on 42 ("don't let billionaires trick you") weakens, but also the strategic reason to vote Yes on 42 weakens. Voters who dislike both may just vote No on all.

Actually, hmm, let me think about the interplay more carefully. PPIC's question order effects: they ask Prop 40 first, then 41, then 42. IGS also asks in order. One more key factor: Early voting composition and Prop 42. Since most Californians vote by mail, and ballots started going out Oct 5, a huge share of votes were cast before the late No-trend.
