The California ballot for a constitutional amendment shows: the title (e.g., "Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.") followed by the summary (the ~100-word "Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer's past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future."). So the actual ballot includes the nullification language. IGS reads this — so IGS may best simulate the actual ballot.

Hmm, that cuts toward the IGS numbers being more realistic (43/45 No+2), with PPIC's title+label-only reading being more favorable to Yes.

2. **The IGS trend**: Sept No 34 → Oct No 45. If this continued into the final week (Oct 26-Nov 2), No could be ahead by more. The No campaign (SEIU) was spending heavily late. The prediction market dropped 18.5 points in the final week — consistent with continued movement toward No.

3. **However**, the Yes campaign's massive ad spending continued through the final week. And the ballot drop-off: many voters vote by mail over multiple weeks; those who voted before late October (a large share — early vote was 27% turnout by Nov 2... hmm, actually that's ballots returned; total turnout might be ~45-50% in this midterm) — those early voters saw the race at an earlier stage. IGS Oct 19-25 includes already-voted respondents. If IGS's already-voted subset shows better Yes numbers than the not-yet-voted, that would suggest the banked vote is more Yes-friendly. I don't have that breakdown though.

4. **Straight-ticket Democratic voting:** In a heavily anti-Trump midterm, Democratic voters will vote the party line. The CA Democratic Party's position: opposed to Props 41/42 (they support Prop 40). Voter guides (Dem party mailers, union mailers) will say No on 42. Republican voter guides say Yes on 42. With Dems ~47-50% of the electorate and most voting No, the math is tight.

Let me try to get the IGS crosstabs by party for Prop 42 to firm this up. The IGS tabulations PDF is at escholarship (403 via fetch). Let me try a different URL form or Google cache. Actually, the earlier search result snippet from the IGS release #2026-22 said: "The latest poll finds 45% now opposing Prop. 42 while 43% are voting Yes, with 12% undecided." The release also mentioned cross-tabs by party maybe. Let me search for "Proposition 42" IGS Democrats Republicans October crosstab.

Actually, let me also check: LA Times article on the IGS poll might have party breakdown. The LA Times piece said: "DiCamillo said... while many voters were unaware the two proposed ballot measures were designed as poison pills to kill the billionaire tax, among those who knew, the opposition was significantly greater."

Let me search for the IGS October release's party breakdown of Prop 42.

Also, let me check the final "Desert Sun election night live updates" page — it might have pre-election analysis. And check for any very late polls (Nov 1-2). The electcademocrats tracker says "November 2 verification: no newer proposition poll located for October 30–November 2."

OK. Let me also try to fetch the IGS tabulations PDF via an alternative URL.

One more consideration — the IGS poll's "already voted" vs "not yet voted": Actually, let me look at the full IGS release text. The escholarship PDF was 403 via direct fetch, but maybe I can find the release hosted elsewhere or search snippets. Let me search for details.

Let me also consider historical analogies for measures backed by massive spending with late-decaying support:
- 2020 Prop 22 (app-based drivers, gig companies spent $200M): polls showed 58-39 yes late → won 58.6%. Money won.
- 2018 Prop 11: passed easily.
- 2020 Prop 25: proponents outspent... failed.
- The billionaires' side spent $368M total on No-on-40/Yes-on-41-42. That's an unprecedented sum. In California initiative politics, the side that outspends 5:1 usually wins IF its message is simple and appealing. "Protect your retirement savings from new taxes" is a simple, appealing message.

Hmm, but the late trend in both polls shows the No message breaking through: "it's a billionaire trick."

Also note: both PPIC (51/47) and AIMSA (50) show Yes around 50-51; only IGS shows 43/45. The IGS poll may be an outlier (or the most accurate). IGS has the most recent field dates (Oct 19-25 vs PPIC's Oct 16-22), and it caught the late trend first.

Weighing everything:

**Case for YES (measure passes):**
- PPIC: 51-47; AIMSA: 50% support.
- Prediction markets: ~56% (Kalshi 57¢, with real volume).
- Yes campaign: $157M+ raised, 5:1 spending advantage, saturation advertising through election day.
- Ballot title/label favorable; "protect retirement savings" framing.
- Newsom endorsement (Oct 9).
- Republicans (84% yes) + independents (53% yes) per PPIC.
- Older voters (dominant in midterms) lean yes.
- Election-night math: ~51-52% plausible.
- Kalshi's "Prop 42 more yes votes than Prop 40" at 66%.

**Case for NO (measure fails):**
- IGS final poll: 43-45 No+2 (most recent, most ballot-realistic wording, historically accurate final pollster).
- Both pollsters show Yes declining and No rising over the final month (PPIC 54→51; IGS No 34→45); momentum is with No.
- 12% undecided in IGS → undecideds break No historically (DiCamillo's own warning).
- Measure below 50% in 2 of 3 final polls; historical base rate: CA initiatives polling ≤51% late usually fail.
- Heavily Democratic midterm electorate (early vote 51% Dem ballots; Dem enthusiasm 71% vs 46% Rep); Dems mostly vote No.
- Democratic Party, Bernie Sanders, labor (SEIU, Teamsters, AFSCME, CA Labor Fed) opposed; their turnout operation is strong in a midterm.
- "Billionaire-funded trick" message resonating late; voters sour on billionaires.
- Editorial boards (LA Times, etc.) likely oppose.
- Prediction market dropped 18.5 points in final week (74→56), suggesting informed money fleeing Yes.

Hmm, this is genuinely close to a coin flip. Let me try to resolve it with more evidence:

1. Get IGS crosstabs by party for Prop 42 (to check if Dem/Ind breakdowns match PPIC).
2. Check editorial endorsements.
3. Maybe check early-vote-related signals or final campaign reports.
4. Check the defirate or nijinn pages for more market details.

Actually — one big thing I should check: the IGS poll's internals on "already voted" voters. Since ~5.8M ballots were already returned by Nov 2 (27% turnout) out of an expected ~12.7M total... wait, the onpointpolitics page said "About 12,687,172 votes are expected." Turnout 2026 midterm maybe ~45% of ~22.8M registered ≈ 10.3M? Hmm, the "12.7M expected" seems high; 2022 CA turnout was ~12.2M (43% of registered? no...). 2022: 12.5M votes? Hmm: 2022 CA general had ~12.2M ballots counted (49% turnout of 24.9M... no). Let me not worry about it.

Ballots returned by Nov 2: 6.25M (3.19+1.72+1.34). That's roughly half the expected total. These were cast when support for 42 was likely a bit higher (before the final-week No surge). The remaining votes (Election Day + late mail) will be cast in the environment captured by the late polls.

2. Let me now also examine: what happens with straight-ticket/"down-ballot dropoff" voters? The Yes side benefits from name-recognition-style voting on a tax ban ("prohibits new taxes" = intuitive yes for many low-info voters). The No side requires voters to understand the "poison pill/billionaire trick" argument — higher-information voting. In midterms with high-information partisan voters, the No argument gets through; but there are still many low-info voters.

3. Another angle: Prop 40's coattails. Since Prop 40 is losing (both polls), the SEIU's message "vote No on 41/42 to save the billionaire tax" has less urgency; but the "No on 41/42" campaign is mainly funded as part of the Yes-on-40 effort. Hmm.

Let me now try to get more specifics on the IGS poll internals. And also look at that "californiatoday.com" guide page, which had a thorough analysis, and the "Where do voters stand on this year's biggest ballot measures" (fiftyplusone.news) aggregation.

Also, I realize I should double-check the Kalshi market's current price as of the latest moment (Nov 2/3). The first search result showed "57% ▼5 Yes 58¢ No 43¢". The nijinn page said 56.0% as of Nov 3, 12:11 AM ET. The defirate page said 56% (Kalshi 57%, Polymarket 54%). So ~56%.

Markets lean Yes at ~56%, but with a sharp downward trend. Public polls average: (43+51+50)/3 ≈ 48% Yes. Adjusted for undecided break (IGS 12% und): maybe 47-49% Yes. That favors No.

But there's an important historical pattern: **late public polls in CA initiative fights with massive ad spending often underestimate the well-funded side.** Examples: 
- 2020 Prop 22: final polls ~58% yes, won 58.6% (accurate, not an upset).
- 2016 Prop 61 (drug pricing): proponents outspent; polls showed it close, it failed 46-54. 
- 2018 Prop 8 (dialysis): industry spent $110M on Yes; final polls ~40% yes; failed 40-60. Money didn't save it.
- 2020 Prop 25 (algorithms): gig companies spent to kill it... polls showed close; failed 41-59.
- 2024 Prop 34: pharma-funded; narrowly passed 50.8%.
- 2024 Prop 32: passed 52.2% after polling 50-53%.

Actually, big money usually wins when it's on the "No" side of a tax measure (status quo bias), but for "Yes" campaigns, money can win too (Prop 22, Prop 34 narrowly). But when late polls show a measure below 50% with No momentum, it usually loses — even with big money (2018 Prop 8, 2020 Prop 25).

The Yes side here is well-funded AND has a naturally appealing anti-tax message AND a favorable ballot title. The No side has the "billionaire trick" counter-message that's clearly landing late.

Hmm, let me look at the age breakdown from PPIC crosstabs, since midterms skew old. From Q29 table 2 (age columns 55+, 35-54, 18-34). I couldn't parse table 2's columns reliably, but earlier I saw in the Q29 second table: "50% 46% 36% 50% 67% 44% 42% 56% 48% 45% 36% 49% / 49% 52% 61% 49% 30% 55% 55% 42% 49% 53% 60% 50%" — the columns there are [Republican, Democratic, Female, Male, Other, Whites, Latinos, 55+, 35-54, 18-34, ...]. Hmm: if col8=55+, col9=35-54, col10=18-34: Yes row (last row): col8=49%?, col9=53%?, col10=60%?? That can't be right — 18-34 most supportive of a tax ban? Unlikely.

Ugh, the extraction column mapping is unreliable. Let me just fetch the PPIC report's "Questions and Responses" section (offset ~20000-40000 in the main PDF) which lists Q29 with party/age breakdowns in a cleaner format.

Actually, the "Questions and Responses" section in PPIC reports typically just gives topline yes/no/DK, not crosstabs. The crosstabs PDF is where subgroups live, and I already have the key subgroup findings from the narrative: "most Republicans and independents would vote yes, while most Democrats would vote no."

Let me now try to get the IGS release's subgroup data. Let me try fetching the escholarship item page via the API or a mirror. Or search for news articles citing IGS party breakdowns for Prop 42.

Let me also check the "fiftyplusone.news" blog that aggregates ballot measure polls — it might have a poll average and analysis.

And the californiatoday.com guide page for Prop 42 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-proposition-42-guide/) — it had good analysis including funding and endorsements. Let me fetch that.","format":"unknown","index":0}]

content.text: Prediction markets (Kalshi ~57%, Polymarket ~54%) lean toward Yes passing, but with a sharp decline in the final week. Let me dig into the IGS poll internals and the detailed guide analysis to firm up my assessment.

California Proposition 42 is asking voters to ban new state taxes on retirement savings and other personal property.
Proposition 42 would amend the California Constitution to bar any new state tax on owning personal property, a category its text defines to include pensions, 401(k)s, IRAs, mutual funds, stocks, business interests, digital assets and intellectual property. It would also bar new state taxes that reach back in time, including any tax "imposed on a taxpayer based upon their residency status on a date prior to the effective date of the tax." Both rules cover taxes enacted on or after January 1, 2026. That reaches Proposition 40 (https://californiatoday.com/news/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-billionaire-tax/), the one-time "billionaire tax" on the same ballot, and the Voter Information Guide warns that if Prop 42 receives more yes votes, Prop 40 "could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters."
California Proposition 42 is drawing $112.8 million from its top contributors, the most of any committee on the November ballot in the FPPC's October 14, 2026 update. Prop 42 is an initiative constitutional amendment (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/) titled the Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act of 2026. Its campaign has $112.8 million from its top contributors, more than any other committee on the ballot, almost all of it from Building a Better California, whose top donors are Google co-founder Sergey Brin and L. John Doerr III. Governor Gavin Newsom endorsed it on October 9. PPIC's September survey found 54% of likely voters in favor and 43% opposed. It is one of 14 measures in our guide to every November proposition (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/), and our billionaire tax explainer (https://californiatoday.com/news/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-billionaire-tax/) covers how Props 40, 41 and 42 interact. This guide covers what Prop 42 would ban, what it would leave alone and who is behind it.

California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) Proposition 42 bans new state taxes on owning retirement accounts, stocks and other personal property:
The core of the measure's text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is one sentence. No state law or constitutional provision enacted on or after January 1, 2026 "may enact, create, impose, or authorize collection of a tax on the ownership or control of retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings, whether held directly or indirectly." The definition of that phrase is broad. It covers pensions, retirement accounts and mutual funds, and "all personal property, whether tangible or intangible," including financial assets, investment accounts, business interests, digital assets, intellectual property and personal belongings.
It does not repeal anything. Any tax "in effect, imposed, and first collected on or before December 31, 2025" is untouched, and the measure says it does not "alter or affect the taxation of real property." The Legislative Analyst's Office (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42.pdf) notes that California already taxes some personal property, such as the vehicle license fee drivers pay each year and the property tax on business equipment. It also notes that while the state taxes the income people earn from financial assets, "there is no tax for simply owning those assets." Prop 42 would keep it that way.

Income tax on wages, interest, dividends and capital gains Unchanged. Proposition 42 bars taxes on the “ownership or control” of assets, not on income they produce or gains when they are sold

A tax keyed to where someone lived on a date before the tax took effect Barred

A retroactive tax passed by initiative Barred, with no emergency exception

Proposition 42 bars new state taxes on owning pensions, 401(k)s, stocks, business stakes and other personal property, and most retroactive taxes. It could cancel Prop 40's billionaire tax, and its $112.8 million campaign is the ballot's largest.

California Proposition 42 is asking voters to ban new state taxes on retirement savings and other personal property.
Proposition 42 would amend the California Constitution to bar any new state tax on owning personal property, a category its text defines to include pensions, 401(k)s, IRAs, mutual funds, stocks, business interests, digital assets and intellectual property. It would also bar new state taxes that reach back in time, including any tax "imposed on a taxpayer based upon their residency status on a date prior to the effective date of the tax." Both rules cover taxes enacted on or after January 1, 2026. That reaches Proposition 40 (https://californiatoday.com/news/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-billionaire-tax/), the one-time "billionaire tax" on the same ballot, and the Voter Information Guide warns that if Prop 42 receives more yes votes, Prop 40 "could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters."
California Proposition 42 is drawing $112.8 million from its top contributors, the most of any committee on the November ballot in the FPPC's October 14, 2026 update. Prop 42 is an initiative constitutional amendment (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/) titled the Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act of 2026. Its campaign has $112.8 million from its top contributors, more than any other committee on the ballot, almost all of it from Building a Better California, whose top donors are Google co-founder Sergey Brin and L. John Doerr III. Governor Gavin Newsom endorsed it on October 9. PPIC's September survey found 54% of likely voters in favor and 43% opposed. It is one of 14 measures in our guide to every November proposition (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/), and our billionaire tax explainer (https://californiatoday.com/news/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-billionaire-tax/) covers how Props 40, 41 and 42 interact. This guide covers what Prop 42 would ban, what it would leave alone and who is behind it.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) Proposition 42 bans new state taxes on owning retirement accounts, stocks and other personal property:
The core of the measure's text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is one sentence. No state law or constitutional provision enacted on or after January 1, 2026 "may enact, create, impose, or authorize collection of a tax on the ownership or control of retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings, whether held directly or indirectly." The definition of that phrase is broad. It covers pensions, retirement accounts and mutual funds, and "all personal property, whether tangible or intangible," including financial assets, investment accounts, business interests, digital assets, intellectual property and personal belongings.
It does not repeal anything. Any tax "in effect, imposed, and first collected on or before December 31, 2025" is untouched, and the measure says it does not "alter or affect the taxation of real property." The Legislative Analyst's Office (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42.pdf) notes that California already taxes some personal property, such as the vehicle license fee drivers pay each year and the property tax on business equipment. It also notes that while the state taxes the income people earn from financial assets, "there is no tax for simply owning those assets." Prop 42 would keep it that way.

Vehicle license fee and property tax on business equipment Unchanged. Both were “in effect, imposed, and first collected” before December 31, 2025, which the measure protects
Property tax on homes and land Unchanged. The measure says it does not “alter or affect the taxation of real property”
Income tax on wages, interest, dividends and capital gains Unchanged. Proposition 42 bars taxes on the “ownership or control” of assets, not on income they produce or gains when they are sold
A new state tax on the value of stocks, funds, business stakes, crypto or intellectual property Barred if enacted on or after January 1, 2026
A new state tax on the value of pensions, 401(k)s, 403(b)s or IRAs Barred if enacted on or after January 1, 2026
A tax keyed to where someone lived on a date before the tax took effect Barred
A retroactive tax passed by the Legislature Barred, except for a look-back of 365 days or less during a declared disaster or fiscal emergency, with the money limited to that emergency
A retroactive tax passed by initiative Barred, with no emergency exception

2026 California Prop 42 guide: "Retirement savings" measure would ban new state taxes on what Californians own
Proposition 42 bars new state taxes on owning pensions, 401(k)s, stocks, business stakes and other personal property, and most retroactive taxes. It could cancel Prop 40's billionaire tax, and its $112.8 million campaign is the ballot's largest.
by
Pat Sharyon | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/pat/)
Updated
October 19, 2026

California Proposition 42 is asking voters to ban new state taxes on retirement savings and other personal property.
Proposition 42 would amend the California Constitution to bar any new state tax on owning personal property, a category its text defines to include pensions, 401(k)s, IRAs, mutual funds, stocks, business interests, digital assets and intellectual property. It would also bar new state taxes that reach back in time, including any tax "imposed on a taxpayer based upon their residency status on a date prior to the effective date of the tax." Both rules cover taxes enacted on or after January 1, 2026. That reaches Proposition 40 (https://californiatoday.com/news/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-billionaire-tax/), the one-time "billionaire tax" on the same ballot, and the Voter Information Guide warns that if Prop 42 receives more yes votes, Prop 40 "could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters."
California Proposition 42 is drawing $112.8 million from its top contributors, the most of any committee on the November ballot in the FPPC's October 14, 2026 update. Prop 42 is an initiative constitutional amendment (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/) titled the Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act of 2026. Its campaign has $112.8 million from its top contributors, more than any other committee on the ballot, almost all of it from Building a Better California, whose top donors are Google co-founder Sergey Brin and L. John Doerr III. Governor Gavin Newsom endorsed it on October 9. PPIC's September survey found 54% of likely voters in favor and 43% opposed. It is one of 14 measures in our guide to every November proposition (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/), and our billionaire tax explainer (https://californiatoday.com/news/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-billionaire-tax/) covers how Props 40, 41 and 42 interact. This guide covers what Prop 42 would ban, what it would leave alone and who is behind it.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) Proposition 42 bans new state taxes on owning retirement accounts, stocks and other personal property:
The core of the measure's text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is one sentence. No state law or constitutional provision enacted on or after January 1, 2026 "may enact, create, impose, or authorize collection of a tax on the ownership or control of retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings, whether held directly or indirectly." The definition of that phrase is broad. It covers pensions, retirement accounts and mutual funds, and "all personal property, whether tangible or intangible," including financial assets, investment accounts, business interests, digital assets, intellectual property and personal belongings.
It does not repeal anything. Any tax "in effect, imposed, and first collected on or before December 31, 2025" is untouched, and the measure says it does not "alter or affect the taxation of real property." The Legislative Analyst's Office (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42.pdf) notes that California already taxes some personal property, such as the vehicle license fee drivers pay each year and the property tax on business equipment. It also notes that while the state taxes the income people earn from financial assets, "there is no tax for simply owning those assets." Prop 42 would keep it that way.
Taxes Proposition 42 would leave alone and taxes it would bar:
Tax Under Proposition 42
Vehicle license fee and property tax on business equipment Unchanged. Both were “in effect, imposed, and first collected” before December 31, 2025, which the measure protects
Property tax on homes and land Unchanged. The measure says it does not “alter or affect the taxation of real property”
Income tax on wages, interest, dividends and capital gains Unchanged. Proposition 42 bars taxes on the “ownership or control” of assets, not on income they produce or gains when they are sold
A new state tax on the value of stocks, funds, business stakes, crypto or intellectual property Barred if enacted on or after January 1, 2026

Try Google cache or the IGS website version. Actually, the IGS website might host the same tabulations: igs.berkeley.edu. Let me search for the direct PDF link on the IGS site.

Also the fiftyplusone.news aggregation might have useful averages. And let me check the Citrin-POLITICO poll (UC Berkeley Citrin Center / Politico) — released Oct 19, might have Props 41/42 numbers.

Let me also think about what more I can learn about the Kalshi market trend. The TruthIndex went from 74.5% to 56% over 7 days. That's a big drop — traders moved on the polls (IGS Oct 29 + PPIC Oct 27-28 + AIMSA Oct 27). But it's still above 50.

Actually, hold on. Let me reconsider the nijinn.io data: "Over the past 7 days, Yes has lost −18.5 on the TruthIndex™, moving to 56.0% as of Nov 3, 2026, 12:11 AM ET." So a week ago (Oct 27) Yes was ~74.5%. The decline came as the October polls dropped. Current: 56%.

Also from the earlier Kalshi search result: "Proposition 42 ... 57% ▼ 5" — so even in the last day, it dropped 5 points.

1. **The Yes side's ad spend is overwhelming**: $157M raised, and they were still spending $8.3M-$18M per week in late October. In the final days, TV saturation. Ads: "Prop 42 protects your retirement and savings from new state taxes. You earned it. Prop 42 protects it." plus firefighters/veterans/seniors imagery. This is a very effective low-information message.

2. **The No side's ads**: SEIU's ~$32M — "billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote No on 42." Effective with Democratic base voters.

3. **Turnout composition**: The question is how many Dems vs. Reps vs. NPPs actually vote. In 2022 midterm: party composition of ballots cast: Dem 46.8%, Rep 26.2%, NPP 23.1%, Other 3.9% (roughly). In 2026, with the Trump backlash and high Dem enthusiasm (71% vs 46%), the Dem share might tick up a bit, maybe 48-50%. The early-vote party split so far: Dem 51.2%, Rep 27.7%, Other 21.5%. Note this is of returned ballots; final will likely be ~49/26/25.

Let me recompute with PPIC October subgroup estimates. I need October subgroup numbers. From September: Rep 74 yes, Ind 61 yes, Dem 39 yes. October (from crosstab fragments): Rep ~84 yes (one of the columns), Dem ~25-32 yes?? Hmm wait, that's a big shift. Let me reconcile.

Actually the PPIC Oct crosstab for Q29 that I parsed: strongly-yes columns col6 (84 yes) and col10 (84 yes); strongly-no col8 (25 yes/74 no) and col11 (32 yes/66 no). Given the Sept numbers (Rep 74, Ind 61, Dem 39) and the Oct narrative ("most Republicans and independents would vote yes, while most Democrats would vote no"), the Oct numbers are probably: Rep ~80%+ yes, Ind ~52-55% yes, Dem ~30-40% yes.

And from Table 21 IGS fragment: "0.55" appears — maybe NPP yes = 55%? And "0.70", "0.84" — Rep yes 70-84%? And "0.19"?? Maybe SF Bay yes 19%? Or Dem yes 29%? The unweighted n row: "1892.00 424.00 ... 390.18 1087.52 0.00". And the Yes row values: "0.43 0.44 0.44 0.55 0.43 0.29 0.47 0.48 0.45 0.37 0.70 0.19 0.84" — these span both regions and parties. That would match PPIC's ~39% Sept. NPP = 0.55? Hmm, but the total is 0.43.

If x = 0.20 and y = 0.45: 0.094 + 0.126 = 0.22 ✓. So maybe Dem Yes ≈ 20% and Ind Yes ≈ 45% in IGS? The "0.19" in the fragment might be Dem Yes = 19%! And "0.47/0.48" might be regions or Ind.

If IGS's Dem Yes is ~20-25% (much lower than PPIC's ~32-39%), that's a big divergence. And Ind Yes maybe 45-48% (vs PPIC's 53-61%).

Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future." — So PPIC DOES read the full label including the nullification language and fiscal impact. So: IGS (PDI voter-file sample, weighted): 43/45. PPIC (Ipsos KnowledgePanel, probability panel): 51/47. Both read similar ballot language. Sampling differences.

IGS's likely voter weighting might be producing a more Democratic electorate than PPIC's. In recent cycles, IGS and PPIC usually agree within a few points; a 8-point gap is unusual. Hmm.

Also the last factor: **ballot roll-off**. Prop 42 is near the end of a 14-measure ballot. Low-propensity voters drop off; the voters who reach Prop 42 tend to be higher-information. Where do voters stand on this year’s biggest ballot measures?
Plus, polls on war, the Supreme Court, and paranormal activity.
Cooper Burton (https://substack.com/@cooperburton) , Mary Radcliffe (https://substack.com/@marywitha4) , and FiftyPlusOne (https://substack.com/@fiftyplusone)

22
5
Share
Welcome to The Trendline, the FiftyPlusOne.news weekly polling roundup. Subscribe (https://blog.fiftyplusone.news/subscribe) to get it delivered straight to your inbox and get bundled access to our polling website (https://fiftyplusone.news/) .
Subscribe
Most of the latest coverage surrounding polling has focused on the battle for control of Congress (https://fiftyplusone.news/forecast/house) , or President Trump’s historically low approval numbers (https://fiftyplusone.news/polls/approval/president) . But there’s far more on the ballot this November than just federal races, including controversial ballot measures surrounding the electoral process, taxes, and transgender rights. These measures can have far-reaching impacts, even for residents of other states (https://digital-release.nbc4i.com/news/local-news/columbus/ohio-sees-increase-in-those-traveling-from-out-of-state-for-an-abortion/) . We don’t have public polling for every measure that will be on voters’ ballots, but we have seen a good amount for some of the most potentially consequential measures of the year. For this week’s Trendline, we’ll be breaking down the latest polling on ballot measures to see which ones stand a chance at passing and how they might impact Americans across the country.
Elections
Multiple states are voting on measures affecting elections and voting in their states, some with the potential to dramatically alter how their residents pick their elected representatives.
In Missouri, Proposition A (https://ballotpedia.org/Missouri_Proposition_A,_Congressional_Map_Referendum_(2026)) gives voters the choice of whether or not to keep a newly passed Republican gerrymander that would almost certainly help the GOP pick up a seat in Congress. (That map was paused by the state Supreme Court last month to let voters weigh in first.) We’ve only seen one recent public poll for the measure, and Missourians appear to be pretty evenly split; in a Saint Louis University/YouGov poll (https://www.slu.edu/research/research-institute/big-ideas/slu-poll/-pdf/slu-poll-august-2026-topline-results.pdf) (Aug. 13 - 24, 2026), 35 percent of likely voters said they would vote to keep the new gerrymander, while 32 percent would reject it, and 33 percent weren’t sure.
Another voting-related ballot measure (https://ballotpedia.org/Missouri_Amendment_6,_Initiative_and_Referendum_Powers_and_Legislative_Change_Requirements_Amendment_(2026)) in Missouri would make it harder for the state legislature to weaken or change the initiative and referendum process, after state lawmakers nullified paid sick leave protections (https://www.komu.com/news/state/paid-sick-leave-requirement-to-end-this-week-employers-are-going-have-a-choice-again/article_beb8c19a-92af-4984-a24d-00faa69ede77.html) voters had passed via initiative. Voters seemed more friendly to this measure, with 48 percent supporting it in the SLU/YouGov poll and 21 percent opposing. Another 32 percent said they weren’t sure.
Maryland also has a redistricting-related measure on the ballot this year; Question 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/Maryland_Question_3,_Provide_That_Nothing_in_State_Constitution_Establishes_Criteria_for_Congressional_Redistricting_Amendment_(2026)) would clarify that state constitutional redistricting requirements apply only to state legislative districts and not congressional ones. Democrats in the state legislature put this measure to voters in the hopes of passing a new gerrymander of their own next year. The two public polls we have on the measure paint a starkly different picture — a Hart Research poll (https://www.thebanner.com/politics-power/state-government/redistricting-ballot-question-poll-GLJQK4NSD5GMDEPNOEPEPY2GKM/) (Sept. 8 - 10, 2026) sponsored by Fight Back MD (which supports the measure) found the measure up slightly, with 40 percent of respondents in favor, 35 percent opposed, and 25 percent unsure. But a Lincoln Park Strategies/Ragnar Research Partners poll (https://www.thebanner.com/politics-power/state-government/maryland-redistricting-poll-3H44RTFBYBA65FQXN2IPYRIH74/) (Sept. 10 - 13, 2026) for Protect Maryland Votes (which opposes the measure) showed the question underwater by double digits, with just 28 percent of Marylanders supporting the measure, 41 percent opposed, and 31 percent unsure.
In California, voters will decide whether to amend the state’s recall election process (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_5,_Eliminate_State_Officer_Recall_Successor_Elections_Amendment_(2026)) to leave offices vacant until a special election can be held to replace a recalled politician, rather than the current system of electing a replacement at the time of the recall. A PPIC poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from last month (Sept. 4 - 10, 2026) showed voters quite opposed to this change, with just 35 percent supporting the measure and 59 percent opposed. Only 5 percent said they weren’t sure.
And in Massachusetts, Bay Staters will vote on whether to overhaul their primary process (https://ballotpedia.org/Massachusetts_Question_3,_Top-Two_Primary_Elections_Initiative_(2026)) and create a single primary system where the top two candidates regardless of party move on to the general election, the same system used in California and Washington. Three recent polls of the question show it passing with varying degrees of strength — a University of Massachusetts Amherst/YouGov poll (https://www.umass.edu/poll/sites/default/files/2026-08/GOPPrimaryStateoftheStateToplinesAug2026MassPoll.pdf?1790267811) (Aug. 5 - 12, 2026) had the measure ahead by 19 points, with 51 percent supporting and 32 opposed to the overhaul. Two September polls also showed the measure ahead, but by a smaller margin. A MassInc/CommonWealth Beacon poll (https://commonwealthbeacon.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Topline-2026-09-CWB-Ballot-Questions-TUES-RELEASE.pdf) (Sept. 14 - 22, 2026) showed 43 percent of respondents in favor of the measure and 36 percent opposed. And in a University of New Hampshire poll (https://scholars.unh.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2007&context=survey_center_polls) (Sept. 17 - 21, 2026), 41 percent of respondents were supportive, while 39 percent were opposed.
Alaska will also hold ( another (https://alaskabeacon.com/2026/07/29/alaskans-to-vote-on-ballot-measure-that-would-overhaul-state-election-system/) ) vote on whether to repeal the state’s top-four ranked-choice primary system (https://ballotpedia.org/Alaska_Ballot_Measure_2,_Repeal_Top-Four_Ranked-Choice_Voting_Initiative_(2026)) and return to a traditional party primary system. We’ve only seen one public poll on the topic so far: a Fabrizio Ward/Impact Research poll (https://www.aarp.org/content/dam/aarp/research/topics/voter-opinion-research/politics/2026-midterm-election-poll-alaska-annotated-questionnaire.doi.10.26419-2fres.01065.017.pdf) for AARP (Sept. 8 - 11, 2026) showed voters closely split just like they were in 2024 (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2024/11/05/us/elections/results-alaska-measure-2-repeal-ranked-choice-voting.html) , with 44 percent in favor of repealing ranked-choice voting and 47 percent opposed.
Taxes
Lots of states will also have voters weigh on tax proposals, some of which have caused quite a stir — California’s Proposition 40 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_40,_One-Time_Wealth_Tax_for_State-Funded_Healthcare,_Education,_and_Food_Assistance_Programs_Initiative_(2026)) chief among them. Also referred to as the “billionaire tax,” the measure would levy a one-time 5 percent tax on individuals with over $1 billion in assets to help fund state programs, including health care and food assistance. The measure has drawn fierce opposition from prominent figures like Gov. Gavin Newsom (https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/newsom-urges-a-national-billionaires-tax-while-fighting-one-in-california) , as well as from the state’s wealthiest residents, who managed to get opposing measures on the same ballot. Propositions 41 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_41,_Prohibit_Excluding_New_State_Taxes_from_Spending_Limit_and_Require_Special_Tax_Audits_Initiative_(2026)) and 42 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_42,_Prohibit_New_Taxes_on_Retirement_Holdings,_Personal_Assets,_and_Savings_and_Limit_Retroactive_Taxes_Initiative_(2026)) would nullify Proposition 40 if either one of them gets a higher share of the vote than 40.
These propositions are by far the ballot measures for which we’ve seen the most public polling this cycle. In an average of polls conducted in August and September, just over 48 percent of respondents said they support Proposition 40, while an average of 41 percent were opposed. Propositions 41 and 42 received a bit less support on average from Californians, but it’ll still be a nail-biter; Proposition 42 in particular is right on the heels of Proposition 40.
In Washington, voters will be asked whether to (https://ballotpedia.org/Washington_Repeal_Tax_on_Household_Income_Over_$1_Million_and_Prohibit_State_and_Local_Taxes_on_Income_Initiative_(2026)) repeal (https://ballotpedia.org/Washington_Repeal_Tax_on_Household_Income_Over_$1_Million_and_Prohibit_State_and_Local_Taxes_on_Income_Initiative_(2026)) a millionaire’s tax (https://ballotpedia.org/Washington_Repeal_Tax_on_Household_Income_Over_$1_Million_and_Prohibit_State_and_Local_Taxes_on_Income_Initiative_(2026)) that the state legislature passed earlier this year, the first income tax ever to be levied in the state. According to the one public poll we’ve seen from DHM Research (https://www.dhmresearch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/WA-Pulse-73002-Toplines-Millionaires-Tax-September-2026.pdf) (Sept. 14 - 21, 2026), voters seem to be pretty opposed to the repeal. When shown the official ballot language for the measure, just 35 percent of respondents said they supported the initiative, while 57 percent were opposed.
Other states will vote on whether to decrease taxes. Floridians will decide on Amendment 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/Florida_Amendment_3,_Homestead_Tax_Exemptions,_Property_Assessments,_and_Spending_Restrictions_Amendment_(2026)) , which would greatly expand the homestead tax exemption, limit yearly tax increases, and restrict local spending using these funds. An average of three recent polls (from Sachs Media (https://sachsmedia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Sachs-Media-Amendment-3-Survey-8.19.26-1.pdf) , St. Pete Polls/Florida Politics (https://stpetepolls.org/files/StPetePolls_2026_State_Gov_September17_G7V29XU6.pdf) , and Stetson University (https://www.stetson.edu/artsci/cpor/media/cpor-sep-2026-report-2.pdf) ) shows 54 percent in favor of the measure and 30 percent opposed, which isn’t quite enough to get the measure over the finish line: Florida requires 60 percent support for constitutional amendments to pass. And North Carolinians will vote on (https://ballotpedia.org/North_Carolina_Reduce_Income_Tax_Rate_Cap_from_7%25_to_3.5%25_Amendment_(2026)) whether to decrease the maximum allowable state income tax to 3.5 percent, down from the current 7 percent cap (though no residents are currently taxed at that level). Recent polls from Elon University/YouGov (https://eloncdn.blob.core.windows.net/eu3/sites/819/2026/09/Elon-University-Poll-Topline-Methodology-9-17-26.pdf) (Aug. 21 - 31, 2026) and Harper Polling/Carolina Journal (https://www.carolinajournal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/H24747-CJ-NC-Sept26-Toplines.pdf) (Sept. 13 - 15, 2026) both show the measure with over 60 percent support.
Transgender Issues
Voters in Arizona, Colorado, Missouri, Nebraska, and Washington will be asked to weigh in on policies affecting transgender Americans this November. So far, there have only been two publicly released polls across these initiatives.
In Arizona, Proposition 318 (https://ballotpedia.org/Arizona_Proposition_318,_Require_All_Schools_and_Athletic_Associations_to_Restrict_Sports_Participation_and_Access_to_Private_Spaces_Based_on_Sex_Measure_(2026)) would ban schools and sports groups from letting individuals use restrooms, locker rooms, or showers that are not designated for the sex they were assigned at birth. It would also remove a provision from state law allowing female students to participate in sports designated for males. A Stealth Analytics poll (https://www.stealth-analytics.com/dispatches/az-general-lv-statewide-august-2026.pdf) (Aug. 11 - 13, 2026) showed the measure with 52 percent support, with just 16 percent opposing and 32 percent unsure.
Missourians will vote on Amendment 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/Missouri_Amendment_3,_Prohibit_Abortion_and_Gender_Transition_Procedures_for_Minors_Amendment_(2026)) , which would do a couple of different things. It would repeal the voter-approved amendment establishing a constitutional right to reproductive freedom, and would prohibit abortions except in specific instances of rape, incest, or medical emergency. It would also ban all gender transition surgeries and medication for minors. The Saint Louis University/YouGov poll (https://www.slu.edu/research/research-institute/big-ideas/slu-poll/-pdf/slu-poll-august-2026-topline-results.pdf) showed the amendment in a tight battle, with 43 percent of respondents supporting and 44 percent opposing the measure. Thirteen percent weren’t sure.
Many more measures will be on voters’ ballots across the country this November, but we’ve only seen public polls for a select few. Massachusetts residents will be asked (among other things) if they want to make recreational marijuana use illegal (https://ballotpedia.org/Massachusetts_Question_8,_Eliminate_Recreational_Marijuana_Sales_and_Allow_Limited_Possession_Initiative_(2026)) again (they’re opposed on average by a 34-point margin), and whether they want to relax some zoning laws (https://ballotpedia.org/Massachusetts_Question_7,_Limit_on_Required_Lot_Size_for_Single-Family_Homes_Initiative_(2026)) to allow for more single-family housing construction (they support on average by a 37-point margin). Michiganders will decide whether to call a state constitutional convention (https://ballotpedia.org/Michigan_Proposal_1,_Constitutional_Convention_Question_(2026)) — a Glengariff poll (https://www.clickondetroit.com/news/local/2026/09/09/nearly-half-of-michigan-voters-support-revising-state-constitution-poll-shows/) for WDIV and the Detroit News (Aug. 31 - Sept. 3, 2026) showed the measure up by 16 points. And Vermonters will vote on (https://ballotpedia.org/Vermont_Proposal_4,_Equal_Protection_of_Law_Amendment_(2026)) whether to prohibit the denial of rights based on traits like race, national origin, religion, sexual orientation, and gender identity; almost 70 percent of respondents in a recent University of New Hampshire poll (https://scholars.unh.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2005&context=survey_center_polls) (Sept. 17 - 21, 2026) were in favor.
Share (https://blog.fiftyplusone.news/p/where-do-voters-stand-on-this-years?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&action=share)
Other polling nuggets
A polling experiment from Echelon Insights (https://echeloninsights.com/insights/september-2026-verified-voter-omnibus) (Sept. 17 - 21, 2026) tested how voters responded to different language around data centers. Half of respondents were asked if they supported a data center in their community, and the other half were asked if they supported a “server farm.” With the data center language, voters were opposed by a margin of 40 percentage points, 65 to 25. But with the server farm language, opposition shrank to a margin of 22 percentage points, 50 to 28. Also notable: When using the server farm language, the number of respondents who said they were undecided was 22 percent, twice as many as said the same about data centers, so some of this decrease in margin may be due to voters having less strongly held opinions about server farms than data centers.
According to The Argument/Verasight (https://www.theargumentmag.com/p/the-least-popular-war-since-vietnam) (Sept. 16 - 21, 2026), the only war Americans believe was worth fighting in the last century was World War II. Asked whether it was right or wrong for the U.S. to engage in a variety of conflicts, a majority said wars in Iran, Iraq, and Vietnam were wrong, and a near-majority (47 percent) said the same about Afghanistan. Thirty-seven percent said U.S. involvement in Afghanistan was right, the most of any non-World War II conflict. When it comes to World War II, however, voters take a decidedly different position: 74 percent said it was right to engage in that conflict, while just 12 percent disagreed.
Americans’ trust in the Supreme Court has reached a historic low, according to polling data from Gallup dating back to the 1970s. Most of the latest coverage surrounding polling has focused on the battle for control of Congress (https://fiftyplusone.news/forecast/house) , or President Trump’s historically low approval numbers (https://fiftyplusone.news/polls/approval/president) . But there’s far more on the ballot this November than just federal races, including controversial ballot measures surrounding the electoral process, taxes, and transgender rights. These measures can have far-reaching impacts, even for residents of other states (https://digital-release.nbc4i.com/news/local-news/columbus/ohio-sees-increase-in-those-traveling-from-out-of-state-for-an-abortion/) . We don’t have public polling for every measure that will be on voters’ ballots, but we have seen a good amount for some of the most potentially consequential measures of the year. For this week’s Trendline, we’ll be breaking down the latest polling on ballot measures to see which ones stand a chance at passing and how they might impact Americans across the country.
Elections
Multiple states are voting on measures affecting elections and voting in their states, some with the potential to dramatically alter how their residents pick their elected representatives.
In Missouri, Proposition A (https://ballotpedia.org/Missouri_Proposition_A,_Congressional_Map_Referendum_(2026)) gives voters the choice of whether or not to keep a newly passed Republican gerrymander that would almost certainly help the GOP pick up a seat in Congress. (That map was paused by the state Supreme Court last month to let voters weigh in first.) We’ve only seen one recent public poll for the measure, and Missourians appear to be pretty evenly split; in a Saint Louis University/YouGov poll (https://www.slu.edu/research/research-institute/big-ideas/slu-poll/-pdf/slu-poll-august-2026-topline-results.pdf) (Aug. 13 - 24, 2026), 35 percent of likely voters said they would vote to keep the new gerrymander, while 32 percent would reject it, and 33 percent weren’t sure.
Another voting-related ballot measure (https://ballotpedia.org/Missouri_Amendment_6,_Initiative_and_Referendum_Powers_and_Legislative_Change_Requirements_Amendment_(2026)) in Missouri would make it harder for the state legislature to weaken or change the initiative and referendum process, after state lawmakers nullified paid sick leave protections (https://www.komu.com/news/state/paid-sick-leave-requirement-to-end-this-week-employers-are-going-have-a-choice-again/article_beb8c19a-92af-4984-a24d-00faa69ede77.html) voters had passed via initiative. Voters seemed more friendly to this measure, with 48 percent supporting it in the SLU/YouGov poll and 21 percent opposing. Another 32 percent said they weren’t sure.
Maryland also has a redistricting-related measure on the ballot this year; Question 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/Maryland_Question_3,_Provide_That_Nothing_in_State_Constitution_Establishes_Criteria_for_Congressional_Redistricting_Amendment_(2026)) would clarify that state constitutional redistricting requirements apply only to state legislative districts and not congressional ones. Democrats in the state legislature put this measure to voters in the hopes of passing a new gerrymander of their own next year. The two public polls we have on the measure paint a starkly different picture — a Hart Research poll (https://www.thebanner.com/politics-power/state-government/redistricting-ballot-question-poll-GLJQK4NSD5GMDEPNOEPEPY2GKM/) (Sept. 8 - 10, 2026) sponsored by Fight Back MD (which supports the measure) found the measure up slightly, with 40 percent of respondents in favor, 35 percent opposed, and 25 percent unsure. But a Lincoln Park Strategies/Ragnar Research Partners poll (https://www.thebanner.com/politics-power/state-government/maryland-redistricting-poll-3H44RTFBYBA65FQXN2IPYRIH74/) (Sept. 10 - 13, 2026) for Protect Maryland Votes (which opposes the measure) showed the question underwater by double digits, with just 28 percent of Marylanders supporting the measure, 41 percent opposed, and 31 percent unsure.
In California, voters will decide whether to amend the state’s recall election process (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_5,_Eliminate_State_Officer_Recall_Successor_Elections_Amendment_(2026)) to leave offices vacant until a special election can be held to replace a recalled politician, rather than the current system of electing a replacement at the time of the recall. A PPIC poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from last month (Sept. 4 - 10, 2026) showed voters quite opposed to this change, with just 35 percent supporting the measure and 59 percent opposed. Only 5 percent said they weren’t sure.
And in Massachusetts, Bay Staters will vote on whether to overhaul their primary process (https://ballotpedia.org/Massachusetts_Question_3,_Top-Two_Primary_Elections_Initiative_(2026)) and create a single primary system where the top two candidates regardless of party move on to the general election, the same system used in California and Washington. Three recent polls of the question show it passing with varying degrees of strength — a University of Massachusetts Amherst/YouGov poll (https://www.umass.edu/poll/sites/default/files/2026-08/GOPPrimaryStateoftheStateToplinesAug2026MassPoll.pdf?1790267811) (Aug. 5 - 12, 2026) had the measure ahead by 19 points, with 51 percent supporting and 32 opposed to the overhaul. Two September polls also showed the measure ahead, but by a smaller margin. A MassInc/CommonWealth Beacon poll (https://commonwealthbeacon.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Topline-2026-09-CWB-Ballot-Questions-TUES-RELEASE.pdf) (Sept. 14 - 22, 2026) showed 43 percent of respondents in favor of the measure and 36 percent opposed. And in a University of New Hampshire poll (https://scholars.unh.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2007&context=survey_center_polls) (Sept. 17 - 21, 2026), 41 percent of respondents were supportive, while 39 percent were opposed.
Alaska will also hold ( another (https://alaskabeacon.com/2026/07/29/alaskans-to-vote-on-ballot-measure-that-would-overhaul-state-election-system/) ) vote on whether to repeal the state’s top-four ranked-choice primary system (https://ballotpedia.org/Alaska_Ballot_Measure_2,_Repeal_Top-Four_Ranked-Choice_Voting_Initiative_(2026)) and return to a traditional party primary system. We’ve only seen one public poll on the topic so far: a Fabrizio Ward/Impact Research poll (https://www.aarp.org/content/dam/aarp/research/topics/voter-opinion-research/politics/2026-midterm-election-poll-alaska-annotated-questionnaire.doi.10.26419-2fres.01065.017.pdf) for AARP (Sept. 8 - 11, 2026) showed voters closely split just like they were in 2024 (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2024/11/05/us/elections/results-alaska-measure-2-repeal-ranked-choice-voting.html) , with 44 percent in favor of repealing ranked-choice voting and 47 percent opposed.
Taxes
Lots of states will also have voters weigh on tax proposals, some of which have caused quite a stir — California’s Proposition 40 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_40,_One-Time_Wealth_Tax_for_State-Funded_Healthcare,_Education,_and_Food_Assistance_Programs_Initiative_(2026)) chief among them. Also referred to as the “billionaire tax,” the measure would levy a one-time 5 percent tax on individuals with over $1 billion in assets to help fund state programs, including health care and food assistance. The measure has drawn fierce opposition from prominent figures like Gov. Gavin Newsom (https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/newsom-urges-a-national-billionaires-tax-while-fighting-one-in-california) , as well as from the state’s wealthiest residents, who managed to get opposing measures on the same ballot. Propositions 41 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_41,_Prohibit_Excluding_New_State_Taxes_from_Spending_Limit_and_Require_Special_Tax_Audits_Initiative_(2026)) and 42 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_42,_Prohibit_New_Taxes_on_Retirement_Holdings,_Personal_Assets,_and_Savings_and_Limit_Retroactive_Taxes_Initiative_(2026)) would nullify Proposition 40 if either one of them gets a higher share of the vote than 40.
These propositions are by far the ballot measures for which we’ve seen the most public polling this cycle. In an average of polls conducted in August and September, just over 48 percent of respondents said they support Proposition 40, while an average of 41 percent were opposed. Propositions 41 and 42 received a bit less support on average from Californians, but it’ll still be a nail-biter; Proposition 42 in particular is right on the heels of Proposition 40.
In Washington, voters will be asked whether to (https://ballotpedia.org/Washington_Repeal_Tax_on_Household_Income_Over_$1_Million_and_Prohibit_State_and_Local_Taxes_on_Income_Initiative_(2026)) repeal (https://ballotpedia.org/Washington_Repeal_Tax_on_Household_Income_Over_$1_Million_and_Prohibit_State_and_Local_Taxes_on_Income_Initiative_(2026)) a millionaire’s tax (https://ballotpedia.org/Washington_Repeal_Tax_on_Household_Income_Over_$1_Million_and_Prohibit_State_and_Local_Taxes_on_Income_Initiative_(2026)) that the state legislature passed earlier this year, the first income tax ever to be levied in the state. According to the one public poll we’ve seen from DHM Research (https://www.dhmresearch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/WA-Pulse-73002-Toplines-Millionaires-Tax-September-2026.pdf) (Sept. 14 - 21, 2026), voters seem to be pretty opposed to the repeal. When shown the official ballot language for the measure, just 35 percent of respondents said they supported the initiative, while 57 percent were opposed.
Other states will vote on whether to decrease taxes. Floridians will decide on Amendment 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/Florida_Amendment_3,_Homestead_Tax_Exemptions,_Property_Assessments,_and_Spending_Restrictions_Amendment_(2026)) , which would greatly expand the homestead tax exemption, limit yearly tax increases, and restrict local spending using these funds. An average of three recent polls (from Sachs Media (https://sachsmedia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Sachs-Media-Amendment-3-Survey-8.19.26-1.pdf) , St. Pete Polls/Florida Politics (https://stpetepolls.org/files/StPetePolls_2026_State_Gov_September17_G7V29XU6.pdf) , and Stetson University (https://www.stetson.edu/artsci/cpor/media/cpor-sep-2026-report-2.pdf) ) shows 54 percent in favor of the measure and 30 percent opposed, which isn’t quite enough to get the measure over the finish line: Florida requires 60 percent support for constitutional amendments to pass. And North Carolinians will vote on (https://ballotpedia.org/North_Carolina_Reduce_Income_Tax_Rate_Cap_from_7%25_to_3.5%25_Amendment_(2026)) whether to decrease the maximum allowable state income tax to 3.5 percent, down from the current 7 percent cap (though no residents are currently taxed at that level). Recent polls from Elon University/YouGov (https://eloncdn.blob.core.windows.net/eu3/sites/819/2026/09/Elon-University-Poll-Topline-Methodology-9-17-26.pdf) (Aug. 21 - 31, 2026) and Harper Polling/Carolina Journal (https://www.carolinajournal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/H24747-CJ-NC-Sept26-Toplines.pdf) (Sept. 13 - 15, 2026) both show the measure with over 60 percent support.
Transgender Issues
Voters in Arizona, Colorado, Missouri, Nebraska, and Washington will be asked to weigh in on policies affecting transgender Americans this November. So far, there have only been two publicly released polls across these initiatives.
In Arizona, Proposition 318 (https://ballotpedia.org/Arizona_Proposition_318,_Require_All_Schools_and_Athletic_Associations_to_Restrict_Sports_Participation_and_Access_to_Private_Spaces_Based_on_Sex_Measure_(2026)) would ban schools and sports groups from letting individuals use restrooms, locker rooms, or showers that are not designated for the sex they were assigned at birth. It would also remove a provision from state law allowing female students to participate in sports designated for males. A Stealth Analytics poll (https://www.stealth-analytics.com/dispatches/az-general-lv-statewide-august-2026.pdf) (Aug. 11 - 13, 2026) showed the measure with 52 percent support, with just 16 percent opposing and 32 percent unsure.
Missourians will vote on Amendment 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/Missouri_Amendment_3,_Prohibit_Abortion_and_Gender_Transition_Procedures_for_Minors_Amendment_(2026)) , which would do a couple of different things. It would repeal the voter-approved amendment establishing a constitutional right to reproductive freedom, and would prohibit abortions except in specific instances of rape, incest, or medical emergency. It would also ban all gender transition surgeries and medication for minors. The Saint Louis University/YouGov poll (https://www.slu.edu/research/research-institute/big-ideas/slu-poll/-pdf/slu-poll-august-2026-topline-results.pdf) showed the amendment in a tight battle, with 43 percent of respondents supporting and 44 percent opposing the measure. Thirteen percent weren’t sure.
Many more measures will be on voters’ ballots across the country this November, but we’ve only seen public polls for a select few. Massachusetts residents will be asked (among other things) if they want to make recreational marijuana use illegal (https://ballotpedia.org/Massachusetts_Question_8,_Eliminate_Recreational_Marijuana_Sales_and_Allow_Limited_Possession_Initiative_(2026)) again (they’re opposed on average by a 34-point margin), and whether they want to relax some zoning laws (https://ballotpedia.org/Massachusetts_Question_7,_Limit_on_Required_Lot_Size_for_Single-Family_Homes_Initiative_(2026)) to allow for more single-family housing construction (they support on average by a 37-point margin). Michiganders will decide whether to call a state constitutional convention (https://ballotpedia.org/Michigan_Proposal_1,_Constitutional_Convention_Question_(2026)) — a Glengariff poll (https://www.clickondetroit.com/news/local/2026/09/09/nearly-half-of-michigan-voters-support-revising-state-constitution-poll-shows/) for WDIV and the Detroit News (Aug. 31 - Sept. 3, 2026) showed the measure up by 16 points. And Vermonters will vote on (https://ballotpedia.org/Vermont_Proposal_4,_Equal_Protection_of_Law_Amendment_(2026)) whether to prohibit the denial of rights based on traits like race, national origin, religion, sexual orientation, and gender identity; almost 70 percent of respondents in a recent University of New Hampshire poll (https://scholars.unh.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2005&context=survey_center_polls) (Sept. 17 - 21, 2026) were in favor.

Other polling nuggets
A polling experiment from Echelon Insights (https://echeloninsights.com/insights/september-2026-verified-voter-omnibus) (Sept. 17 - 21, 2026) tested how voters responded to different language around data centers. Half of respondents were asked if they supported a data center in their community, and the other half were asked if they supported a “server farm.” With the data center language, voters were opposed by a margin of 40 percentage points, 65 to 25. But with the server farm language, opposition shrank to a margin of 22 percentage points, 50 to 28. Also notable: When using the server farm language, the number of respondents who said they were undecided was 22 percent, twice as many as said the same about data centers, so some of this decrease in margin may be due to voters having less strongly held opinions about server farms than data centers.
According to The Argument/Verasight (https://www.theargumentmag.com/p/the-least-popular-war-since-vietnam) (Sept. 16 - 21, 2026), the only war Americans believe was worth fighting in the last century was World War II. Asked whether it was right or wrong for the U.S. to engage in a variety of conflicts, a majority said wars in Iran, Iraq, and Vietnam were wrong, and a near-majority (47 percent) said the same about Afghanistan. Thirty-seven percent said U.S. involvement in Afghanistan was right, the most of any non-World War II conflict. When it comes to World War II, however, voters take a decidedly different position: 74 percent said it was right to engage in that conflict, while just 12 percent disagreed.
Americans’ trust in the Supreme Court has reached a historic low, according to polling data from Gallup dating back to the 1970s. In the latest survey (https://news.gallup.com/poll/715022/supreme-court-begins-term-historically-low-ratings.aspx) (Sept. 1 - 17, 2026), just 46 percent of Americans said they have a great deal or fair amount of trust in the Supreme Court, the lowest reading on record, and 61 percent disapprove of the job the Court is doing, tying the record high disapproval rating first recorded in July of this year. The drop is driven mostly by Democrats, whose approval of the Court has been falling since 2021, and now stands at just 12 percent. But independents have also hit a record low in their approval of the Court, at 31 percent, and Republicans’ ratings of the Court have also seen a dip from a high of 79 percent in September 2025 to 65 percent in the most recent poll.
