Welcome to The Trendline, the FiftyPlusOne.news weekly polling roundup. Subscribe (https://blog.fiftyplusone.news/subscribe) to get it delivered straight to your inbox and get bundled access to our polling website (https://fiftyplusone.news/) .
Subscribe
Most of the latest coverage surrounding polling has focused on the battle for control of Congress (https://fiftyplusone.news/forecast/house) , or President Trump’s historically low approval numbers (https://fiftyplusone.news/polls/approval/president) . But there’s far more on the ballot this November than just federal races, including controversial ballot measures surrounding the electoral process, taxes, and transgender rights. These measures can have far-reaching impacts, even for residents of other states (https://digital-release.nbc4i.com/news/local-news/columbus/ohio-sees-increase-in-those-traveling-from-out-of-state-for-an-abortion/) . We don’t have public polling for every measure that will be on voters’ ballots, but we have seen a good amount for some of the most potentially consequential measures of the year. For this week’s Trendline, we’ll be breaking down the latest polling on ballot measures to see which ones stand a chance at passing and how they might impact Americans across the country.
Elections
Multiple states are voting on measures affecting elections and voting in their states, some with the potential to dramatically alter how their residents pick their elected representatives.
In Missouri, Proposition A (https://ballotpedia.org/Missouri_Proposition_A,_Congressional_Map_Referendum_(2026)) gives voters the choice of whether or not to keep a newly passed Republican gerrymander that would almost certainly help the GOP pick up a seat in Congress. (That map was paused by the state Supreme Court last month to let voters weigh in first.) We’ve only seen one recent public poll for the measure, and Missourians appear to be pretty evenly split; in a Saint Louis University/YouGov poll (https://www.slu.edu/research/research-institute/big-ideas/slu-poll/-pdf/slu-poll-august-2026-topline-results.pdf) (Aug. 13 - 24, 2026), 35 percent of likely voters said they would vote to keep the new gerrymander, while 32 percent would reject it, and 33 percent weren’t sure.
Another voting-related ballot measure (https://ballotpedia.org/Missouri_Amendment_6,_Initiative_and_Referendum_Powers_and_Legislative_Change_Requirements_Amendment_(2026)) in Missouri would make it harder for the state legislature to weaken or change the initiative and referendum process, after state lawmakers nullified paid sick leave protections (https://www.komu.com/news/state/paid-sick-leave-requirement-to-end-this-week-employers-are-going-have-a-choice-again/article_beb8c19a-92af-4984-a24d-00faa69ede77.html) voters had passed via initiative. Voters seemed more friendly to this measure, with 48 percent supporting it in the SLU/YouGov poll and 21 percent opposing. Another 32 percent said they weren’t sure.
Maryland also has a redistricting-related measure on the ballot this year; Question 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/Maryland_Question_3,_Provide_That_Nothing_in_State_Constitution_Establishes_Criteria_for_Congressional_Redistricting_Amendment_(2026)) would clarify that state constitutional redistricting requirements apply only to state legislative districts and not congressional ones. Democrats in the state legislature put this measure to voters in the hopes of passing a new gerrymander of their own next year. The two public polls we have on the measure paint a starkly different picture — a Hart Research poll (https://www.thebanner.com/politics-power/state-government/redistricting-ballot-question-poll-GLJQK4NSD5GMDEPNOEPEPY2GKM/) (Sept. 8 - 10, 2026) sponsored by Fight Back MD (which supports the measure) found the measure up slightly, with 40 percent of respondents in favor, 35 percent opposed, and 25 percent unsure. But a Lincoln Park Strategies/Ragnar Research Partners poll (https://www.thebanner.com/politics-power/state-government/maryland-redistricting-poll-3H44RTFBYBA65FQXN2IPYRIH74/) (Sept. 10 - 13, 2026) for Protect Maryland Votes (which opposes the measure) showed the question underwater by double digits, with just 28 percent of Marylanders supporting the measure, 41 percent opposed, and 31 percent unsure.
In California, voters will decide whether to amend the state’s recall election process (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_5,_Eliminate_State_Officer_Recall_Successor_Elections_Amendment_(2026)) to leave offices vacant until a special election can be held to replace a recalled politician, rather than the current system of electing a replacement at the time of the recall. A PPIC poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from last month (Sept. 4 - 10, 2026) showed voters quite opposed to this change, with just 35 percent supporting the measure and 59 percent opposed. Only 5 percent said they weren’t sure.
And in Massachusetts, Bay Staters will vote on whether to overhaul their primary process (https://ballotpedia.org/Massachusetts_Question_3,_Top-Two_Primary_Elections_Initiative_(2026)) and create a single primary system where the top two candidates regardless of party move on to the general election, the same system used in California and Washington. Three recent polls of the question show it passing with varying degrees of strength — a University of Massachusetts Amherst/YouGov poll (https://www.umass.edu/poll/sites/default/files/2026-08/GOPPrimaryStateoftheStateToplinesAug2026MassPoll.pdf?1790267811) (Aug. 5 - 12, 2026) had the measure ahead by 19 points, with 51 percent supporting and 32 opposed to the overhaul. Two September polls also showed the measure ahead, but by a smaller margin. A MassInc/CommonWealth Beacon poll (https://commonwealthbeacon.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Topline-2026-09-CWB-Ballot-Questions-TUES-RELEASE.pdf) (Sept. 14 - 22, 2026) showed 43 percent of respondents in favor of the measure and 36 percent opposed. And in a University of New Hampshire poll (https://scholars.unh.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2007&context=survey_center_polls) (Sept. 17 - 21, 2026), 41 percent of respondents were supportive, while 39 percent were opposed.
Alaska will also hold ( another (https://alaskabeacon.com/2026/07/29/alaskans-to-vote-on-ballot-measure-that-would-overhaul-state-election-system/) ) vote on whether to repeal the state’s top-four ranked-choice primary system (https://ballotpedia.org/Alaska_Ballot_Measure_2,_Repeal_Top-Four_Ranked-Choice_Voting_Initiative_(2026)) and return to a traditional party primary system. We’ve only seen one public poll on the topic so far: a Fabrizio Ward/Impact Research poll (https://www.aarp.org/content/dam/aarp/research/topics/voter-opinion-research/politics/2026-midterm-election-poll-alaska-annotated-questionnaire.doi.10.26419-2fres.01065.017.pdf) for AARP (Sept. 8 - 11, 2026) showed voters closely split just like they were in 2024 (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2024/11/05/us/elections/results-alaska-measure-2-repeal-ranked-choice-voting.html) , with 44 percent in favor of repealing ranked-choice voting and 47 percent opposed.
Taxes
Lots of states will also have voters weigh on tax proposals, some of which have caused quite a stir — California’s Proposition 40 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_40,_One-Time_Wealth_Tax_for_State-Funded_Healthcare,_Education,_and_Food_Assistance_Programs_Initiative_(2026)) chief among them. Also referred to as the “billionaire tax,” the measure would levy a one-time 5 percent tax on individuals with over $1 billion in assets to help fund state programs, including health care and food assistance. The measure has drawn fierce opposition from prominent figures like Gov. Gavin Newsom (https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/newsom-urges-a-national-billionaires-tax-while-fighting-one-in-california) , as well as from the state’s wealthiest residents, who managed to get opposing measures on the same ballot. Propositions 41 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_41,_Prohibit_Excluding_New_State_Taxes_from_Spending_Limit_and_Require_Special_Tax_Audits_Initiative_(2026)) and 42 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_42,_Prohibit_New_Taxes_on_Retirement_Holdings,_Personal_Assets,_and_Savings_and_Limit_Retroactive_Taxes_Initiative_(2026)) would nullify Proposition 40 if either one of them gets a higher share of the vote than 40.
These propositions are by far the ballot measures for which we’ve seen the most public polling this cycle. In an average of polls conducted in August and September, just over 48 percent of respondents said they support Proposition 40, while an average of 41 percent were opposed. Propositions 41 and 42 received a bit less support on average from Californians, but it’ll still be a nail-biter; Proposition 42 in particular is right on the heels of Proposition 40.
In Washington, voters will be asked whether to (https://ballotpedia.org/Washington_Repeal_Tax_on_Household_Income_Over_$1_Million_and_Prohibit_State_and_Local_Taxes_on_Income_Initiative_(2026)) repeal (https://ballotpedia.org/Washington_Repeal_Tax_on_Household_Income_Over_$1_Million_and_Prohibit_State_and_Local_Taxes_on_Income_Initiative_(2026)) a millionaire’s tax (https://ballotpedia.org/Washington_Repeal_Tax_on_Household_Income_Over_$1_Million_and_Prohibit_State_and_Local_Taxes_on_Income_Initiative_(2026)) that the state legislature passed earlier this year, the first income tax ever to be levied in the state. According to the one public poll we’ve seen from DHM Research (https://www.dhmresearch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/WA-Pulse-73002-Toplines-Millionaires-Tax-September-2026.pdf) (Sept. 14 - 21, 2026), voters seem to be pretty opposed to the repeal. When shown the official ballot language for the measure, just 35 percent of respondents said they supported the initiative, while 57 percent were opposed.
Other states will vote on whether to decrease taxes. Floridians will decide on Amendment 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/Florida_Amendment_3,_Homestead_Tax_Exemptions,_Property_Assessments,_and_Spending_Restrictions_Amendment_(2026)) , which would greatly expand the homestead tax exemption, limit yearly tax increases, and restrict local spending using these funds. An average of three recent polls (from Sachs Media (https://sachsmedia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Sachs-Media-Amendment-3-Survey-8.19.26-1.pdf) , St. Pete Polls/Florida Politics (https://stpetepolls.org/files/StPetePolls_2026_State_Gov_September17_G7V29XU6.pdf) , and Stetson University (https://www.stetson.edu/artsci/cpor/media/cpor-sep-2026-report-2.pdf) ) shows 54 percent in favor of the measure and 30 percent opposed, which isn’t quite enough to get the measure over the finish line: Florida requires 60 percent support for constitutional amendments to pass. And North Carolinians will vote on (https://ballotpedia.org/North_Carolina_Reduce_Income_Tax_Rate_Cap_from_7%25_to_3.5%25_Amendment_(2026)) whether to decrease the maximum allowable state income tax to 3.5 percent, down from the current 7 percent cap (though no residents are currently taxed at that level). Recent polls from Elon University/YouGov (https://eloncdn.blob.core.windows.net/eu3/sites/819/2026/09/Elon-University-Poll-Topline-Methodology-9-17-26.pdf) (Aug. 21 - 31, 2026) and Harper Polling/Carolina Journal (https://www.carolinajournal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/H24747-CJ-NC-Sept26-Toplines.pdf) (Sept. 13 - 15, 2026) both show the measure with over 60 percent support.
Transgender Issues
Voters in Arizona, Colorado, Missouri, Nebraska, and Washington will be asked to weigh in on policies affecting transgender Americans this November. So far, there have only been two publicly released polls across these initiatives.
In Arizona, Proposition 318 (https://ballotpedia.org/Arizona_Proposition_318,_Require_All_Schools_and_Athletic_Associations_to_Restrict_Sports_Participation_and_Access_to_Private_Spaces_Based_on_Sex_Measure_(2026)) would ban schools and sports groups from letting individuals use restrooms, locker rooms, or showers that are not designated for the sex they were assigned at birth. It would also remove a provision from state law allowing female students to participate in sports designated for males. A Stealth Analytics poll (https://www.stealth-analytics.com/dispatches/az-general-lv-statewide-august-2026.pdf) (Aug. 11 - 13, 2026) showed the measure with 52 percent support, with just 16 percent opposing and 32 percent unsure.
Missourians will vote on Amendment 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/Missouri_Amendment_3,_Prohibit_Abortion_and_Gender_Transition_Procedures_for_Minors_Amendment_(2026)) , which would do a couple of different things. It would repeal the voter-approved amendment establishing a constitutional right to reproductive freedom, and would prohibit abortions except in specific instances of rape, incest, or medical emergency. It would also ban all gender transition surgeries and medication for minors. The Saint Louis University/YouGov poll (https://www.slu.edu/research/research-institute/big-ideas/slu-poll/-pdf/slu-poll-august-2026-topline-results.pdf) showed the amendment in a tight battle, with 43 percent of respondents supporting and 44 percent opposing the measure. Thirteen percent weren’t sure.
Many more measures will be on voters’ ballots across the country this November, but we’ve only seen public polls for a select few. Massachusetts residents will be asked (among other things) if they want to make recreational marijuana use illegal (https://ballotpedia.org/Massachusetts_Question_8,_Eliminate_Recreational_Marijuana_Sales_and_Allow_Limited_Possession_Initiative_(2026)) again (they’re opposed on average by a 34-point margin), and whether they want to relax some zoning laws (https://ballotpedia.org/Massachusetts_Question_7,_Limit_on_Required_Lot_Size_for_Single-Family_Homes_Initiative_(2026)) to allow for more single-family housing construction (they support on average by a 37-point margin). Michiganders will decide whether to call a state constitutional convention (https://ballotpedia.org/Michigan_Proposal_1,_Constitutional_Convention_Question_(2026)) — a Glengariff poll (https://www.clickondetroit.com/news/local/2026/09/09/nearly-half-of-michigan-voters-support-revising-state-constitution-poll-shows/) for WDIV and the Detroit News (Aug. 31 - Sept. 3, 2026) showed the measure up by 16 points. And Vermonters will vote on (https://ballotpedia.org/Vermont_Proposal_4,_Equal_Protection_of_Law_Amendment_(2026)) whether to prohibit the denial of rights based on traits like race, national origin, religion, sexual orientation, and gender identity; almost 70 percent of respondents in a recent University of New Hampshire poll (https://scholars.unh.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2005&context=survey_center_polls) (Sept. 17 - 21, 2026) were in favor.
Share (https://blog.fiftyplusone.news/p/where-do-voters-stand-on-this-years?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&action=share)
Other polling nuggets
A polling experiment from Echelon Insights (https://echeloninsights.com/insights/september-2026-verified-voter-omnibus) (Sept. 17 - 21, 2026) tested how voters responded to different language around data centers. Half of respondents were asked if they supported a data center in their community, and the other half were asked if they supported a “server farm.” With the data center language, voters were opposed by a margin of 40 percentage points, 65 to 25. But with the server farm language, opposition shrank to a margin of 22 percentage points, 50 to 28. Also notable: When using the server farm language, the number of respondents who said they were undecided was 22 percent, twice as many as said the same about data centers, so some of this decrease in margin may be due to voters having less strongly held opinions about server farms than data centers.
According to The Argument/Verasight (https://www.theargumentmag.com/p/the-least-popular-war-since-vietnam) (Sept. 16 - 21, 2026), the only war Americans believe was worth fighting in the last century was World War II. Asked whether it was right or wrong for the U.S. to engage in a variety of conflicts, a majority said wars in Iran, Iraq, and Vietnam were wrong, and a near-majority (47 percent) said the same about Afghanistan. Thirty-seven percent said U.S. involvement in Afghanistan was right, the most of any non-World War II conflict. When it comes to World War II, however, voters take a decidedly different position: 74 percent said it was right to engage in that conflict, while just 12 percent disagreed.
Americans’ trust in the Supreme Court has reached a historic low, according to polling data from Gallup dating back to the 1970s. In the latest survey (https://news.gallup.com/poll/715022/supreme-court-begins-term-historically-low-ratings.aspx) (Sept. 1 - 17, 2026), just 46 percent of Americans said they have a great deal or fair amount of trust in the Supreme Court, the lowest reading on record, and 61 percent disapprove of the job the Court is doing, tying the record high disapproval rating first recorded in July of this year. The drop is driven mostly by Democrats, whose approval of the Court has been falling since 2021, and now stands at just 12 percent. But independents have also hit a record low in their approval of the Court, at 31 percent, and Republicans’ ratings of the Court have also seen a dip from a high of 79 percent in September 2025 to 65 percent in the most recent poll.
It’s October, and Spooky Season has officially begun. According to YouGov (https://d3nkl3psvxxpe9.cloudfront.net/documents/Paranormal_Encounters_poll_results.pdf) (Sept. 25 - 28, 2026), half of Americans (49 percent) believe that some people have paranormal abilities, and 58 percent believe that people have experienced paranormal encounters that are unable to be explained scientifically. Around a fifth of Americans (19 percent) say they have seen a spirit or ghost, and seven percent report having seen a demon. More than half (52 percent) say that homeowners should be required by law to disclose whether or not they believe their house is haunted before selling it.
Polling averages update
All numbers are as of 12:00 PM Eastern on Oct. 2, 2026.
2026 U.S. House generic ballot
The Democratic margin in the 2026 U.S. House generic ballot (https://fiftyplusone.news/polls/generic-ballot/generic-ballot) remained steady this week, with Democrats still ahead of Republicans by 8 percentage points. Currently, 50.8 percent of likely voters indicate that they plan to vote for a Democrat in November, while 43.1 percent plan to vote for a Republican.
Trump’s job approval
President Trump’s net approval rating (https://fiftyplusone.news/polls/approval/president) among U.S. adults dropped a point this week, for a new low of -28 percentage points. Most of the latest coverage surrounding polling has focused on the battle for control of Congress (https://fiftyplusone.news/forecast/house) , or President Trump’s historically low approval numbers (https://fiftyplusone.news/polls/approval/president) . But there’s far more on the ballot this November than just federal races, including controversial ballot measures surrounding the electoral process, taxes, and transgender rights. These measures can have far-reaching impacts, even for residents of other states (https://digital-release.nbc4i.com/news/local-news/columbus/ohio-sees-increase-in-those-traveling-from-out-of-state-for-an-abortion/) . We don’t have public polling for every measure that will be on voters’ ballots, but we have seen a good amount for some of the most potentially consequential measures of the year. For this week’s Trendline, we’ll be breaking down the latest polling on ballot measures to see which ones stand a chance at passing and how they might impact Americans across the country.
Elections
Multiple states are voting on measures affecting elections and voting in their states, some with the potential to dramatically alter how their residents pick their elected representatives.
In Missouri, Proposition A (https://ballotpedia.org/Missouri_Proposition_A,_Congressional_Map_Referendum_(2026)) gives voters the choice of whether or not to keep a newly passed Republican gerrymander that would almost certainly help the GOP pick up a seat in Congress. (That map was paused by the state Supreme Court last month to let voters weigh in first.) We’ve only seen one recent public poll for the measure, and Missourians appear to be pretty evenly split; in a Saint Louis University/YouGov poll (https://www.slu.edu/research/research-institute/big-ideas/slu-poll/-pdf/slu-poll-august-2026-topline-results.pdf) (Aug. 13 - 24, 2026), 35 percent of likely voters said they would vote to keep the new gerrymander, while 32 percent would reject it, and 33 percent weren’t sure.
Another voting-related ballot measure (https://ballotpedia.org/Missouri_Amendment_6,_Initiative_and_Referendum_Powers_and_Legislative_Change_Requirements_Amendment_(2026)) in Missouri would make it harder for the state legislature to weaken or change the initiative and referendum process, after state lawmakers nullified paid sick leave protections (https://www.komu.com/news/state/paid-sick-leave-requirement-to-end-this-week-employers-are-going-have-a-choice-again/article_beb8c19a-92af-4984-a24d-00faa69ede77.html) voters had passed via initiative. Voters seemed more friendly to this measure, with 48 percent supporting it in the SLU/YouGov poll and 21 percent opposing. Another 32 percent said they weren’t sure.
Maryland also has a redistricting-related measure on the ballot this year; Question 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/Maryland_Question_3,_Provide_That_Nothing_in_State_Constitution_Establishes_Criteria_for_Congressional_Redistricting_Amendment_(2026)) would clarify that state constitutional redistricting requirements apply only to state legislative districts and not congressional ones. Democrats in the state legislature put this measure to voters in the hopes of passing a new gerrymander of their own next year. The two public polls we have on the measure paint a starkly different picture — a Hart Research poll (https://www.thebanner.com/politics-power/state-government/redistricting-ballot-question-poll-GLJQK4NSD5GMDEPNOEPEPY2GKM/) (Sept. 8 - 10, 2026) sponsored by Fight Back MD (which supports the measure) found the measure up slightly, with 40 percent of respondents in favor, 35 percent opposed, and 25 percent unsure. But a Lincoln Park Strategies/Ragnar Research Partners poll (https://www.thebanner.com/politics-power/state-government/maryland-redistricting-poll-3H44RTFBYBA65FQXN2IPYRIH74/) (Sept. 10 - 13, 2026) for Protect Maryland Votes (which opposes the measure) showed the question underwater by double digits, with just 28 percent of Marylanders supporting the measure, 41 percent opposed, and 31 percent unsure.
In California, voters will decide whether to amend the state’s recall election process (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_5,_Eliminate_State_Officer_Recall_Successor_Elections_Amendment_(2026)) to leave offices vacant until a special election can be held to replace a recalled politician, rather than the current system of electing a replacement at the time of the recall. A PPIC poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from last month (Sept. 4 - 10, 2026) showed voters quite opposed to this change, with just 35 percent supporting the measure and 59 percent opposed. Only 5 percent said they weren’t sure.
And in Massachusetts, Bay Staters will vote on whether to overhaul their primary process (https://ballotpedia.org/Massachusetts_Question_3,_Top-Two_Primary_Elections_Initiative_(2026)) and create a single primary system where the top two candidates regardless of party move on to the general election, the same system used in California and Washington. Three recent polls of the question show it passing with varying degrees of strength — a University of Massachusetts Amherst/YouGov poll (https://www.umass.edu/poll/sites/default/files/2026-08/GOPPrimaryStateoftheStateToplinesAug2026MassPoll.pdf?1790267811) (Aug. 5 - 12, 2026) had the measure ahead by 19 points, with 51 percent supporting and 32 opposed to the overhaul. Two September polls also showed the measure ahead, but by a smaller margin. A MassInc/CommonWealth Beacon poll (https://commonwealthbeacon.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Topline-2026-09-CWB-Ballot-Questions-TUES-RELEASE.pdf) (Sept. 14 - 22, 2026) showed 43 percent of respondents in favor of the measure and 36 percent opposed. And in a University of New Hampshire poll (https://scholars.unh.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2007&context=survey_center_polls) (Sept. 17 - 21, 2026), 41 percent of respondents were supportive, while 39 percent were opposed.
Alaska will also hold ( another (https://alaskabeacon.com/2026/07/29/alaskans-to-vote-on-ballot-measure-that-would-overhaul-state-election-system/) ) vote on whether to repeal the state’s top-four ranked-choice primary system (https://ballotpedia.org/Alaska_Ballot_Measure_2,_Repeal_Top-Four_Ranked-Choice_Voting_Initiative_(2026)) and return to a traditional party primary system. We’ve only seen one public poll on the topic so far: a Fabrizio Ward/Impact Research poll (https://www.aarp.org/content/dam/aarp/research/topics/voter-opinion-research/politics/2026-midterm-election-poll-alaska-annotated-questionnaire.doi.10.26419-2fres.01065.017.pdf) for AARP (Sept. 8 - 11, 2026) showed voters closely split just like they were in 2024 (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2024/11/05/us/elections/results-alaska-measure-2-repeal-ranked-choice-voting.html) , with 44 percent in favor of repealing ranked-choice voting and 47 percent opposed.
Taxes
Lots of states will also have voters weigh on tax proposals, some of which have caused quite a stir — California’s Proposition 40 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_40,_One-Time_Wealth_Tax_for_State-Funded_Healthcare,_Education,_and_Food_Assistance_Programs_Initiative_(2026)) chief among them. Also referred to as the “billionaire tax,” the measure would levy a one-time 5 percent tax on individuals with over $1 billion in assets to help fund state programs, including health care and food assistance. The measure has drawn fierce opposition from prominent figures like Gov. Gavin Newsom (https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/newsom-urges-a-national-billionaires-tax-while-fighting-one-in-california) , as well as from the state’s wealthiest residents, who managed to get opposing measures on the same ballot. Propositions 41 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_41,_Prohibit_Excluding_New_State_Taxes_from_Spending_Limit_and_Require_Special_Tax_Audits_Initiative_(2026)) and 42 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_42,_Prohibit_New_Taxes_on_Retirement_Holdings,_Personal_Assets,_and_Savings_and_Limit_Retroactive_Taxes_Initiative_(2026)) would nullify Proposition 40 if either one of them gets a higher share of the vote than 40.
These propositions are by far the ballot measures for which we’ve seen the most public polling this cycle. In an average of polls conducted in August and September, just over 48 percent of respondents said they support Proposition 40, while an average of 41 percent were opposed. Propositions 41 and 42 received a bit less support on average from Californians, but it’ll still be a nail-biter; Proposition 42 in particular is right on the heels of Proposition 40.
In Washington, voters will be asked whether to (https://ballotpedia.org/Washington_Repeal_Tax_on_Household_Income_Over_$1_Million_and_Prohibit_State_and_Local_Taxes_on_Income_Initiative_(2026)) repeal (https://ballotpedia.org/Washington_Repeal_Tax_on_Household_Income_Over_$1_Million_and_Prohibit_State_and_Local_Taxes_on_Income_Initiative_(2026)) a millionaire’s tax (https://ballotpedia.org/Washington_Repeal_Tax_on_Household_Income_Over_$1_Million_and_Prohibit_State_and_Local_Taxes_on_Income_Initiative_(2026)) that the state legislature passed earlier this year, the first income tax ever to be levied in the state. According to the one public poll we’ve seen from DHM Research (https://www.dhmresearch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/WA-Pulse-73002-Toplines-Millionaires-Tax-September-2026.pdf) (Sept. 14 - 21, 2026), voters seem to be pretty opposed to the repeal. When shown the official ballot language for the measure, just 35 percent of respondents said they supported the initiative, while 57 percent were opposed.
Other states will vote on whether to decrease taxes. Floridians will decide on Amendment 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/Florida_Amendment_3,_Homestead_Tax_Exemptions,_Property_Assessments,_and_Spending_Restrictions_Amendment_(2026)) , which would greatly expand the homestead tax exemption, limit yearly tax increases, and restrict local spending using these funds. An average of three recent polls (from Sachs Media (https://sachsmedia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Sachs-Media-Amendment-3-Survey-8.19.26-1.pdf) , St. Pete Polls/Florida Politics (https://stpetepolls.org/files/StPetePolls_2026_State_Gov_September17_G7V29XU6.pdf) , and Stetson University (https://www.stetson.edu/artsci/cpor/media/cpor-sep-2026-report-2.pdf) ) shows 54 percent in favor of the measure and 30 percent opposed, which isn’t quite enough to get the measure over the finish line: Florida requires 60 percent support for constitutional amendments to pass. And North Carolinians will vote on (https://ballotpedia.org/North_Carolina_Reduce_Income_Tax_Rate_Cap_from_7%25_to_3.5%25_Amendment_(2026)) whether to decrease the maximum allowable state income tax to 3.5 percent, down from the current 7 percent cap (though no residents are currently taxed at that level). Recent polls from Elon University/YouGov (https://eloncdn.blob.core.windows.net/eu3/sites/819/2026/09/Elon-University-Poll-Topline-Methodology-9-17-26.pdf) (Aug. 21 - 31, 2026) and Harper Polling/Carolina Journal (https://www.carolinajournal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/H24747-CJ-NC-Sept26-Toplines.pdf) (Sept. 13 - 15, 2026) both show the measure with over 60 percent support.
Transgender Issues
Voters in Arizona, Colorado, Missouri, Nebraska, and Washington will be asked to weigh in on policies affecting transgender Americans this November. So far, there have only been two publicly released polls across these initiatives.
In Arizona, Proposition 318 (https://ballotpedia.org/Arizona_Proposition_318,_Require_All_Schools_and_Athletic_Associations_to_Restrict_Sports_Participation_and_Access_to_Private_Spaces_Based_on_Sex_Measure_(2026)) would ban schools and sports groups from letting individuals use restrooms, locker rooms, or showers that are not designated for the sex they were assigned at birth. It would also remove a provision from state law allowing female students to participate in sports designated for males. A Stealth Analytics poll (https://www.stealth-analytics.com/dispatches/az-general-lv-statewide-august-2026.pdf) (Aug. 11 - 13, 2026) showed the measure with 52 percent support, with just 16 percent opposing and 32 percent unsure.
Missourians will vote on Amendment 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/Missouri_Amendment_3,_Prohibit_Abortion_and_Gender_Transition_Procedures_for_Minors_Amendment_(2026)) , which would do a couple of different things. It would repeal the voter-approved amendment establishing a constitutional right to reproductive freedom, and would prohibit abortions except in specific instances of rape, incest, or medical emergency. It would also ban all gender transition surgeries and medication for minors. The Saint Louis University/YouGov poll (https://www.slu.edu/research/research-institute/big-ideas/slu-poll/-pdf/slu-poll-august-2026-topline-results.pdf) showed the amendment in a tight battle, with 43 percent of respondents supporting and 44 percent opposing the measure. Thirteen percent weren’t sure.
Many more measures will be on voters’ ballots across the country this November, but we’ve only seen public polls for a select few. Massachusetts residents will be asked (among other things) if they want to make recreational marijuana use illegal (https://ballotpedia.org/Massachusetts_Question_8,_Eliminate_Recreational_Marijuana_Sales_and_Allow_Limited_Possession_Initiative_(2026)) again (they’re opposed on average by a 34-point margin), and whether they want to relax some zoning laws (https://ballotpedia.org/Massachusetts_Question_7,_Limit_on_Required_Lot_Size_for_Single-Family_Homes_Initiative_(2026)) to allow for more single-family housing construction (they support on average by a 37-point margin). Michiganders will decide whether to call a state constitutional convention (https://ballotpedia.org/Michigan_Proposal_1,_Constitutional_Convention_Question_(2026)) — a Glengariff poll (https://www.clickondetroit.com/news/local/2026/09/09/nearly-half-of-michigan-voters-support-revising-state-constitution-poll-shows/) for WDIV and the Detroit News (Aug. 31 - Sept. 3, 2026) showed the measure up by 16 points. And Vermonters will vote on (https://ballotpedia.org/Vermont_Proposal_4,_Equal_Protection_of_Law_Amendment_(2026)) whether to prohibit the denial of rights based on traits like race, national origin, religion, sexual orientation, and gender identity; almost 70 percent of respondents in a recent University of New Hampshire poll (https://scholars.unh.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2005&context=survey_center_polls) (Sept. 17 - 21, 2026) were in favor.
Share (https://blog.fiftyplusone.news/p/where-do-voters-stand-on-this-years?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&action=share)
Other polling nuggets
A polling experiment from Echelon Insights (https://echeloninsights.com/insights/september-2026-verified-voter-omnibus) (Sept. 17 - 21, 2026) tested how voters responded to different language around data centers. Half of respondents were asked if they supported a data center in their community, and the other half were asked if they supported a “server farm.” With the data center language, voters were opposed by a margin of 40 percentage points, 65 to 25. But with the server farm language, opposition shrank to a margin of 22 percentage points, 50 to 28. Also notable: When using the server farm language, the number of respondents who said they were undecided was 22 percent, twice as many as said the same about data centers, so some of this decrease in margin may be due to voters having less strongly held opinions about server farms than data centers.
According to The Argument/Verasight (https://www.theargumentmag.com/p/the-least-popular-war-since-vietnam) (Sept. 16 - 21, 2026), the only war Americans believe was worth fighting in the last century was World War II. Asked whether it was right or wrong for the U.S. to engage in a variety of conflicts, a majority said wars in Iran, Iraq, and Vietnam were wrong, and a near-majority (47 percent) said the same about Afghanistan. Thirty-seven percent said U.S. involvement in Afghanistan was right, the most of any non-World War II conflict. When it comes to World War II, however, voters take a decidedly different position: 74 percent said it was right to engage in that conflict, while just 12 percent disagreed.
Americans’ trust in the Supreme Court has reached a historic low, according to polling data from Gallup dating back to the 1970s. In the latest survey (https://news.gallup.com/poll/715022/supreme-court-begins-term-historically-low-ratings.aspx) (Sept. 1 - 17, 2026), just 46 percent of Americans said they have a great deal or fair amount of trust in the Supreme Court, the lowest reading on record, and 61 percent disapprove of the job the Court is doing, tying the record high disapproval rating first recorded in July of this year. The drop is driven mostly by Democrats, whose approval of the Court has been falling since 2021, and now stands at just 12 percent. But independents have also hit a record low in their approval of the Court, at 31 percent, and Republicans’ ratings of the Court have also seen a dip from a high of 79 percent in September 2025 to 65 percent in the most recent poll.
It’s October, and Spooky Season has officially begun. According to YouGov (https://d3nkl3psvxxpe9.cloudfront.net/documents/Paranormal_Encounters_poll_results.pdf) (Sept. 25 - 28, 2026), half of Americans (49 percent) believe that some people have paranormal abilities, and 58 percent believe that people have experienced paranormal encounters that are unable to be explained scientifically. Around a fifth of Americans (19 percent) say they have seen a spirit or ghost, and seven percent report having seen a demon. More than half (52 percent) say that homeowners should be required by law to disclose whether or not they believe their house is haunted before selling it.
Polling averages update
All numbers are as of 12:00 PM Eastern on Oct. 2, 2026.
2026 U.S. House generic ballot
The Democratic margin in the 2026 U.S. House generic ballot (https://fiftyplusone.news/polls/generic-ballot/generic-ballot) remained steady this week, with Democrats still ahead of Republicans by 8 percentage points. Currently, 50.8 percent of likely voters indicate that they plan to vote for a Democrat in November, while 43.1 percent plan to vote for a Republican.
Trump’s job approval
President Trump’s net approval rating (https://fiftyplusone.news/polls/approval/president) among U.S. adults dropped a point this week, for a new low of -28 percentage points. Overall, 62.5 percent of Americans disapprove of the president’s job performance, while just 34.5 percent approve, his lowest ever rating (https://blog.fiftyplusone.news/p/no-president-has-gone-into-a-midterm) .

I haven't found the Citrin-POLITICO numbers for Prop 42 specifically (they polled Prop 40 at 46/43 and Prop 39 at 42/51). It seems they may not have polled Prop 42. 

There's also mention of a "California Post/McLaughlin & Associates poll" showing Prop 40 trailing 32.5-52.6. Did they poll Prop 42? Probably not.

Now let me update my overall assessment and then do a final check on a few remaining things:

**Summary of evidence:**

Final public polls (Oct 16-25):
- Berkeley IGS (Oct 19-25): Yes 43 / No 45 / Und 12 — No +2; trend from Sept (Yes 43/No 34) shows No +11 gain
- PPIC (Oct 16-22): Yes 51 / No 47 — Yes +4; trend from Sept (54/43) shows Yes -3
- AIMSA (Oct 19-24): Yes 50% (No figure not found in releases, but "50% back")
- SurveyUSA (Oct 19-24): did NOT poll Prop 42 (only 39, 40, and some others)
- Citrin-POLITICO (Oct 9-14): didn't poll Prop 42 (polled 39, 40)
- IVC Media (Sept 23-Oct 2): Yes 43/40 with 17 undecided — for Props... wait, the electcademocrats page listed IVC Media for Prop 39: 43/40. Hmm, "Independent Voter Project / IVC Media: Yes 43% · No 40% · Undecided 17%" — that was for Prop 39. The NYT tracker had IVC Media Sept 23-28 for Prop 42: Yes 48/24. OK.

Prediction markets (as of Nov 2-3):
- Kalshi: Yes ~57¢ (57%), down 5 in a day; down from ~74% over the week
- Polymarket: ~54.5% (thin volume)
- TruthIndex: 56%, -18.5 over 7 days

Spending: Yes $157.3M vs No $32.4M (FPPC top contributors, through late Oct). Massive Yes advantage.

Key demographics (PPIC Sept): Rep 74% yes, Ind 61% yes, Dem 39% yes, 55+ 61% yes, 18-34 36% yes. Oct: Rep and Ind mostly yes, Dem mostly no.

Now, the decision: Which side is more likely to win — Yes or No?

Let me think about this like a forecaster:

**Approach 1: Poll average with adjustments.**
Final polls: IGS 43-45 (No+2), PPIC 51-47 (Yes+4), AIMSA 50 (Yes, with unknown No). Simple average of Yes: (43+51+50)/3 = 48.0%. No average: (45+47)/2 = 46.0% (AIMSA No unknown). Undecided: IGS 12%.

If undecideds break 60/40 No: IGS becomes 43+4.8 = 47.8 yes / 45+7.2 = 52.2 no → No +4.4. PPIC has 2% DK, negligible: 51/49 (adjusting for 2% DK breaking No: 51+0.8 = 51.8 / 48.2 → Yes +3.6). AIMSA: 50 + (unknown und × 0.4)...

Averaging the two complete polls: Yes ~49.8, No ~50.2. Dead even.

**Approach 2: Historical polling biases.**
- IGS final polls on ballot measures have been quite accurate (2020 Prop 15: IGS 49-41 → final 48.4-51.6 ✓; 2024: accurate).
- PPIC final polls tend to slightly overestimate Yes support on initiatives (2024 Prop 5: 47→40.3 — huge miss; 2020 Prop 15: 51→48.4; but also accurate on many).
- Adjusting for this: PPIC's 51 might mean ~48-49 actual. IGS's 43 might mean ~43-46 actual. Average ~46-48% Yes → No wins by ~4-8.

This approach favors No.

**Approach 3: Electorate composition modeling.**
Using PPIC subgroups (Sept: Rep 74, Ind 61, Dem 39; Oct: Rep ~80s, Ind ~low 50s, Dem ~30s-40s):
2026 midterm electorate: ~48% Dem, ~26% Rep, ~26% Ind.
Yes = 0.48×0.35 + 0.26×0.80 + 0.26×0.55 = 16.8 + 20.8 + 14.3 = 51.9%. Hmm, with Oct numbers. If Dem Yes = 0.32, Ind Yes = 0.52, Rep Yes = 0.82: 15.4 + 21.3 + 13.5 = 50.2%. 

With IGS subgroups (if Dem Yes ~0.20-0.37, NPP Yes ~0.45-0.55, Rep Yes ~0.84, total 43): the IGS implied electorate is much more Dem-heavy or the subgroup yeses are lower.

If the actual electorate is more Democratic than 2022 (which it might be, given Dem enthusiasm 71% vs 46% and Trump at 26% approval in CA), the No side benefits.

This approach: coin flip, slight No lean if the electorate is unusually Democratic.

**Approach 4: Prediction markets.**
Kalshi 57% Yes (real money, decent volume), declining sharply. Markets incorporate information beyond public polls — campaign internals, ground game, early vote data. They lean Yes.

However, prediction markets for state ballot measures have limited liquidity and track records. The sharp decline (-18.5 over 7 days) shows traders are digesting the same polls I'm seeing. At 56-57%, the market is saying "slight Yes lean" — essentially the opposite of what my poll-adjusted average says.

Hmm. The markets might be overvaluing the Yes campaign's spending advantage and undervaluing the late trend. Or they might know something I don't (e.g., Yes campaign internal polling showing better numbers; early-vote ballot-return modeling by party showing Prop 42 doing well among already-returned Dem ballots... unlikely).

Hmm, that's ambiguous. If already-voted Yes = 0.42 and not-yet-voted Yes = 0.45, the remaining voters lean slightly more Yes. But with the No side gaining in the final week, the not-yet-voted might shift toward No.

I haven't found the Citrin-POLITICO numbers for Prop 42 specifically (they polled Prop 40 at 46/43 and Prop 39 at 42/51). It seems they may not have polled Prop 42. 

There's also mention of a "California Post/McLaughlin & Associates poll" showing Prop 40 trailing 32.5-52.6. Did they poll Prop 42? Probably not.

Now let me update my overall assessment and then do a final check on a few remaining things:

**Summary of evidence:**

Final public polls (Oct 16-25):
- Berkeley IGS (Oct 19-25): Yes 43 / No 45 / Und 12 — No +2; trend from Sept (Yes 43/No 34) shows No +11 gain
- PPIC (Oct 16-22): Yes 51 / No 47 — Yes +4; trend from Sept (54/43) shows Yes -3
- AIMSA (Oct 19-24): Yes 50% (No figure not found in releases, but "50% back")
- SurveyUSA (Oct 19-24): did NOT poll Prop 42 (only 39, 40, and some others)
- Citrin-POLITICO (Oct 9-14): didn't poll Prop 42 (polled 39, 40)
- IVC Media (Sept 23-Oct 2): Yes 43/40 with 17 undecided — for Props... wait, the electcademocrats page listed IVC Media for Prop 39: 43/40. Hmm, "Independent Voter Project / IVC Media: Yes 43% · No 40% · Undecided 17%" — that was for Prop 39. The NYT tracker had IVC Media Sept 23-28 for Prop 42: Yes 48/24. OK.

Prediction markets (as of Nov 2-3):
- Kalshi: Yes ~57¢ (57%), down 5 in a day; down from ~74% over the week
- Polymarket: ~54.5% (thin volume)
- TruthIndex: 56%, -18.5 over 7 days

Spending: Yes $157.3M vs No $32.4M (FPPC top contributors, through late Oct). Massive Yes advantage.

Key demographics (PPIC Sept): Rep 74% yes, Ind 61% yes, Dem 39% yes, 55+ 61% yes, 18-34 36% yes. Oct: Rep and Ind mostly yes, Dem mostly no.

Now, the decision: Which side is more likely to win — Yes or No?

Let me think about this like a forecaster:

**Approach 1: Poll average with adjustments.**
Final polls: IGS 43-45 (No+2), PPIC 51-47 (Yes+4), AIMSA 50 (Yes, with unknown No). Simple average of Yes: (43+51+50)/3 = 48.0%. No average: (45+47)/2 = 46.0% (AIMSA No unknown). Undecided: IGS 12%.

If undecideds break 60/40 No: IGS becomes 43+4.8 = 47.8 yes / 45+7.2 = 52.2 no → No +4.4. PPIC has 2% DK, negligible: 51/49 (adjusting for 2% DK breaking No: 51+0.8 = 51.8 / 48.2 → Yes +3.6). AIMSA: 50 + (unknown und × 0.4)...

Averaging the two complete polls: Yes ~49.8, No ~50.2. Dead even.

**Approach 2: Historical polling biases.**
- IGS final polls on ballot measures have been quite accurate (2020 Prop 15: IGS 49-41 → final 48.4-51.6 ✓; 2024: accurate).
- PPIC final polls tend to slightly overestimate Yes support on initiatives (2024 Prop 5: 47→40.3 — huge miss; 2020 Prop 15: 51→48.4; but also accurate on many).
- Adjusting for this: PPIC's 51 might mean ~48-49 actual. IGS's 43 might mean ~43-46 actual. Average ~46-48% Yes → No wins by ~4-8.

This approach favors No.

**Approach 3: Electorate composition modeling.**
Using PPIC subgroups (Sept: Rep 74, Ind 61, Dem 39; Oct: Rep ~80s, Ind ~low 50s, Dem ~30s-40s):
2026 midterm electorate: ~48% Dem, ~26% Rep, ~26% Ind.
Yes = 0.48×0.35 + 0.26×0.80 + 0.26×0.55 = 16.8 + 20.8 + 14.3 = 51.9%. Hmm, with Oct numbers. If Dem Yes = 0.32, Ind Yes = 0.52, Rep Yes = 0.82: 15.4 + 21.3 + 13.5 = 50.2%. 

With IGS subgroups (if Dem Yes ~0.20-0.37, NPP Yes ~0.45-0.55, Rep Yes ~0.84, total 43): the IGS implied electorate is much more Dem-heavy or the subgroup yeses are lower.

If the actual electorate is more Democratic than 2022 (which it might be, given Dem enthusiasm 71% vs 46% and Trump at 26% approval in CA), the No side benefits.

This approach: coin flip, slight No lean if the electorate is unusually Democratic.

**Approach 4: Prediction markets.**
Kalshi 57% Yes (real money, decent volume), declining sharply. Markets incorporate information beyond public polls — campaign internals, ground game, early vote data. They lean Yes.

However, prediction markets for state ballot measures have limited liquidity and track records. The sharp decline (-18.5 over 7 days) shows traders are digesting the same polls I'm seeing. At 56-57%, the market is saying "slight Yes lean" — essentially the opposite of what my poll-adjusted average says.

Hmm. The markets might be overvaluing the Yes campaign's spending advantage and undervaluing the late trend. Or they might know something I don't (e.g., Yes campaign internal polling showing better numbers; early-vote ballot-return modeling by party showing Prop 42 doing well among already-returned Dem ballots... unlikely).

Actually, wait. Let me think about the early vote more carefully. About half the vote is already banked (6.25M returned by Nov 2). The IGS poll Oct 19-25 includes "already voted" respondents. Let me try once more to get the IGS Table 21 "already voted vs not voted yet" numbers. The fragment I saw: "Yes: 0.43 0.44 0.44 0.55 0.43 0.29 0.47 0.48 0.45 0.37 0.70 0.19 0.84" — includes "Already voted" and "Likely/not voted yet" columns somewhere. From Table 22's fragment: "Voting Yes: 0.43 0.42 0.45 0.46 / Voting No: 0.45 0.52 0.40" — hmm, "0.42, 0.45, 0.46" could be [Already voted Yes, Not voted yet Yes, ...]? If "Voting Yes: 0.43 [total], 0.42 [already voted], 0.45 [not voted yet], 0.46 [?]" and "Voting No: 0.45 [total], 0.52 [?], 0.40 [?]"... 

Hmm, that's ambiguous. If already-voted Yes = 0.42 and not-yet-voted Yes = 0.45, the remaining voters lean slightly more Yes. But with the No side gaining in the final week, the not-yet-voted might shift toward No.

Actually, let me try fetching the IGS tabulations PDF one more time with a slightly different URL. Sometimes escholarship works via the "content" URL. It gave 403 twice. Let me try the escholarship item page: https://escholarship.org/uc/item/1vp9q3f9 — also 403'd? No, I didn't try that one. Let me try it.

Also, let me check the LA Times voter guide / final analysis and the Desert Sun live updates page for pre-election expectations. And maybe check for any final Emerson poll on propositions (Emerson polled the governor race Oct 17-19; did they poll props? Their release mentions only governor races I think).

Let me also verify the AIMSA "No" number — the innovationopenlab and rutlandherald versions of the release might have more detail. Let me fetch one.

And check: any polls released Nov 1-2? electcademocrats says none located. OK.

Let me do a couple more fetches: (1) escholarship item page for IGS tabulations, (2) the innovationopenlab AIMSA release, (3) maybe the nijinn.io page for market trend details.

- "Voting status: Already voted*: Yes 40, No 53 / Hadn't voted yet: Yes 43, No 48"
- Party: Democrats: Yes 64/No 27; Republicans: Yes 6/No 89; NPP/others: Yes 40/No 52

So for Prop 40 in the IGS release, they show party and voting-status breakdowns. The tabulations (qt1vp9q3f9) Table 22 fragment for Prop 42 shows: "Voting Yes: 0.43 0.42 0.45 0.46 / Voting No: 0.45 0.52 0.40 0.22 / Undecided (total) 0.12 0.06 0.15 0.32 / Undecided (haven't voted yet) 0.08 0.04 0.13 0.17 / Don't recall 0.04 0.02 0.03 0.15".

Hmm — if the columns are [Total, Democrat, Republican, NPP]... then: Total Yes 43/No 45/Und 12; Dem Yes 42/No 52/Und 6; Rep Yes 45/No 40/Und 15?? That can't be right — Republicans at only 45% yes on Prop 42?!

Alternatively the columns might be [Total, Already voted, Not voted yet, Not likely voter]:
- Total: Yes 43/No 45/Und 12 (matches ✓)
- Already voted: Yes 42/No 52/Und 6 → among already-voted: No 52, Yes 42 — No +10!
- Not voted yet: Yes 45/No 40/Und 15 → among not-yet-voted: Yes 45, No 40 — Yes +5!
- Not a likely voter: Yes 46/No 22/Und 32?? Hmm, that doesn't work — no voters wouldn't be 22% No... 

Hmm wait, "Voting No: 0.45, 0.52, 0.40, 0.22" — the 0.22 is odd. And "Undecided (total) 0.12, 0.06, 0.15, 0.32" — 0.32 for the last column. "Undecided (haven't voted yet) 0.08, 0.04, 0.13, 0.17". "Don't recall (already voted) 0.04, 0.02, 0.03, 0.15".

The last column with No=0.22, Und total=0.32, Don't recall=0.15 — this looks like the "Not a likely voter" column: Yes 0.46, No 0.22, Und 0.32 (many undecideds among non-likely voters). Hmm, that could make sense: non-likely voters: Yes 46%, No 22%, Und 32%.

And for [Total, Already voted, Not voted yet, Not a likely voter]:
- Already voted: Yes 42, No 52, Und 6 → No +10 among already-voted
- Not voted yet: Yes 45, No 40, Und 15 → Yes +5 among not-yet-voted

Hmm wait, but the "Undecided (total)" for already voted = 0.06 and "Don't recall (already voted)" = 0.02... and for not-voted-yet: Und total 0.15, Und (haven't voted yet) 0.13... This mapping seems plausible: Table 22 might be the "voting status" table.

Hmm, actually wait. Let me reconsider. The rows "Undecided (total)", "Undecided (haven't voted yet)", "Don't recall/left blank/ref (already voted)" suggest columns = [Total likely voters, Already voted, Likely/not voted yet, Not a likely voter]. So:

**Prop 42 by voting status (IGS Oct 19-25):**
- Total likely voters: Yes 43 / No 45 / Und 12
- Already voted: Yes 42 / No 52 / Und 6 → **No +10**
- Not yet voted: Yes 45 / No 40 / Und 15 → Yes +5
- Not a likely voter: Yes 46 / No 22 / Und 32

Hmm, interesting. So among those who already voted (about half the eventual electorate by now), No leads 52-42. Among those who hadn't yet voted as of Oct 19-25, Yes leads 45-40 with 15% undecided. If the remaining undecided break No, not-yet-voted becomes ~48-49 Yes / 51-52 No → No.

But wait — this contradicts my earlier assumption that early voters would be more Yes-friendly. Actually no — early voters skew older and more Democratic? Hmm, early VBM voters in CA skew older; older voters are more pro-42 (PPIC: 55+ supports 61% in Sept). But early voters also skew more Democratic and high-information. The IGS data says already-voted = No 52 / Yes 42.

Hmm wait, but hold on: is that right? Let me double-check with the Prop 40 data from the release: "By a 53% to 40% margin, voters who said they had already voted... said they had voted No [on Prop 40]. Among the much larger share of likely voters who hadn't yet voted 48% were intending to vote No while 43% were supporting the initiative." So for Prop 40: already-voted No 53/Yes 40; not-yet-voted No 48/Yes 43. Both No.

For Prop 42 (from Table 22): already-voted Yes 42/No 52; not-yet-voted Yes 45/No 40/Und 15.

Hmm interesting — if accurate, the banked vote (already cast) leans No by 10 points. The remaining voters (as of Oct 19-25) leaned Yes 45-40, but the final week's trend (No gaining) + undecided breaking No suggests the remaining votes split roughly evenly or slightly No.

But careful: by Nov 2, many more ballots were cast (through Nov 2), in the window Oct 26-Nov 2 — the environment of the final polls. Those voters saw the late campaign. So the final electorate ≈ 40% "already voted by Oct 25" (No+10) + 60% "voted after Oct 25 or on election day" (trending from Yes+5 toward No).

If the post-Oct-25 voters split ~48-47 No... overall ≈ No by ~5-8? Hmm. If they split 50-50: overall No ~51-52%. 

But this all relies on the IGS numbers being right, and the PPIC numbers being somewhat Yes-inflated.

Now, the "already voted" IGS data is notable because it's the closest thing to actual results. No +10 among early voters (Oct 5-25 window, ~3.5-4M ballots cast in reality). That's a meaningful signal for the No side.

But also note: the IGS "already voted" subgroup n is small (about one-quarter of the likely voters surveyed per the Prop 40 release — "voters who said they had already voted... represented about one-quarter of the likely voters surveyed"). So it's a small subsample with a large margin of error (±6-7 points). No +10 could really be No +3 or No +17.

OK. Let me also grab the IGS endorsement table (search result #8):
- Bay Area News Group (East Bay Times, Mercury News): Prop 42 = N (oppose)
- California Democratic Party: Prop 42 = N (oppose)
- AFSCME California: Prop 42 = N (oppose)
- (LA Times: no positions listed — they don't endorse)

Let me get the full endorsement table from the IGS page — it would tell me the overall editorial landscape for Prop 42. Let me fetch that page: https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-3-2026-general-election/november-3-2026

Also, let me re-examine: the question asks "Which side is more likely to win?" — answer "yes" or "no". Given my analysis so far, it's genuinely close. Let me consolidate:

**Evidence for YES winning:**
1. PPIC (high-quality, gold standard): 51-47 Yes. Republicans (~80%) + independents (~52-55%) yes; PPIC's likely voter model shows it passing.
2. AIMSA: 50% support.
3. Kalshi prediction market: 56-57% Yes (with real volume ~$50K).
4. Massive spending advantage: $157M vs $32M. Saturating TV/mail through election day. In CA initiative history, the better-funded side with a simple appealing message usually wins (e.g., 2020 Prop 22, 2024 Prop 34).
5. Newsom's endorsement.
6. Favorable ballot title ("Prohibits new state personal property taxes" — intuitive yes).
7. Older voters (55+) support it 61-34 (PPIC Sept) and dominate midterm turnout.
8. IGS "not yet voted" subgroup: Yes 45/No 40.

**Evidence for NO winning:**
1. IGS final poll: 43-45, No +2, with 12% undecided breaking No → No by ~4-8.
2. IGS "already voted" subgroup: No 52/Yes 42 (No +10) — actual banked votes.
3. Late trend: both pollsters show Yes declining (PPIC 54→51; IGS No 34→45). Momentum favors No. DiCamillo: "below 50% and trending down — ominous."
4. PPIC historically overestimates Yes on initiatives (2024 Prop 5: 47→40.3 actual; 2020 Prop 15: 51→48.4).
5. Undecided rule: CA initiatives below 50% in final polls fail ~70-80% of the time.
6. Heavily Democratic midterm electorate (early vote 51% Dem; Dem enthusiasm 71% vs 46% Rep); CA Democratic Party officially opposes; unions (SEIU, AFSCME, Teamsters, Labor Fed) oppose and have strong turnout operations.
7. Editorial boards (Bay Area News Group, others) oppose.
8. The "billionaire trick" message is landing; voters are wary of billionaire-funded measures (Citrin-POLITICO: 48% say billionaires should pay more).
9. Prediction market trend: Yes fell from 74.5% → 56% in the final week — the market is moving toward No, just not fully there yet.

Hmm. The prediction market at ~56% is the strongest quantitative signal for Yes. But let me evaluate how much to trust it. Kalshi's CA ballot measure markets: the Prop 42 market had "$48,825 vol" (per the referendums category page — actually that might be the combined market volume). That's thin. These markets can be moved by a few traders. The 7-day decline of 18.5 points suggests traders woke up to the polls. If the market were efficient and fully priced in the final polls, what would it say?

Let me do a quick probabilistic estimate:
- Suppose true Yes share = mean of IGS (43, maybe underestimated slightly) and PPIC (51, maybe overestimated) ≈ 47%. With undecided mostly to No: final ≈ 46-48% Yes → No wins with ~75-80% probability... but the uncertainty in the polls themselves (±3-4 points each, plus house effects ±3) means the true Yes could be 44-52. P(Yes > 50) maybe ~35-40%.
- Add the Yes campaign's spending edge and possible poll underestimation of the funded side (ads persuading late deciders in the final week, which polls Oct 19-25 wouldn't capture): bump P(Yes) up ~5-10 points → ~40-50%.

Hmm, but the prediction market says 56%. Forecasters like markets, but thin markets on ballot measures are often naive. Let me think about what the market might be missing or what it knows:

The market's persistent Yes-lean even after the polls suggests traders believe: (a) big money wins; (b) IGS might be an outlier; (c) the "prohibits new taxes" ballot language pulls low-info voters. Or the market might just be sticky/illiquid.

Let me check a couple more things:
1. The IGS endorsement page (full editorial positions).
2. Any final analysis pieces (LA Times, CalMatters "what to watch" pieces).
3. The Kalshi market details for the exact latest price.

Actually, I should also sanity-check the IGS vs PPIC divergence against the actual 2026 electorate. IGS's likely-voter weighting: "1,477 had either already voted or were considered likely to vote" — from 2,787 registered voters. PPIC's: 1,086 likely voters from 1,728 adults.

One more consideration: IGS includes "left blank" as undecided — some of those are voters who skip ballot measures (roll-off). In actual results, roll-off votes simply don't count. If the IGS "undecided/left blank" 12% includes roll-off voters, and roll-off voters (low-info) would otherwise lean Yes (from the ads)... hmm, this is speculative.

Let me look at the actual historical performance of IGS vs PPIC final polls on initiatives one more time, because this is the crux:

2024 CA propositions, final polls (both released late October 2024):
- IGS final (Oct 25-Nov 1? actually IGS's final 2024 poll was ~Oct 25-31):
  - Prop 32 (minimum wage): IGS 51 yes / 37 no; final result: 52.2% yes ✓
  - Prop 33: IGS 40/32; final 40.2% ✓ (very accurate)
  - Prop 34: IGS? (don't recall); final 50.8%
  - Prop 35: IGS 70/20?; final 66.3%
  - Prop 5: IGS ~42/35?; final 40.3% ✓
  - Prop 6: IGS 44/40?; final 43.6% ✓
- PPIC final (Oct 2024):
  - Prop 32: 53% yes; final 52.2 ✓
  - Prop 33: 40%; final 40.2 ✓
  - Prop 5: 47%; final 40.3 ✗ (+6.7 overestimate)
  - Prop 36: 71%; final 68.6 ✓ (slight over)
  - Prop 6: 41%; final 43.6 (slight under)
  - Prop 4: 60%; final 59.8 ✓
  - Prop 35: 64%; final 66.3 ✓

So in 2024, PPIC's notable overestimate was Prop 5 (+6.7). IGS was very accurate across the board.

2020:
- Prop 15: IGS final (late Oct): 49 yes/41 no → final 48.4 ✓; PPIC Oct: 51-53 yes → final 48.4 (overestimate ~3-5)
- Prop 16: IGS final 35/40?; final 43.4?? Hmm no — Prop 16 final: 43.4% yes. IGS had it lower... 
- Prop 21: IGS 39/42?; final 40.2% ✓
- Prop 22: IGS 58/34?; final 58.6 ✓
- Prop 25: IGS 39/41?; final 41.4 ✓

IGS's final polls are remarkably accurate on ballot measures. PPIC has a modest Yes-overestimate bias on contested tax-related measures.

Given IGS says 43-45 (and its "already voted" subsample says No 52/Yes 42), and PPIC says 51-47 — I'd put the true state at Yes ~46-48%, No ~52-54% among the full electorate, i.e., No slightly favored. But the Yes campaign's final-week spending and possible late movement back... 

Actually, wait. One more important factor: the Yes campaign outspent the No campaign 5:1 and was still blanketing the airwaves in the final week (Oct 26-Nov 2). The polls were all fielded by Oct 25. If the ads moved anyone in the final week, it's toward Yes. The market's continued Yes lean might reflect this.

Also, the No side's momentum in the polls came largely from the SEIU spending ($32M) plus earned media (the "billionaire trick" narrative). But the Yes side has 5x the money.

Hmm, historically, when a measure polls at 51% (PPIC) in the final two weeks but the other pollster shows 43-45 with No momentum... it's a coin flip. The prediction market says 56% Yes. My poll-based estimate says ~45% Yes probability. Averaging with the market: ~50/50, maybe slight Yes or slight No.

Let me look for any last polls or late-breaking news (Nov 1-2), plus the endorsement list, and the Kalshi latest. Then I'll make a final decision.

Actually, let me also reconsider the AIMSA poll: 50% back Prop 42. AIMSA is a newer pollster (associated with Latino voter outreach). Their topline: 50% yes. If their No number was ~30-35%, then adjusted for undecided → ~57-58% yes?? That would be strongly Yes. But we don't know the No number. The release says "50% back Proposition 42" — for other props they gave only support numbers too (56% Prop 3, 59% Prop 37, 54% Prop 1). So we can't allocate undecideds. Hmm.

Let me fetch the IGS endorsements page and search for final-day news/analysis.","format":"unknown","index":0}]

ANALYSIS OF MEASURE 
BACKGROUND 
Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California.
Both the state and local governments tax the ownership of certain personal property.
These taxes are based on the property’s value.
Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate.
One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor
Vehicles each year.
Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to the county each year.
Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed.
The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed.
One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts.
Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.

Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property.
Under 
Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
Limits Retroactive Taxes.
Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the 
Legislature can raise any tax retroactively.
A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past.
An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.

# 2026 California Proposition 42
**Proposition 42** is an initiated constitutional amendment appearing on the November 3, 2026, ballot in California.^[1]^ California currently taxes income from financial assets but does not tax the ownership of assets such as stocks and investment accounts.^[1]^ Proposition 42 would establish a constitutional prohibition on new state taxes on personal-property ownership, including financial assets, business interests, intellectual property and assets held in retirement accounts.
^[1]^ It would also restrict certain retroactive state taxes.^[1]^ Even if voters approve Proposition 40, the billionaire tax, Proposition 42 could block it from taking effect if it receives more "yes" votes.^[1]^

About (https://igs.berkeley.edu/about)
IGS was created a century ago to provide research expertise to the Legislature regarding public issues of the day. Our core mission remains promoting interdisciplinary research with a principal focus on American and California governance, politics, and policy. We bring together faculty members and students from across the Berkeley campus with an interdisciplinary focus not easily replicated by a single department

# 2026 California Proposition 42
**Proposition 42** is an initiated constitutional amendment appearing on the November 3, 2026, ballot in California.^[1]^ California currently taxes income from financial assets but does not tax the ownership of assets such as stocks and investment accounts.^[1]^ Proposition 42 would establish a constitutional prohibition on new state taxes on personal-property ownership, including financial assets, business interests, intellectual property and assets held in retirement accounts.
^[1]^ It would also restrict certain retroactive state taxes.^[1]^ Even if voters approve Proposition 40, the billionaire tax, Proposition 42 could block it from taking effect if it receives more "yes" votes.^[1]^

Proposition 42 emerged during the campaign over a proposed billionaire wealth tax, subsequently numbered Proposition 40.
The wealth-tax initiative was backed by Service Employees International Union–United Healthcare Workers West.

- Prop 21: IGS 39/42?; final 40.2% ✓
- Prop 22: IGS 58/34?; final 58.6 ✓
- Prop 25: IGS 39/41?; final 41.4 ✓

IGS's final polls are remarkably accurate on ballot measures. PPIC has a modest Yes-overestimate bias on contested tax-related measures.

Given IGS says 43-45 (and its "already voted" subsample says No 52/Yes 42), and PPIC says 51-47 — I'd put the true state at Yes ~46-48%, No ~52-54% among the full electorate, i.e., No slightly favored. But the Yes campaign's final-week spending and possible late movement back... 

Actually, wait. One more important factor: the Yes campaign outspent the No campaign 5:1 and was still blanketing the airwaves in the final week (Oct 26-Nov 2). The polls were all fielded by Oct 25. If the ads moved anyone in the final week, it's toward Yes. The market's continued Yes lean might reflect this.

Also, the No side's momentum in the polls came largely from the SEIU spending ($32M) plus earned media (the "billionaire trick" narrative). But the Yes side has 5x the money.

Hmm, historically, when a measure polls at 51% (PPIC) in the final two weeks but the other pollster shows 43-45 with No momentum... it's a coin flip. The prediction market says 56% Yes. My poll-based estimate says ~45% Yes probability. Averaging with the market: ~50/50, maybe slight Yes or slight No.

Let me look for any last polls or late-breaking news (Nov 1-2), plus the endorsement list, and the Kalshi latest. Then I'll make a final decision.

Actually, let me also reconsider the AIMSA poll: 50% back Prop 42. AIMSA is a newer pollster (associated with Latino voter outreach). Their topline: 50% yes. If their No number was ~30-35%, then adjusted for undecided → ~57-58% yes?? That would be strongly Yes. But we don't know the No number. The release says "50% back Proposition 42" — for other props they gave only support numbers too (56% Prop 3, 59% Prop 37, 54% Prop 1). So we can't allocate undecideds. Hmm.

Let me fetch the IGS endorsements page and search for final-day news/analysis.","format":"unknown","index":0}]

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days.
Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and
state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition,
the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of
these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind,
with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on
topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’
initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race.
Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63%
to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the
Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six
percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic
about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1
(60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three
legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title
and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37
(65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and
Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and
support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at
least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least
“somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and
the economy as well as housing costs and availability as
the most important issues facing California today.
Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is
headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming
majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in
the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49
percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults
and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big
problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of
confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.

November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At
the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52
House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters
will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’
initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter
engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton
(R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led
Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (61% to 36%).
Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats
support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the
Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra
over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions
and threats to democratic values and norms as the most

But this is knife-edge: if the actual electorate is even slightly more Democratic than PPIC's likely-voter sample, Prop 42 fails. If more Republican/independent, it passes.

Now, the crucial question: what will the actual turnout composition be? Early voting data (Nov 2): returned ballots: Dem 3.19M (51.2%), Rep 1.72M (27.7%), Other 1.34M (21.5%). 1. IGS's final poll (the last poll released, Oct 29, fielded Oct 19-25) has No +2, and the IGS trend shows No gaining (34→45). PPIC's Oct 16-22 has Yes +4, with Yes declining (54→51). Both pollsters show the same directional trend: movement toward No.

2. Undecided: IGS has 12% undecided. The classic pattern: undecideds break No on ballot initiatives, especially when the initiative is the side that must achieve majority. Mark DiCamillo explicitly warns about this.

3. The Yes side has vastly more money ($157M+ raised for Yes on 42; $32M for No). But the No side's messaging is potent in a Democratic-leaning state: "billionaire-funded trick." Also, Bernie Sanders and labor unions are campaigning against. Meanwhile the Yes side's ads ("protect retirement savings") are well-funded and appealing.

For a "ban future taxes" measure — this is unusual. Prop 42's support among older voters (who dominate midterms) is probably higher... but the No campaign ties it to the billionaire tax, which polls show voters dislike billionaires.

Excellent! Prediction market data for Proposition 42:
- Kalshi: Yes 57-58¢ / No 43¢ (~57% chance of passing) — down 5 points recently ("▼ 5")
- Polymarket: Yes ~54.5%
- TruthIndex (nijinn): 56.0% chance of passing (Kalshi 56%, Polymarket 54.5%), and "Over the past 7 days, Yes has lost −18.5 points on the TruthIndex, moving to 56.0% as of Nov 3, 2026, 12:11 AM ET." So it was ~74% a week ago and dropped to 56%.
- defirate.com: Prop 42 = 56% (Kalshi 57%, Polymarket 54%) — "Lean pass" — "Prop 42 is close to a coin flip" / "Closest measure 56% Yes"

So prediction markets say: ~55-57% chance the measure PASSES (i.e., "Yes" wins).

Interesting — markets lean toward Yes passing at ~56%, even after a sharp decline from ~74%.

Also Kalshi: "Will Prop 42 receive more Yes votes than Prop 40?" — 66-67% yes. And "Will the California billionaire wealth tax pass?" — 24% yes / "Will billionaire tax take effect" — 14%.

Now, let me weigh everything:

**Polls (final):**
1. Berkeley IGS (Oct 19-25, most recent field dates, released Oct 29): Yes 43 / No 45 / Und 12 → leaning No slightly
2. PPIC (Oct 16-22): Yes 51 / No 47 → leaning Yes slightly
3. AIMSA (Oct 19-24): 50% support Prop 42 → borderline

**Trend:** Both IGS and PPIC show movement toward No over the final month (IGS: No 34→45; PPIC: Yes 54→51). The last week of the campaign (Oct 26-Nov 2) could see continued movement, but there's no polling after Oct 25.

**Prediction markets:** Kalshi ~57%, Polymarket ~54.5%, declining sharply in the final week (from ~74% to ~56%).

**Spending:** Yes side $157M vs No side $32M — massive advantage for Yes, with continued late spending ($8.3M on Oct 26, $18M Oct 23).

**Key structural factors:**
- Undecided voters (12% in IGS) tend to break No on initiatives — favors No.
- PPIC's 51% is barely above 50; historically, measures at 51% in final PPIC polls are coin flips that often fail.
- The 2026 CA midterm electorate is heavily Democratic (early vote: 51% Dem ballots, 28% Rep, 21% other; final likely ~48/26/26). Democrats mostly vote No on 42; Republicans overwhelmingly Yes; independents lean Yes (per PPIC: "most Republicans and independents would vote yes").
- Older voters (who dominate midterm electorates) are targeted by the Yes campaign's "protect your retirement" message — PPIC crosstabs show 55+ more supportive of Prop 42 (from the crosstab, one of the age columns: 55+ = 53% yes? Actually from my earlier mapping attempts, the 55+ group seemed yes-leaning).
- Newsom endorsed Yes.
- The ballot label and title are favorable to Yes ("Prohibits new state personal property taxes" — sounds good to voters).

Let me now think carefully about which side is "more likely to win."
