2026 California Prop 42 guide: "Retirement savings" measure would ban new state taxes on what Californians own
Proposition 42 bars new state taxes on owning pensions, 401(k)s, stocks, business stakes and other personal property, and most retroactive taxes. It could cancel Prop 40's billionaire tax, and its $112.8 million campaign is the ballot's largest.
by
Pat Sharyon | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/pat/)
Updated
October 19, 2026
Link copied!
Copy failed!
California Proposition 42 is asking voters to ban new state taxes on retirement savings and other personal property.
Proposition 42 would amend the California Constitution to bar any new state tax on owning personal property, a category its text defines to include pensions, 401(k)s, IRAs, mutual funds, stocks, business interests, digital assets and intellectual property. It would also bar new state taxes that reach back in time, including any tax "imposed on a taxpayer based upon their residency status on a date prior to the effective date of the tax." Both rules cover taxes enacted on or after January 1, 2026. That reaches Proposition 40 (https://californiatoday.com/news/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-billionaire-tax/), the one-time "billionaire tax" on the same ballot, and the Voter Information Guide warns that if Prop 42 receives more yes votes, Prop 40 "could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters."
California Proposition 42 is drawing $112.8 million from its top contributors, the most of any committee on the November ballot in the FPPC's October 14, 2026 update. Prop 42 is an initiative constitutional amendment (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/) titled the Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act of 2026. Its campaign has $112.8 million from its top contributors, more than any other committee on the ballot, almost all of it from Building a Better California, whose top donors are Google co-founder Sergey Brin and L. John Doerr III. Governor Gavin Newsom endorsed it on October 9. PPIC's September survey found 54% of likely voters in favor and 43% opposed. It is one of 14 measures in our guide to every November proposition (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/), and our billionaire tax explainer (https://californiatoday.com/news/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-billionaire-tax/) covers how Props 40, 41 and 42 interact. This guide covers what Prop 42 would ban, what it would leave alone and who is behind it.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) Proposition 42 bans new state taxes on owning retirement accounts, stocks and other personal property:
The core of the measure's text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is one sentence. No state law or constitutional provision enacted on or after January 1, 2026 "may enact, create, impose, or authorize collection of a tax on the ownership or control of retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings, whether held directly or indirectly." The definition of that phrase is broad. It covers pensions, retirement accounts and mutual funds, and "all personal property, whether tangible or intangible," including financial assets, investment accounts, business interests, digital assets, intellectual property and personal belongings.
It does not repeal anything. Any tax "in effect, imposed, and first collected on or before December 31, 2025" is untouched, and the measure says it does not "alter or affect the taxation of real property." The Legislative Analyst's Office (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42.pdf) notes that California already taxes some personal property, such as the vehicle license fee drivers pay each year and the property tax on business equipment. It also notes that while the state taxes the income people earn from financial assets, "there is no tax for simply owning those assets." Prop 42 would keep it that way.
Taxes Proposition 42 would leave alone and taxes it would bar:
Tax Under Proposition 42
Vehicle license fee and property tax on business equipment Unchanged. Both were “in effect, imposed, and first collected” before December 31, 2025, which the measure protects
Property tax on homes and land Unchanged. The measure says it does not “alter or affect the taxation of real property”
Income tax on wages, interest, dividends and capital gains Unchanged. Proposition 42 bars taxes on the “ownership or control” of assets, not on income they produce or gains when they are sold
A new state tax on the value of stocks, funds, business stakes, crypto or intellectual property Barred if enacted on or after January 1, 2026
A new state tax on the value of pensions, 401(k)s, 403(b)s or IRAs Barred if enacted on or after January 1, 2026
A tax keyed to where someone lived on a date before the tax took effect Barred
A retroactive tax passed by the Legislature Barred, except for a look-back of 365 days or less during a declared disaster or fiscal emergency, with the money limited to that emergency
A retroactive tax passed by initiative Barred, with no emergency exception

Most of the latest coverage surrounding polling has focused on the battle for control of Congress (https://fiftyplusone.news/forecast/house) , or President Trump’s historically low approval numbers (https://fiftyplusone.news/polls/approval/president) . But there’s far more on the ballot this November than just federal races, including controversial ballot measures surrounding the electoral process, taxes, and transgender rights. These measures can have far-reaching impacts, even for residents of other states (https://digital-release.nbc4i.com/news/local-news/columbus/ohio-sees-increase-in-those-traveling-from-out-of-state-for-an-abortion/) . We don’t have public polling for every measure that will be on voters’ ballots, but we have seen a good amount for some of the most potentially consequential measures of the year. For this week’s Trendline, we’ll be breaking down the latest polling on ballot measures to see which ones stand a chance at passing and how they might impact Americans across the country.
Elections
Multiple states are voting on measures affecting elections and voting in their states, some with the potential to dramatically alter how their residents pick their elected representatives.
In Missouri, Proposition A (https://ballotpedia.org/Missouri_Proposition_A,_Congressional_Map_Referendum_(2026)) gives voters the choice of whether or not to keep a newly passed Republican gerrymander that would almost certainly help the GOP pick up a seat in Congress. (That map was paused by the state Supreme Court last month to let voters weigh in first.) We’ve only seen one recent public poll for the measure, and Missourians appear to be pretty evenly split; in a Saint Louis University/YouGov poll (https://www.slu.edu/research/research-institute/big-ideas/slu-poll/-pdf/slu-poll-august-2026-topline-results.pdf) (Aug. 13 - 24, 2026), 35 percent of likely voters said they would vote to keep the new gerrymander, while 32 percent would reject it, and 33 percent weren’t sure.
Another voting-related ballot measure (https://ballotpedia.org/Missouri_Amendment_6,_Initiative_and_Referendum_Powers_and_Legislative_Change_Requirements_Amendment_(2026)) in Missouri would make it harder for the state legislature to weaken or change the initiative and referendum process, after state lawmakers nullified paid sick leave protections (https://www.komu.com/news/state/paid-sick-leave-requirement-to-end-this-week-employers-are-going-have-a-choice-again/article_beb8c19a-92af-4984-a24d-00faa69ede77.html) voters had passed via initiative. Voters seemed more friendly to this measure, with 48 percent supporting it in the SLU/YouGov poll and 21 percent opposing. Another 32 percent said they weren’t sure.
Maryland also has a redistricting-related measure on the ballot this year; Question 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/Maryland_Question_3,_Provide_That_Nothing_in_State_Constitution_Establishes_Criteria_for_Congressional_Redistricting_Amendment_(2026)) would clarify that state constitutional redistricting requirements apply only to state legislative districts and not congressional ones. Democrats in the state legislature put this measure to voters in the hopes of passing a new gerrymander of their own next year. The two public polls we have on the measure paint a starkly different picture — a Hart Research poll (https://www.thebanner.com/politics-power/state-government/redistricting-ballot-question-poll-GLJQK4NSD5GMDEPNOEPEPY2GKM/) (Sept. 8 - 10, 2026) sponsored by Fight Back MD (which supports the measure) found the measure up slightly, with 40 percent of respondents in favor, 35 percent opposed, and 25 percent unsure. But a Lincoln Park Strategies/Ragnar Research Partners poll (https://www.thebanner.com/politics-power/state-government/maryland-redistricting-poll-3H44RTFBYBA65FQXN2IPYRIH74/) (Sept. 10 - 13, 2026) for Protect Maryland Votes (which opposes the measure) showed the question underwater by double digits, with just 28 percent of Marylanders supporting the measure, 41 percent opposed, and 31 percent unsure.
In California, voters will decide whether to amend the state’s recall election process (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_5,_Eliminate_State_Officer_Recall_Successor_Elections_Amendment_(2026)) to leave offices vacant until a special election can be held to replace a recalled politician, rather than the current system of electing a replacement at the time of the recall. A PPIC poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from last month (Sept. 4 - 10, 2026) showed voters quite opposed to this change, with just 35 percent supporting the measure and 59 percent opposed. Only 5 percent said they weren’t sure.
And in Massachusetts, Bay Staters will vote on whether to overhaul their primary process (https://ballotpedia.org/Massachusetts_Question_3,_Top-Two_Primary_Elections_Initiative_(2026)) and create a single primary system where the top two candidates regardless of party move on to the general election, the same system used in California and Washington. Three recent polls of the question show it passing with varying degrees of strength — a University of Massachusetts Amherst/YouGov poll (https://www.umass.edu/poll/sites/default/files/2026-08/GOPPrimaryStateoftheStateToplinesAug2026MassPoll.pdf?1790267811) (Aug. 5 - 12, 2026) had the measure ahead by 19 points, with 51 percent supporting and 32 opposed to the overhaul. Two September polls also showed the measure ahead, but by a smaller margin. A MassInc/CommonWealth Beacon poll (https://commonwealthbeacon.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Topline-2026-09-CWB-Ballot-Questions-TUES-RELEASE.pdf) (Sept. 14 - 22, 2026) showed 43 percent of respondents in favor of the measure and 36 percent opposed. And in a University of New Hampshire poll (https://scholars.unh.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2007&context=survey_center_polls) (Sept. 17 - 21, 2026), 41 percent of respondents were supportive, while 39 percent were opposed.
Alaska will also hold ( another (https://alaskabeacon.com/2026/07/29/alaskans-to-vote-on-ballot-measure-that-would-overhaul-state-election-system/) ) vote on whether to repeal the state’s top-four ranked-choice primary system (https://ballotpedia.org/Alaska_Ballot_Measure_2,_Repeal_Top-Four_Ranked-Choice_Voting_Initiative_(2026)) and return to a traditional party primary system. We’ve only seen one public poll on the topic so far: a Fabrizio Ward/Impact Research poll (https://www.aarp.org/content/dam/aarp/research/topics/voter-opinion-research/politics/2026-midterm-election-poll-alaska-annotated-questionnaire.doi.10.26419-2fres.01065.017.pdf) for AARP (Sept. 8 - 11, 2026) showed voters closely split just like they were in 2024 (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2024/11/05/us/elections/results-alaska-measure-2-repeal-ranked-choice-voting.html) , with 44 percent in favor of repealing ranked-choice voting and 47 percent opposed.
Taxes
Lots of states will also have voters weigh on tax proposals, some of which have caused quite a stir — California’s Proposition 40 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_40,_One-Time_Wealth_Tax_for_State-Funded_Healthcare,_Education,_and_Food_Assistance_Programs_Initiative_(2026)) chief among them. Also referred to as the “billionaire tax,” the measure would levy a one-time 5 percent tax on individuals with over $1 billion in assets to help fund state programs, including health care and food assistance. The measure has drawn fierce opposition from prominent figures like Gov. Gavin Newsom (https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/newsom-urges-a-national-billionaires-tax-while-fighting-one-in-california) , as well as from the state’s wealthiest residents, who managed to get opposing measures on the same ballot. Propositions 41 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_41,_Prohibit_Excluding_New_State_Taxes_from_Spending_Limit_and_Require_Special_Tax_Audits_Initiative_(2026)) and 42 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_42,_Prohibit_New_Taxes_on_Retirement_Holdings,_Personal_Assets,_and_Savings_and_Limit_Retroactive_Taxes_Initiative_(2026)) would nullify Proposition 40 if either one of them gets a higher share of the vote than 40.
These propositions are by far the ballot measures for which we’ve seen the most public polling this cycle. In an average of polls conducted in August and September, just over 48 percent of respondents said they support Proposition 40, while an average of 41 percent were opposed. Propositions 41 and 42 received a bit less support on average from Californians, but it’ll still be a nail-biter; Proposition 42 in particular is right on the heels of Proposition 40.
In Washington, voters will be asked whether to (https://ballotpedia.org/Washington_Repeal_Tax_on_Household_Income_Over_$1_Million_and_Prohibit_State_and_Local_Taxes_on_Income_Initiative_(2026)) repeal (https://ballotpedia.org/Washington_Repeal_Tax_on_Household_Income_Over_$1_Million_and_Prohibit_State_and_Local_Taxes_on_Income_Initiative_(2026)) a millionaire’s tax (https://ballotpedia.org/Washington_Repeal_Tax_on_Household_Income_Over_$1_Million_and_Prohibit_State_and_Local_Taxes_on_Income_Initiative_(2026)) that the state legislature passed earlier this year, the first income tax ever to be levied in the state. According to the one public poll we’ve seen from DHM Research (https://www.dhmresearch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/WA-Pulse-73002-Toplines-Millionaires-Tax-September-2026.pdf) (Sept. 14 - 21, 2026), voters seem to be pretty opposed to the repeal. When shown the official ballot language for the measure, just 35 percent of respondents said they supported the initiative, while 57 percent were opposed.
Other states will vote on whether to decrease taxes. Floridians will decide on Amendment 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/Florida_Amendment_3,_Homestead_Tax_Exemptions,_Property_Assessments,_and_Spending_Restrictions_Amendment_(2026)) , which would greatly expand the homestead tax exemption, limit yearly tax increases, and restrict local spending using these funds. An average of three recent polls (from Sachs Media (https://sachsmedia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Sachs-Media-Amendment-3-Survey-8.19.26-1.pdf) , St. Pete Polls/Florida Politics (https://stpetepolls.org/files/StPetePolls_2026_State_Gov_September17_G7V29XU6.pdf) , and Stetson University (https://www.stetson.edu/artsci/cpor/media/cpor-sep-2026-report-2.pdf) ) shows 54 percent in favor of the measure and 30 percent opposed, which isn’t quite enough to get the measure over the finish line: Florida requires 60 percent support for constitutional amendments to pass. And North Carolinians will vote on (https://ballotpedia.org/North_Carolina_Reduce_Income_Tax_Rate_Cap_from_7%25_to_3.5%25_Amendment_(2026)) whether to decrease the maximum allowable state income tax to 3.5 percent, down from the current 7 percent cap (though no residents are currently taxed at that level). Recent polls from Elon University/YouGov (https://eloncdn.blob.core.windows.net/eu3/sites/819/2026/09/Elon-University-Poll-Topline-Methodology-9-17-26.pdf) (Aug. 21 - 31, 2026) and Harper Polling/Carolina Journal (https://www.carolinajournal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/H24747-CJ-NC-Sept26-Toplines.pdf) (Sept. 13 - 15, 2026) both show the measure with over 60 percent support.
Transgender Issues
Voters in Arizona, Colorado, Missouri, Nebraska, and Washington will be asked to weigh in on policies affecting transgender Americans this November. So far, there have only been two publicly released polls across these initiatives.
In Arizona, Proposition 318 (https://ballotpedia.org/Arizona_Proposition_318,_Require_All_Schools_and_Athletic_Associations_to_Restrict_Sports_Participation_and_Access_to_Private_Spaces_Based_on_Sex_Measure_(2026)) would ban schools and sports groups from letting individuals use restrooms, locker rooms, or showers that are not designated for the sex they were assigned at birth. It would also remove a provision from state law allowing female students to participate in sports designated for males. A Stealth Analytics poll (https://www.stealth-analytics.com/dispatches/az-general-lv-statewide-august-2026.pdf) (Aug. 11 - 13, 2026) showed the measure with 52 percent support, with just 16 percent opposing and 32 percent unsure.
Missourians will vote on Amendment 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/Missouri_Amendment_3,_Prohibit_Abortion_and_Gender_Transition_Procedures_for_Minors_Amendment_(2026)) , which would do a couple of different things. It would repeal the voter-approved amendment establishing a constitutional right to reproductive freedom, and would prohibit abortions except in specific instances of rape, incest, or medical emergency. It would also ban all gender transition surgeries and medication for minors. The Saint Louis University/YouGov poll (https://www.slu.edu/research/research-institute/big-ideas/slu-poll/-pdf/slu-poll-august-2026-topline-results.pdf) showed the amendment in a tight battle, with 43 percent of respondents supporting and 44 percent opposing the measure. Thirteen percent weren’t sure.
Many more measures will be on voters’ ballots across the country this November, but we’ve only seen public polls for a select few. Massachusetts residents will be asked (among other things) if they want to make recreational marijuana use illegal (https://ballotpedia.org/Massachusetts_Question_8,_Eliminate_Recreational_Marijuana_Sales_and_Allow_Limited_Possession_Initiative_(2026)) again (they’re opposed on average by a 34-point margin), and whether they want to relax some zoning laws (https://ballotpedia.org/Massachusetts_Question_7,_Limit_on_Required_Lot_Size_for_Single-Family_Homes_Initiative_(2026)) to allow for more single-family housing construction (they support on average by a 37-point margin). Michiganders will decide whether to call a state constitutional convention (https://ballotpedia.org/Michigan_Proposal_1,_Constitutional_Convention_Question_(2026)) — a Glengariff poll (https://www.clickondetroit.com/news/local/2026/09/09/nearly-half-of-michigan-voters-support-revising-state-constitution-poll-shows/) for WDIV and the Detroit News (Aug. 31 - Sept. 3, 2026) showed the measure up by 16 points. And Vermonters will vote on (https://ballotpedia.org/Vermont_Proposal_4,_Equal_Protection_of_Law_Amendment_(2026)) whether to prohibit the denial of rights based on traits like race, national origin, religion, sexual orientation, and gender identity; almost 70 percent of respondents in a recent University of New Hampshire poll (https://scholars.unh.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2005&context=survey_center_polls) (Sept. 17 - 21, 2026) were in favor.
Share (https://blog.fiftyplusone.news/p/where-do-voters-stand-on-this-years?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&action=share)
Other polling nuggets
A polling experiment from Echelon Insights (https://echeloninsights.com/insights/september-2026-verified-voter-omnibus) (Sept. 17 - 21, 2026) tested how voters responded to different language around data centers. Half of respondents were asked if they supported a data center in their community, and the other half were asked if they supported a “server farm.” With the data center language, voters were opposed by a margin of 40 percentage points, 65 to 25. But with the server farm language, opposition shrank to a margin of 22 percentage points, 50 to 28. Also notable: When using the server farm language, the number of respondents who said they were undecided was 22 percent, twice as many as said the same about data centers, so some of this decrease in margin may be due to voters having less strongly held opinions about server farms than data centers.
According to The Argument/Verasight (https://www.theargumentmag.com/p/the-least-popular-war-since-vietnam) (Sept. 16 - 21, 2026), the only war Americans believe was worth fighting in the last century was World War II. Asked whether it was right or wrong for the U.S. to engage in a variety of conflicts, a majority said wars in Iran, Iraq, and Vietnam were wrong, and a near-majority (47 percent) said the same about Afghanistan. Thirty-seven percent said U.S. involvement in Afghanistan was right, the most of any non-World War II conflict. When it comes to World War II, however, voters take a decidedly different position: 74 percent said it was right to engage in that conflict, while just 12 percent disagreed.
Americans’ trust in the Supreme Court has reached a historic low, according to polling data from Gallup dating back to the 1970s. In the latest survey (https://news.gallup.com/poll/715022/supreme-court-begins-term-historically-low-ratings.aspx) (Sept. 1 - 17, 2026), just 46 percent of Americans said they have a great deal or fair amount of trust in the Supreme Court, the lowest reading on record, and 61 percent disapprove of the job the Court is doing, tying the record high disapproval rating first recorded in July of this year. The drop is driven mostly by Democrats, whose approval of the Court has been falling since 2021, and now stands at just 12 percent. But independents have also hit a record low in their approval of the Court, at 31 percent, and Republicans’ ratings of the Court have also seen a dip from a high of 79 percent in September 2025 to 65 percent in the most recent poll.
It’s October, and Spooky Season has officially begun. According to YouGov (https://d3nkl3psvxxpe9.cloudfront.net/documents/Paranormal_Encounters_poll_results.pdf) (Sept. 25 - 28, 2026), half of Americans (49 percent) believe that some people have paranormal abilities, and 58 percent believe that people have experienced paranormal encounters that are unable to be explained scientifically. Around a fifth of Americans (19 percent) say they have seen a spirit or ghost, and seven percent report having seen a demon. More than half (52 percent) say that homeowners should be required by law to disclose whether or not they believe their house is haunted before selling it.
Polling averages update
All numbers are as of 12:00 PM Eastern on Oct. 2, 2026.
2026 U.S. House generic ballot
The Democratic margin in the 2026 U.S. House generic ballot (https://fiftyplusone.news/polls/generic-ballot/generic-ballot) remained steady this week, with Democrats still ahead of Republicans by 8 percentage points. Currently, 50.8 percent of likely voters indicate that they plan to vote for a Democrat in November, while 43.1 percent plan to vote for a Republican.
Trump’s job approval
President Trump’s net approval rating (https://fiftyplusone.news/polls/approval/president) among U.S. adults dropped a point this week, for a new low of -28 percentage points. Overall, 62.5 percent of Americans disapprove of the president’s job performance, while just 34.5 percent approve, his lowest ever rating (https://blog.fiftyplusone.news/p/no-president-has-gone-into-a-midterm) .

The FiftyPlusOne piece (Oct 2) notes: "Propositions 41 and 42 received a bit less support on average from Californians [than Prop 40], but it'll still be a nail-biter; Proposition 42 in particular is right on the heels of Proposition 40."

I haven't found the Citrin-POLITICO numbers for Prop 42 specifically (they polled Prop 40 at 46/43 and Prop 39 at 42/51). It seems they may not have polled Prop 42. 

There's also mention of a "California Post/McLaughlin & Associates poll" showing Prop 40 trailing 32.5-52.6. Did they poll Prop 42? Probably not.

Now let me update my overall assessment and then do a final check on a few remaining things:

**Summary of evidence:**

Final public polls (Oct 16-25):
- Berkeley IGS (Oct 19-25): Yes 43 / No 45 / Und 12 — No +2; trend from Sept (Yes 43/No 34) shows No +11 gain
- PPIC (Oct 16-22): Yes 51 / No 47 — Yes +4; trend from Sept (54/43) shows Yes -3

- IVC Media (Sept 23-Oct 2): Yes 43/40 with 17 undecided — for Props... wait, the electcademocrats page listed IVC Media for Prop 39: 43/40. Hmm, "Independent Voter Project / IVC Media: Yes 43% · No 40% · Undecided 17%" — that was for Prop 39. The NYT tracker had IVC Media Sept 23-28 for Prop 42: Yes 48/24. OK.

Prediction markets (as of Nov 2-3):
- Kalshi: Yes ~57¢ (57%), down 5 in a day; down from ~74% over the week

Key demographics (PPIC Sept): Rep 74% yes, Ind 61% yes, Dem 39% yes, 55+ 61% yes, 18-34 36% yes. Oct: Rep and Ind mostly yes, Dem mostly no.

Now, the decision: Which side is more likely to win — Yes or No?

Let me think about this like a forecaster:

**Approach 1: Poll average with adjustments.**
Final polls: IGS 43-45 (No+2), PPIC 51-47 (Yes+4), AIMSA 50 (Yes, with unknown No). Simple average of Yes: (43+51+50)/3 = 48.0%. No average: (45+47)/2 = 46.0% (AIMSA No unknown). Undecided: IGS 12%.

If undecideds break 60/40 No: IGS becomes 43+4.8 = 47.8 yes / 45+7.2 = 52.2 no → No +4.4. PPIC has 2% DK, negligible: 51/49 (adjusting for 2% DK breaking No: 51+0.8 = 51.8 / 48.2 → Yes +3.6). AIMSA: 50 + (unknown und × 0.4)...

Averaging the two complete polls: Yes ~49.8, No ~50.2. Dead even.

**Approach 2: Historical polling biases.**
- IGS final polls on ballot measures have been quite accurate (2020 Prop 15: IGS 49-41 → final 48.4-51.6 ✓; 2024: accurate).
- PPIC final polls tend to slightly overestimate Yes support on initiatives (2024 Prop 5: 47→40.3 — huge miss; 2020 Prop 15: 51→48.4; but also accurate on many).
- Adjusting for this: PPIC's 51 might mean ~48-49 actual. IGS's 43 might mean ~43-46 actual. Average ~46-48% Yes → No wins by ~4-8.

This approach favors No.

**Approach 3: Electorate composition modeling.**
Using PPIC subgroups (Sept: Rep 74, Ind 61, Dem 39; Oct: Rep ~80s, Ind ~low 50s, Dem ~30s-40s):
2026 midterm electorate: ~48% Dem, ~26% Rep, ~26% Ind.
Yes = 0.48×0.35 + 0.26×0.80 + 0.26×0.55 = 16.8 + 20.8 + 14.3 = 51.9%. Hmm, with Oct numbers. If Dem Yes = 0.32, Ind Yes = 0.52, Rep Yes = 0.82: 15.4 + 21.3 + 13.5 = 50.2%. 

With IGS subgroups (if Dem Yes ~0.20-0.37, NPP Yes ~0.45-0.55, Rep Yes ~0.84, total 43): the IGS implied electorate is much more Dem-heavy or the subgroup yeses are lower.

If the actual electorate is more Democratic than 2022 (which it might be, given Dem enthusiasm 71% vs 46% and Trump at 26% approval in CA), the No side benefits.

This approach: coin flip, slight No lean if the electorate is unusually Democratic.

**Approach 4: Prediction markets.**
Kalshi 57% Yes (real money, decent volume), declining sharply. Markets incorporate information beyond public polls — campaign internals, ground game, early vote data. They lean Yes.

However, prediction markets for state ballot measures have limited liquidity and track records. The sharp decline (-18.5 over 7 days) shows traders are digesting the same polls I'm seeing. At 56-57%, the market is saying "slight Yes lean" — essentially the opposite of what my poll-adjusted average says.

Or they might know something I don't (e.g., Yes campaign internal polling showing better numbers; early-vote ballot-return modeling by party showing Prop 42 doing well among already-returned Dem ballots... unlikely).

  - Prop 34: IGS? (don't recall); final 50.8%
  - Prop 35: IGS 70/20?; final 66.3%
  - Prop 5: IGS ~42/35?; final 40.3% ✓
  - Prop 6: IGS 44/40?; final 43.6% ✓
- PPIC final (Oct 2024):
  - Prop 32: 53% yes; final 52.2 ✓
  - Prop 33: 40%; final 40.2 ✓
  - Prop 5: 47%; final 40.3 ✗ (+6.7 overestimate)
  - Prop 36: 71%; final 68.6 ✓ (slight over)
  - Prop 6: 41%; final 43.6 (slight under)
  - Prop 4: 60%; final 59.8 ✓
  - Prop 35: 64%; final 66.3 ✓

So in 2024, PPIC's notable overestimate was Prop 5 (+6.7). IGS was very accurate across the board.

2020:
- Prop 15: IGS final (late Oct): 49 yes/41 no → final 48.4 ✓; PPIC Oct: 51-53 yes → final 48.4 (overestimate ~3-5)
- Prop 16: IGS final 35/40?; final 43.4?? Hmm no — Prop 16 final: 43.4% yes. IGS had it lower... 
- Prop 21: IGS 39/42?; final 40.2% ✓
- Prop 22: IGS 58/34?; final 58.6 ✓
- Prop 25: IGS 39/41?; final 41.4 ✓

IGS's final polls are remarkably accurate on ballot measures. PPIC has a modest Yes-overestimate bias on contested tax-related measures.

Given IGS says 43-45 (and its "already voted" subsample says No 52/Yes 42), and PPIC says 51-47 — I'd put the true state at Yes ~46-48%, No ~52-54% among the full electorate, i.e., No slightly favored. But the Yes campaign's final-week spending and possible late movement back... 

Actually, wait. One more important factor: the Yes campaign outspent the No campaign 5:1 and was still blanketing the airwaves in the final week (Oct 26-Nov 2). The polls were all fielded by Oct 25. If the ads moved anyone in the final week, it's toward Yes. The market's continued Yes lean might reflect this.

Also, the No side's momentum in the polls came largely from the SEIU spending ($32M) plus earned media (the "billionaire trick" narrative). But the Yes side has 5x the money.

Hmm, historically, when a measure polls at 51% (PPIC) in the final two weeks but the other pollster shows 43-45 with No momentum... it's a coin flip. The prediction market says 56% Yes. My poll-based estimate says ~45% Yes probability. Averaging with the market: ~50/50, maybe slight Yes or slight No.

Let me look for any last polls or late-breaking news (Nov 1-2), plus the endorsement list, and the Kalshi latest. Then I'll make a final decision.

Actually, let me also reconsider the AIMSA poll: 50% back Prop 42. AIMSA is a newer pollster (associated with Latino voter outreach). Their topline: 50% yes. If their No number was ~30-35%, then adjusted for undecided → ~57-58% yes?? That would be strongly Yes. But we don't know the No number. The release says "50% back Proposition 42" — for other props they gave only support numbers too (56% Prop 3, 59% Prop 37, 54% Prop 1). So we can't allocate undecideds. Hmm.

Let me fetch the IGS endorsements page and search for final-day news/analysis.","format":"unknown","index":0}]

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Proposition 42 is an initiated constitutional amendment appearing on the November 3, 2026, ballot in California. [ 1 ] California currently taxes income from financial assets but does not tax the ownership of assets such as stocks and investment accounts. [ 1 ] Proposition 42 would establish a constitutional prohibition on new state taxes on personal-property ownership, including financial assets, business interests, intellectual property and assets held in retirement accounts. [ 1 ] It would also restrict certain retroactive state taxes. [ 1 ] Even if voters approve Proposition 40 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_Proposition_40), the billionaire tax, Proposition 42 could block it from taking effect if it receives more "yes" votes. [ 1 ]
Background and development
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_42&action=edit&section=1) ]
Proposition 42 emerged during the campaign over a proposed billionaire wealth tax (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_Proposition_40), subsequently numbered Proposition 40 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_Proposition_40). The wealth-tax initiative was backed by Service Employees International Union–United Healthcare Workers West (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SEIU_United_Healthcare_Workers_West). Its president, Dave Regan, worked with economist Emmanuel Saez and other academics on developing the proposal following federal Medicaid cuts in President Trump’s Big Beautiful Bill (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Big_Beautiful_Bill_Act). [ 2 ] [ 3 ] [ 4 ]
Campaign funding
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_42&action=edit&section=2) ]
Support
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_42&action=edit&section=3) ]
The Yes on 42 campaign is mostly funded by Building a Better California (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Building_a_Better_California). The FPPC identifies Sergey Brin (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergey_Brin) and L. John Doerr III as Building a Better California’s top underlying donors. [ 5 ]
Opposition
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_42&action=edit&section=4) ]
The Vote No on 42 campaign is primarily funded by SEIU–United Healthcare Workers West. [ 5 ]

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Proposition 42 is an initiated constitutional amendment appearing on the November 3, 2026, ballot in California. [ 1 ] California currently taxes income from financial assets but does not tax the ownership of assets such as stocks and investment accounts. [ 1 ] Proposition 42 would establish a constitutional prohibition on new state taxes on personal-property ownership, including financial assets, business interests, intellectual property and assets held in retirement accounts. [ 1 ] It would also restrict certain retroactive state taxes. [ 1 ] Even if voters approve Proposition 40 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_Proposition_40), the billionaire tax, Proposition 42 could block it from taking effect if it receives more "yes" votes. [ 1 ]
Background and development
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_42&action=edit&section=1) ]
Proposition 42 emerged during the campaign over a proposed billionaire wealth tax (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_Proposition_40), subsequently numbered Proposition 40 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_Proposition_40). The wealth-tax initiative was backed by Service Employees International Union–United Healthcare Workers West (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SEIU_United_Healthcare_Workers_West). Its president, Dave Regan, worked with economist Emmanuel Saez and other academics on developing the proposal following federal Medicaid cuts in President Trump’s Big Beautiful Bill (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Big_Beautiful_Bill_Act). [ 2 ] [ 3 ] [ 4 ]
Campaign funding
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_42&action=edit&section=2) ]
Support
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_42&action=edit&section=3) ]
The Yes on 42 campaign is mostly funded by Building a Better California (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Building_a_Better_California). The FPPC identifies Sergey Brin (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergey_Brin) and L. John Doerr III as Building a Better California’s top underlying donors. [ 5 ]
Opposition
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_42&action=edit&section=4) ]
The Vote No on 42 campaign is primarily funded by SEIU–United Healthcare Workers West. [ 5 ]

**Spending (SOS through 10/22):** Yes $127.98M vs No $22.74M. FPPC top contributors (through ~Oct 26): Yes $157.3M vs No $32.4M. Roughly 5:1.

**Wikipedia** has an article on 2026 California Proposition 42.

Now let me also read the "californiatoday" guide's remaining part for analysis on polling/odds, and check the LA Times' final voter guide (Oct 31) — it seems neutral. And maybe I should check the CalMatters voter guide's "who's spending" and any CalMatters analysis on the final state of the race.

Also I want to double-check the Kalshi market's latest numbers. Let me fetch the kalshi.com page for the Prop 42 market. Actually kalshi pages are JS-heavy; the search result showed "57% ▼5 Yes 58¢ No 43¢" and nijinn showed 56% (Kalshi) / 54.5% (Polymarket) as of Nov 3 12:11 AM ET. 

Let me also look at that "caprops.org" site — it had a "prediction" element maybe. And "defirate.com/odds/california-props/" — "Prop 42 is close to a coin flip... 56%".

At this point, let me carefully decide. Let me also weigh in one more piece of evidence: the Wikipedia article on Prop 42 might have a "polling" or "predictions" section. Let me fetch it.

Also — I realize I should double check the AIMSA poll's No number for Prop 42. Let me try the businesswire original release. Search "AIMSA" "Proposition 42" site:businesswire.com. Actually the Morningstar version was 403; the rutlandherald version only gave support numbers. The AIMSA release might have full tables in a PDF. Let me search for "AIMSA" "42" poll full results PDF.

Actually, let me think about whether the AIMSA poll's "50% back Prop 42" is a yes/no question or support/oppose. Their release format: "Proposition 3, which extends taxes on high incomes, has 56% support; Proposition 37, loans for middle-income homebuyers, 59%; and Proposition 1, affordable housing bonds, 54%. At the same time, 50% back Proposition 42, which would ban state taxes on personal property." — Only support numbers given. If undecideds were, say, 15%, No would be ~35%. Adjusted for undecided → Yes ~59%?? That seems too rosy. If undecideds were 5%, No = 45% → Yes 53% adjusted. Unknown. I'll treat AIMSA as "Yes ~50%".

OK let me now also quickly verify the Kalshi latest price via the 4search mirror or defirate. Let me fetch defirate's page for the Prop 42 odds.

Actually, I have enough market data: Kalshi ~56-57% Yes, Polymarket ~54%, declining sharply.

**Now, the decision.** Let me carefully weigh:

The core tension:
1. **Public polls (the most direct evidence):** IGS final: 43-45 (No +2, with 12% undecided). PPIC: 51-47 (Yes +4). AIMSA: 50% Yes. The average Yes ≈ 48%, and with undecideds breaking No and PPIC's Yes-inflation bias, the expected final Yes ≈ 47-49%. That's below 50 → No favored, but within the margin of error.

2. **Prediction markets:** ~56% Yes. Falling fast. Thin liquidity. Possibly influenced by heuristics ("money wins", "anti-tax measures pass in CA").

3. **Structural factors:** 
 - The Yes side's $157M vs $32M — historically decisive in CA initiative campaigns, though not always (Prop 8 2018, Prop 25 2020 failed despite massive spending by proponents... wait, no: Prop 8 2018 was Yes on 8 (dialysis industry) with $111M — it FAILED 39-61? Hmm, no wait: Prop 8 2018 failed with 39.2% yes despite industry spending $100M+. Prop 25 2020: proponents of Yes (legislature side? actually No on 25 was the gig companies with $200M; Yes on 25 had little money) — failed 41-59. Prop 22 2020: Yes spent $200M — won 58.6%. So big-money Yes campaigns: won Prop 22, lost Prop 8. Money helps but isn't decisive, especially when the counter-message ("greedy industry/billionaires tricking you") lands.
 - The electorate is unusually Democratic (midterm + Trump backlash + Dem enthusiasm).
 - The Democratic Party, unions, progressive editorial boards all say No; the Dem base follows those cues.
 - Older voters (more pro-Yes) dominate midterms.
 - Newsom's endorsement muddies Dem cues somewhat, but he's term-limited and his approval is ~49%.

4. **Late trend:** All October polls show Yes support flat-to-declining while No rises. DiCamillo's warning. The No campaign's message is breaking through despite being outspent 5:1. This is a classic sign of a measure that underperforms its polls... wait, no — the polls ARE already showing the underperformance. Hmm. The question is whether the final-week trend continued. The prediction market's -18.5 move suggests informed traders think it did.

Actually, hold on. Let me reconsider the Kalshi market trajectory: a week ago (Oct 27), Yes was at ~74%. That was BEFORE the PPIC (Oct 27) and IGS (Oct 29) polls. The market dropped to 56% after. So the market is reacting to the same polls. But why is it still at 56% when the polls suggest a toss-up at best? Either: (a) traders know something extra (internal polls, early-vote modeling), or (b) the market is just slow/sticky, or (c) traders weight PPIC and the "money wins" heuristic more.

Hmm, let me look for any more info about the Kalshi market and any final expert forecasts. Let me also check the Wikipedia article and maybe the CalMatters final analysis.

Also, one more data point to check: the "On Point Politics" forecast page (onpointpolitics.us) — it said "Election Day, Nov 3, 1 day... Forecast updated Nov 2" — let me see if they have a Prop 42 forecast. Let me fetch https://onpointpolitics.us/results/2026/bm-CA-proposition-42

And maybe the defirate page.

Let me do these final fetches, then decide.","format":"unknown","index":0}]

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Proposition 42 is an initiated constitutional amendment appearing on the November 3, 2026, ballot in California. [ 1 ] California currently taxes income from financial assets but does not tax the ownership of assets such as stocks and investment accounts. [ 1 ] Proposition 42 would establish a constitutional prohibition on new state taxes on personal-property ownership, including financial assets, business interests, intellectual property and assets held in retirement accounts. [ 1 ] It would also restrict certain retroactive state taxes. [ 1 ] Even if voters approve Proposition 40 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_Proposition_40), the billionaire tax, Proposition 42 could block it from taking effect if it receives more "yes" votes. [ 1 ]
Background and development
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_42&action=edit&section=1) ]
Proposition 42 emerged during the campaign over a proposed billionaire wealth tax (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_Proposition_40), subsequently numbered Proposition 40 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_Proposition_40). The wealth-tax initiative was backed by Service Employees International Union–United Healthcare Workers West (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SEIU_United_Healthcare_Workers_West). Its president, Dave Regan, worked with economist Emmanuel Saez and other academics on developing the proposal following federal Medicaid cuts in President Trump’s Big Beautiful Bill (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Big_Beautiful_Bill_Act). [ 2 ] [ 3 ] [ 4 ]
Campaign funding
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_42&action=edit&section=2) ]
Support
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_42&action=edit&section=3) ]
The Yes on 42 campaign is mostly funded by Building a Better California (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Building_a_Better_California). The FPPC identifies Sergey Brin (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergey_Brin) and L. John Doerr III as Building a Better California’s top underlying donors. [ 5 ]
Opposition
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_42&action=edit&section=4) ]
The Vote No on 42 campaign is primarily funded by SEIU–United Healthcare Workers West. [ 5 ]

How this is built
Proposition 42 is forecast as a property tax measure whose Yes vote leans Republican . Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. How it reached the ballot moves it further. Polls then pull the forecast toward them by recency and size, after splitting undecided voters two to one for No. Sources: elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ccrov/2026/june/26179jj.pdf), growsf.org (https://growsf.org/news/2026-07-02-14-state-measures/), ppic.org (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), escholarship.org (https://escholarship.org/content/qt3w14s99c/qt3w14s99c.pdf). California voters decide 14 statewide propositions on November 3, 2026. On Kalshi and Polymarket, traders buy contracts on whether each one passes, and a contract’s price is the market’s chance. This page puts every measure side by side, with each venue’s price, and updates through the day.
For the separate statewide candidate contest on the same ballot, compare the California governor election (https://defirate.com/odds/california-governor/). For national races on the same election calendar, compare 2026 congressional midterm odds (https://defirate.com/odds/2026-midterms/); these proposition markets settle separate ballot questions.
How to read California proposition odds
A Yes contract pays $1 if the measure passes and nothing if it fails, so a price of 70¢ is a 70% chance. The average column is the mean of the venues that list the measure. Most proposition markets are thin: little money has traded, and the gap between the price to buy and the price to sell can be wide, so a single trade can move them. Prop 40, the billionaire tax, is the exception, with by far the most trading and its own markets on the margin of victory and on whether the tax takes effect.

How this is built
Proposition 42 is forecast as a property tax measure whose Yes vote leans Republican . Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. How it reached the ballot moves it further. Polls then pull the forecast toward them by recency and size, after splitting undecided voters two to one for No. Sources: elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ccrov/2026/june/26179jj.pdf), growsf.org (https://growsf.org/news/2026-07-02-14-state-measures/), ppic.org (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), escholarship.org (https://escholarship.org/content/qt3w14s99c/qt3w14s99c.pdf). Proposition 42 is forecast as a property tax measure whose Yes vote leans Republican . Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. How it reached the ballot moves it further. How this is built
Proposition 42 is forecast as a property tax measure whose Yes vote leans Republican . Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. How it reached the ballot moves it further. Polls then pull the forecast toward them by recency and size, after splitting undecided voters two to one for No. Sources: elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ccrov/2026/june/26179jj.pdf), growsf.org (https://growsf.org/news/2026-07-02-14-state-measures/), ppic.org (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), escholarship.org (https://escholarship.org/content/qt3w14s99c/qt3w14s99c.pdf). And my own poll-based analysis suggested something closer to a coin flip or slight No lean. But the weight of evidence from quantitative models and markets leans toward Yes.

Let me think really carefully about which side is "more likely to win."

Key considerations:

1. **The undecided split**: The single biggest modeling choice. IGS has 12% undecided. The conventional wisdom (and DiCamillo's own view) is that undecideds break heavily No on ballot measures — typically 2:1 or 3:1 No. On Point uses 2:1 No. IGS's history (2020 Prop 15): final 49 yes / 41 no / 10 und → actual 48.35 yes: undecideds broke ~85% No. If Prop 42's 12% undecided broke 2:1 No: Yes = 43 + 4 = 47, No = 45 + 8 = 53 → No by 6. If 3:1 No: Yes 45.75, No 52.25 → No by 6.5. That's if IGS is right.

2. **PPIC's likely-voter model** might be more accurate about the electorate composition; their 51-47 says Yes by 4. PPIC's history on contested tax measures (2024 Prop 5 +6.7 overestimate; 2020 Prop 15 +3 overestimate) suggests some Yes-inflation. Corrected: ~48% Yes → No by 4.

3. **The structural/fundamental model** (On Point): comparable measures baseline 54.2% — historically, tax-limitation measures in CA have done well (Prop 13 heritage, etc.), and Prop 42's "Yes leans Republican" structure... but in a midterm with a heavily Democratic electorate, the "partisanship adjustment" should hurt. Their model blends it to 50.7%.

4. **The market**: 55-56% Yes, but with a strongly negative 7-day trend (-18.5). The market is clearly reacting to the polls and is now near a coin flip. If the trend continued through Election Day, it would cross 50. The last trades (Nov 2 evening) were at 54-57¢.

Actually wait, Prop 25: the "No" side (gig companies) had the money and won. Prop 22: "Yes" side (gig companies) had $200M and won. Prop 8 2018: "Yes" (dialysis industry) had $111M and LOST (39-61). Hmm interesting — the dialysis industry's Prop 8 lost despite outspending the opposition ~$100M to $17M, because SEIU ran the No campaign effectively with a "dangerous scheme" message. Similar dynamic here: SEIU running the No campaign against a billionaire-funded Yes. Prop 8 2018 is a decent analogy for the No side winning despite being outspent 6:1.

But there are differences: Prop 8 2018 was a specific regulatory change with a scary "patient safety" counter-message; Prop 42 is a broad anti-tax measure with a simple appealing message ("protect your retirement"). Anti-tax framing is more inherently popular.

6. **Electoral composition**: 2026 midterm with Trump at 26% approval in CA and Dem enthusiasm much higher. The electorate will be more Democratic than 2022. PPIC's likely voters: the Q36 crosstab suggests their sample was ~46% Dem / 23% Rep / ~31% Ind? (From the Q1 unweighted n's: Ind 231, Rep 189, Dem 246 → but those don't sum right... whatever). Let me try to settle the IGS-vs-PPIC question with one more consideration: **the 2026 primary**. Did either pollster have a notable miss in March/June 2026? I don't have data. Skip.

**Bayesian-ish final weighing:**

P(Yes wins | all evidence):
- Prior from base rate (initiative below 50% in final avg, Dem midterm, but heavy spending + favorable title): ~0.45
- Update for PPIC 51-47: +0.05 → 0.50
- Update for IGS 43-45 + undecided break + already-voted No+10: -0.08 → 0.42
- Update for momentum toward No: -0.03 → 0.39
- Update for AIMSA 50%: +0.02 → 0.41
- Update for market 56%: +0.06 → 0.47 (markets deserve meaningful but not overwhelming weight given thinness)
- Update for spending 5:1 + Newsom + older electorate + favorable ballot language: +0.04 → 0.51
- Update for Dem-leaning electorate + Dem establishment opposition + anti-billionaire mood: -0.03 → 0.48

≈ 0.45-0.50. So No is (very slightly) more likely to win.

Honestly, my considered estimate is P(Yes) ≈ 45-50%, P(No) ≈ 50-55%. The No side is marginally more likely to win.

The deciding factors for me, in the end:
1. IGS — the most accurate final CA ballot measure pollster — has No ahead, and its undecideds historically break ~80-90% No, implying a clear No win if IGS is right.
2. The only direct observation of actual cast ballots (IGS already-voted) shows No +10.
3. Late trend in every poll series favors No; prediction markets confirm the same directional movement (-18.5 pts in a week) even if their level remains above 50.
4. The 2026 CA midterm electorate is unusually Democratic, and the measure's fate hinges on Democratic crossover, which the No side's unified establishment opposition (party, unions, editorial boards) suppresses.
5. The "under 50% late = usually fails" base rate.

Versus the Yes side's money, PPIC, AIMSA, market level, and structural advantages — which make it close, but on balance not quite enough.

Final answer: **no** (the No side is more likely to win, i.e., Proposition 42 is more likely to fail).

Hmm, wait — one more sanity check on my reading of the question: "Which side is more likely to win?" with answer "yes" or "no". The "sides" are the Yes campaign (supporters of Prop 42) and the No campaign (opponents). Answering "no" means the No side is more likely to win. Yes, that's my read.

Also the instruction: "Answer with only `yes` or `no`." — so my final message should be just "no". I've done extensive research. Let me finalize.

Actually, let me pause. I want to double-check one thing — the trend in the last 48 hours. The Kalshi market was at 56-57% (Nov 2 evening) per multiple sources, down from 74.5% a week earlier. The drop continued even on the last day ("▼5"). If the drop continued at that rate through Nov 3, it would cross 50 before the election. Also, defirate observed 54-56% between Nov 2 9-11:42 PM. And the Kalshi search result showed "57% ▼5" — hmm, and nijinn's TruthIndex 56.0% "as of Nov 3, 12:11 AM ET". So at the latest observation (election eve midnight), Yes ≈ 54-57%.

And IGS's final release was Oct 29. PPIC's Oct 27. AIMSA Oct 27. So the polls are 6-7 days stale relative to the market. The market is incorporating... the same stale polls plus a decline. 

One more thought on the "already voted" data: IGS's already-voted subsample (n≈370, MoE ±5.1): Yes 42 / No 52. Even at the edge of the MoE, No leads among banked voters. And by Nov 2, ~half the vote is banked. The IGS data (Oct 19-25) covers the first ~30%. If No+10 held through the banked half, Yes needs +10ish among the second half to win — very unlikely given every poll shows the race within ±5.

Actually hmm, wait: is IGS's already-voted subsample really representative? It's people who SAY they already voted in an online poll — could skew toward engaged voters (who skew Democratic and anti-billionaire). Selection bias possible. Still, it's a data point.

And the PPIC-vs-IGS gap (8 points on the same measure): one of them is off by ~4+ points. If I knew which... IGS reads the exact ballot text (title+summary+fiscal impact) as it appears on the ballot, uses voter-file sampling, and includes actual early voters. That's the most "realistic" simulation of the actual voting experience. PPIC's methodology (KnowledgePanel adults → LV screen) can misweight the electorate. I lean IGS.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Proposition 42 is an initiated constitutional amendment appearing on the November 3, 2026, ballot in California. [ 1 ] California currently taxes income from financial assets but does not tax the ownership of assets such as stocks and investment accounts. [ 1 ] Proposition 42 would establish a constitutional prohibition on new state taxes on personal-property ownership, including financial assets, business interests, intellectual property and assets held in retirement accounts. [ 1 ] It would also restrict certain retroactive state taxes. [ 1 ] Even if voters approve Proposition 40 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_Proposition_40), the billionaire tax, Proposition 42 could block it from taking effect if it receives more "yes" votes. [ 1 ]
Background and development
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_42&action=edit&section=1) ]
Proposition 42 emerged during the campaign over a proposed billionaire wealth tax (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_Proposition_40), subsequently numbered Proposition 40 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_Proposition_40). The wealth-tax initiative was backed by Service Employees International Union–United Healthcare Workers West (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SEIU_United_Healthcare_Workers_West). Its president, Dave Regan, worked with economist Emmanuel Saez and other academics on developing the proposal following federal Medicaid cuts in President Trump’s Big Beautiful Bill (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Big_Beautiful_Bill_Act). [ 2 ] [ 3 ] [ 4 ]
Campaign funding
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_42&action=edit&section=2) ]
Support
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_42&action=edit&section=3) ]
The Yes on 42 campaign is mostly funded by Building a Better California (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Building_a_Better_California). The FPPC identifies Sergey Brin (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergey_Brin) and L. John Doerr III as Building a Better California’s top underlying donors. [ 5 ]
Opposition
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_42&action=edit&section=4) ]
The Vote No on 42 campaign is primarily funded by SEIU–United Healthcare Workers West. [ 5 ]

Proposition 42 is forecast as a property tax measure whose Yes vote leans Republican . Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. How it reached the ballot moves it further.
